Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 1
A 58-year-old man comes to the clinic because of fatigue and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss over 3 months. He drank heavily for 20 years but quit last year. His liver is firm and palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is high, and CT shows a liver mass. A biopsy shows malignant hepatocytes, each containing several large, prominent nucleoli. Which of the following processes is most likely increased in these structures?
A. Ribosome subunit assembly
B. Basal body formation
C. Hydrogen peroxide breakdown
D. Ubiquitinated protein degradation
E. Long-chain fatty acid oxidation
Answer: A. Ribosome subunit assembly
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Nucleolus and ribosomes
Why this is correct:
The prominent structures are nucleoli, the site of rRNA transcription, pre-RNA processing, and ribosome subunit assembly. Cells with high protein synthesis, such as cancer cells and liver cells, tend to have more nucleoli.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Basal bodies form when centrioles attach to the inner plasma membrane of non-dividing cells, not in the nucleus.
C. Hydrogen peroxide is broken down by catalase in peroxisomes.
D. Ubiquitinated proteins are degraded by proteasomes.
E. Beta oxidation of long-chain fatty acids takes place in peroxisomes.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 2
A 24-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of fever, cough, and green sputum for 4 days. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), and she has crackles over the right lower lobe. Chest x-ray shows consolidation. She is started on an antibiotic that binds the small ribosomal subunit of bacteria without affecting her own ribosomes. Which of the following correctly describes bacterial and human ribosomes?
A. Bacterial 80S (40S and 60S); human 70S (30S and 50S)
B. Bacterial 70S (30S and 50S); human 80S (40S and 60S)
C. Bacterial 70S (30S and 50S); human 70S (30S and 50S)
D. Bacterial 80S (40S and 60S); human 80S (40S and 60S)
E. Bacterial 70S (40S and 30S); human 80S (50S and 60S)
Answer: B. Bacterial 70S (30S and 50S); human 80S (40S and 60S)
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Nucleolus and ribosomes; Ribosome sites, elongation, and termination
Why this is correct:
Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made of a 30S small subunit and a 50S large subunit. Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, made of a 40S small subunit and a 60S large subunit. This difference lets antibiotics such as aminoglycosides and tetracyclines bind the bacterial 30S subunit without harming human ribosomes.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. This reverses the two ribosome types.
C. Human ribosomes are 80S, which is why the drug spares them.
D. Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, not 80S.
E. The subunits are mixed up; the bacterial subunits are 30S and 50S, and the human subunits are 40S and 60S.
Objective: Describe the mechanisms of action of major classes of antimicrobial drugs and recommend appropriate antibiotic treatments for infectious diseases based on patient factors, pathogens involved, and pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drugs (CBO 1.4)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 3
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of developmental regression and an enlarging abdomen. His parents are first cousins. He has coarse facial features, and his liver is palpable 5 cm below the costal margin. Studies of his fibroblasts show that material delivered to a highly acidic organelle accumulates because the organelle's enzymes can't break it down. Which of the following is the origin of this organelle?
A. Free ribosomes in the cytosol
B. Centrioles near the nucleus
C. The Golgi body
D. The plasma membrane, through scramblase activity
E. The nucleolus
Answer: C. The Golgi body
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Lysosomes vs. peroxisomes; Lysosomal targeting and storage diseases
Why this is correct:
The acidic organelle that fails to digest delivered material is the lysosome, and this child has a lysosomal storage disease. Lysosomes originate from the Golgi body, and their enzymes are made on the rough ER and then passed to the Golgi, where they're tagged with mannose-6-phosphate for delivery.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Free ribosomes make peroxisomal enzymes, and peroxisomes don't originate from the Golgi.
B. Centrioles form basal bodies in non-dividing cells, not lysosomes.
D. Scramblases move phospholipids between membrane leaflets; they don't form organelles.
E. The nucleolus assembles ribosome subunits.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 4
A 6-month-old girl is brought to the clinic because of poor feeding and floppiness since birth. She has a large anterior fontanelle, marked hypotonia, and a liver palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. She has had two seizures. Serum very-long-chain fatty acids and branched-chain fatty acids are high. Which of the following organelles is most likely defective?
A. Proteasome
B. Lysosome
C. Mitochondrion
D. Peroxisome
E. Nucleolus
Answer: D. Peroxisome
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Lysosomes vs. peroxisomes; Zellweger syndrome, adrenoleukodystrophy, and Refsum disease
Why this is correct:
Peroxisomes carry out beta oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids and alpha oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids, so both accumulate when peroxisomes don't work. This infant's hypotonia, hepatomegaly, seizures, and facial findings fit Zellweger syndrome, in which functional peroxisomes are absent.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Proteasomes degrade ubiquitinated proteins and don't oxidize fatty acids.
B. Lysosomal defects cause storage of undigested material, not very-long-chain and branched-chain fatty acids.
C. Very-long-chain fatty acids have to be shortened in the peroxisome before mitochondria can handle them, and branched-chain fatty acids need peroxisomal alpha oxidation.
E. The nucleolus assembles ribosome subunits.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 5
A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department after a radiation exposure at work. He has redness and peeling of the skin on his forearms and mild nausea. Pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg. His lymphocyte count is low. As his cells neutralize reactive oxygen species, hydrogen peroxide forms, and an enzyme in one organelle converts it to water. Which of the following enzymes and organelles are responsible?
A. Proteases in proteasomes
B. Glycosylases in the nucleolus
C. Catalase in peroxisomes
D. Acid hydrolases in lysosomes
E. Catalase in lysosomes
Answer: C. Catalase in peroxisomes
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Lysosomes vs. peroxisomes
Why this is correct:
Peroxisomal catalase decomposes hydrogen peroxide, which forms as free radicals are neutralized, into water.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Proteasomes degrade ubiquitinated proteins.
B. Glycosylases remove damaged bases during base excision repair; they don't break down hydrogen peroxide.
D. Lysosomal acid hydrolases digest delivered material.
E. Catalase is a peroxisomal enzyme, not a lysosomal one.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 6
A 12-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of progressive loss of vision. He had extra fingers removed in infancy. His BMI is above the 97th percentile, and ultrasound shows kidney cysts. Genetic testing shows a defect in the projection that forms when a centriole attaches to the inner side of the plasma membrane in a non-dividing cell. Which of the following does this structure form in most non-dividing cells?
A. A motile cilium with a 9+2 arrangement
B. A nucleolus
C. A microvillus
D. A nonmotile primary cilium
E. A lysosome
Answer: D. A nonmotile primary cilium
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Centrioles and basal bodies; Ciliopathies
Why this is correct:
In non-dividing cells, centrioles attach to the inner plasma membrane to form a basal body. A basal body can form the base of a flagellum or beating cilium, but in most cells it forms a nonmotile primary cilium. Vision loss, polydactyly, obesity, and kidney cysts fit Bardet-Biedl syndrome, a primary cilia disorder.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Motile 9+2 cilia form only in specific tissues such as airway epithelium and the female reproductive tract.
B. The nucleolus is a nuclear structure for ribosome assembly.
C. Microvilli are built from actin filaments made by formins, not from basal bodies.
E. Lysosomes originate from the Golgi.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 7
A researcher studies mature red blood cells collected from a healthy 30-year-old blood donor. The cells have no nucleus, mitochondria, or ribosomes, yet they still degrade damaged proteins that have been tagged with ubiquitin. Which of the following structures do these cells retain?
A. Rough endoplasmic reticulum
B. Proteasomes
C. Mitochondria
D. Lysosomes
E. Peroxisomes
Answer: B. Proteasomes
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Proteasomes
Why this is correct:
Mature red blood cells have proteasomes and no other organelles. The proteasome's regulatory particle binds ubiquitin, and its core particle degrades the tagged protein.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Red cells have no rough ER.
C. Red cells have no mitochondria, which is why they rely on glycolysis for ATP.
D. Red cells have no lysosomes.
E. Red cells have no peroxisomes.
Objective: Demonstrate knowledge of normal and abnormal structure and function of the hematological, system on the macroscopic, microscopic, and biochemical levels (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 8
A 65-year-old man with lymphoma receives his first cycle of chemotherapy. Two days later, his tumor cells are undergoing apoptosis. As calcium enters the dying cells, a negatively charged phospholipid that normally sits on the inner leaflet appears on the cell surface and signals macrophages to engulf the cells. Which of the following phospholipids is exposed, and which enzymes expose it?
A. Phosphatidylserine, exposed by scramblases
B. Phosphatidylcholine, exposed by flippases
C. Sphingomyelin, exposed by floppases
D. Phosphatidylethanolamine, exposed by flippases
E. Phosphatidylserine, exposed by flippases
Answer: A. Phosphatidylserine, exposed by scramblases
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Membrane phospholipid asymmetry; Intrinsic apoptosis and caspases
Why this is correct:
PS, PE, and PI normally sit on the inner leaflet. An influx of calcium can make scramblases display PS on the outer leaflet, which signals apoptosis. Annexin V binds this exposed PS, which is how apoptotic cells are detected.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. PC already sits on the outer leaflet, and flippases move lipids inward.
C. Sphingomyelin already sits on the outer leaflet.
D. PE is an inner-leaflet lipid, but flippases move lipids inward, and PS is the apoptotic signal.
E. Flippases move lipids inward; scramblases are what expose PS.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 9
A 34-year-old woman with a mitochondrial disorder brings her two children for evaluation. She has mild hearing loss and diabetes. Her son has seizures, muscle weakness, high serum lactate, and lesions in both basal ganglia on MRI. Her daughter has only mild exercise intolerance, and her serum lactate is normal. Both children inherited the same mitochondrial mutation from their mother. Which of the following best explains the difference in severity?
A. Lyonization
B. Anticipation
C. Heteroplasmy
D. Genomic imprinting
E. Gene conversion
Answer: C. Heteroplasmy
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Heteroplasmy and the microsomal fraction
Why this is correct:
Heteroplasmy is the reason the severity of a mitochondrial mutation changes from one child to another in the same family. Each child inherits a different mix of mutant and normal mitochondria.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Lyonization is random X inactivation by Xist, which affects X-linked genes, not mitochondrial DNA.
B. Anticipation is earlier onset with each generation, usually from expanding trinucleotide repeats.
D. Imprinting silences one parent's copy of a nuclear gene through methylation.
E. Gene conversion happens when mismatch repair changes one allele into another during recombination.
Objective: Illustrate the molecular basis of human genome instability and articulate the principles of inheritance of single gene mutations, cancer genetics, and genetic counseling (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 10
A researcher studies drug metabolism in liver tissue from a 50-year-old man with alcohol use disorder. The tissue is homogenized and centrifuged, and a fraction of small vesicles derived from the smooth and rough ER, the Golgi body, and the plasma membrane is collected to measure drug-metabolizing enzymes. Which of the following is this fraction called?
A. The nuclear fraction
B. The mitochondrial fraction
C. The microsomal fraction
D. The peroxisomal fraction
E. The proteasomal fraction
Answer: C. The microsomal fraction
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Heteroplasmy and the microsomal fraction
Why this is correct:
The microsomal fraction is made of vesicles derived from the smooth and rough ER, the Golgi body, and the plasma membrane that form during centrifugation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A nuclear fraction would contain nuclei, not membrane vesicles from the ER and Golgi.
B. A mitochondrial fraction would contain mitochondria rather than ER, Golgi, and plasma membrane vesicles.
D. Peroxisomes are separate organelles and don't define this vesicle mix.
E. Proteasomes are protein complexes, not membrane vesicles.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cell Structure & Organelles
Question 11
A 60-year-old woman with multiple myeloma is started on bortezomib, a drug that blocks the structure responsible for degrading damaged or unneeded proteins. She has back pain, anemia, and high serum calcium. Which of the following components of this structure binds ubiquitin?
A. The 30S subunit
B. The regulatory particle
C. The core particle
D. Catalase
E. Lysosomal hydrolases
Answer: B. The regulatory particle
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Proteasomes
Why this is correct:
Bortezomib blocks the proteasome. The proteasome's regulatory particle (RP, regulatory proteins) binds ubiquitin, and its core particle (CP, core proteins) does the degrading.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The 30S subunit is the small subunit of the bacterial ribosome.
C. The core particle degrades the protein but isn't the part that binds ubiquitin.
D. Catalase is a peroxisomal enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide.
E. Lysosomal hydrolases digest material in lysosomes and don't bind ubiquitin.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes
Question 12
A 42-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of episodes of flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing for 6 months. She has a murmur over the right side of the heart. Urine 5-HIAA is high, and CT shows liver masses from a neuroendocrine tumor that makes large amounts of serotonin. She also has a scaly rash on sun-exposed skin. Which of the following amino acids is most likely depleted, causing her rash?
A. Beta-alanine
B. Tryptophan
C. Tyrosine
D. Histidine
E. Leucine
Answer: B. Tryptophan
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Amino acid derivatives
Why this is correct:
Tryptophan is the precursor of serotonin, niacin, and melatonin. A tumor that makes large amounts of serotonin uses up tryptophan, leaving less for niacin, and niacin deficiency causes the sun-exposed rash.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Beta-alanine is the precursor of coenzyme A.
C. Tyrosine is the precursor of catecholamines, thyroxine, and melanin.
D. Histidine is the precursor of histamine.
E. Leucine is an essential, ketogenic amino acid and isn't a niacin precursor.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes
Question 13
A 3-week-old girl is brought to the clinic for follow-up of an abnormal newborn screen. She was born at term and is feeding well. She has fairer skin than her parents. Serum phenylalanine is high. Which of the following amino acids, normally made from phenylalanine, is most likely deficient?
A. Tryptophan
B. Beta-alanine
C. Tyrosine
D. Histidine
E. Lysine
Answer: C. Tyrosine
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Amino acid derivatives; Phenylketonuria
Why this is correct:
Phenylalanine is converted to tyrosine, which becomes conditionally essential when that step fails, as in phenylketonuria. Tyrosine is the precursor of dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, thyroxine, and melanin, so low tyrosine explains her fair skin.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Tryptophan is essential and is the precursor of serotonin, niacin, and melatonin.
B. Beta-alanine is the precursor of coenzyme A.
D. Histidine is essential and is the precursor of histamine.
E. Lysine is essential and purely ketogenic; it isn't made from phenylalanine.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes
Question 14
A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with hives, itching, and lip swelling 20 minutes after eating shellfish. Pulse is 104/min, and blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. She has diffuse raised wheals and mild wheezing. Her symptoms are driven by a mediator released from mast cells that is made from an amino acid. Which of the following amino acids is the precursor of this mediator?
A. Beta-alanine
B. Leucine
C. Tyrosine
D. Histidine
E. Tryptophan
Answer: D. Histidine
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Amino acid derivatives; Type I hypersensitivity
Why this is correct:
Histamine, the main early mediator released by mast cells in a type I reaction, is made from histidine.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Beta-alanine is the precursor of coenzyme A.
B. Leucine is a ketogenic amino acid and isn't a mediator precursor.
C. Tyrosine makes catecholamines such as epinephrine, which treats anaphylaxis rather than causing it.
E. Tryptophan makes serotonin, niacin, and melatonin.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes
Question 16
A 16-year-old girl comes to the clinic because of fatigue and thinning hair 6 months after starting a restrictive diet of mostly fruit and rice. She runs cross-country. Her BMI is 17.8, and serum albumin is low. A dietitian notes that her diet is low in amino acids her body can't synthesize. Which of the following groups contains only essential amino acids?
A. Proline, arginine, methionine, and threonine
B. Tyrosine, cysteine, glutamine, and leucine
C. Phenylalanine, valine, threonine, and lysine
D. Aspartate, glutamate, valine, and histidine
E. Alanine, glycine, serine, and lysine
Answer: C. Phenylalanine, valine, threonine, and lysine
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Essential, ketogenic, and glucogenic amino acids; Amino acid categories and plant diets
Why this is correct:
The essential amino acids are phenylalanine, valine, tryptophan, threonine, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, leucine, and lysine (PVT TIM HaLL). All four in this choice are on that list.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Proline and arginine aren't on the essential list.
B. Tyrosine is conditional because it's made from phenylalanine, and cysteine and glutamine aren't essential.
D. Aspartate and glutamate aren't essential.
E. Alanine, glycine, and serine aren't essential.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 17
A 5-year-old boy with seizures that haven't responded to two medications is started on a ketogenic diet. His dietitian builds the protein portion around amino acids whose carbon skeletons can be converted only to ketone bodies and never to glucose. Which of the following amino acids are purely ketogenic?
A. Leucine and lysine
B. Tryptophan and threonine
C. Histidine and valine
D. Isoleucine and phenylalanine
E. Alanine and glycine
Answer: A. Leucine and lysine
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Essential, ketogenic, and glucogenic amino acids
Why this is correct:
Leucine and lysine are the ketogenic amino acids (the two L's).
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Tryptophan and threonine are both glucogenic and ketogenic.
C. Histidine and valine aren't among the ketogenic amino acids.
D. Isoleucine and phenylalanine are both glucogenic and ketogenic.
E. Alanine and glycine aren't among the ketogenic amino acids.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes
Question 18
A researcher studying protein metabolism in adults with type 2 diabetes tracks amino acids whose carbon skeletons can be used to make both glucose and ketone bodies. Which of the following groups contains only amino acids that are both glucogenic and ketogenic?
A. Histidine, valine, and methionine
B. Leucine, lysine, isoleucine, and threonine
C. Leucine and lysine
D. Isoleucine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and threonine
E. Tyrosine, histidine, and lysine
Answer: D. Isoleucine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and threonine
Order: First
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Essential, ketogenic, and glucogenic amino acids
Why this is correct:
Isoleucine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, and threonine (TTIP) are both glucogenic and ketogenic.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Histidine, valine, and methionine aren't in the TTIP group.
B. Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic, so this group is mixed.
C. Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic.
E. Lysine is purely ketogenic, and tyrosine and histidine aren't in the TTIP group.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes
Question 19
A resident reviewing an endocrine workup reads the amino acid sequence of a short peptide fragment reported by the laboratory. The attending reminds her that protein sequences are always written in one standard direction. Which of the following is that direction?
A. From the N terminus to the C terminus
B. From the 3' end to the 5' end
C. From the C terminus to the N terminus
D. From the lightest to the heaviest amino acid
E. From the 5' end to the 3' end
Answer: A. From the N terminus to the C terminus
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Essential, ketogenic, and glucogenic amino acids
Why this is correct:
Peptide sequences are written from the N terminus to the C terminus, the same direction in which a chain grows during translation.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. 3' and 5' ends describe nucleic acids, not proteins.
C. This reverses the convention.
D. Sequences are written in chain order, not by amino acid size.
E. 5' to 3' describes how nucleic acids are written and synthesized, not proteins.
Objective: Identify functional groups unique to proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and apply the underlying principles as to how these biomolecules communicate with one another in health and disease (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes
Question 20
A 46-year-old man with alcohol use disorder starts a medication to help him stop drinking. Two weeks later, he drinks at a party and within minutes develops flushing, a pounding headache, nausea, and palpitations. Pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg. He is flushed and diaphoretic but alert. Which of the following best explains how his medication causes these symptoms?
A. It competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, so ethanol builds up
B. It inhibits electron transport chain enzymes, so lactate builds up
C. It inhibits peroxisomal catalase, so hydrogen peroxide builds up
D. It speeds acetic acid production, so the blood turns acidic
E. It irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up
Answer: E. It irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Disulfiram, fomepizole, and ALDH2 deficiency
Why this is correct:
Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, which normally converts acetaldehyde to acetic acid. Acetaldehyde builds up and causes severe hangover-like symptoms, which discourages drinking.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Competitive inhibition of alcohol dehydrogenase is how fomepizole works, and it would reduce acetaldehyde, not increase it.
B. Electron transport chain inhibition is the mechanism of cyanide, not disulfiram.
C. Catalase isn't the target of disulfiram.
D. Blocking aldehyde dehydrogenase lowers acetic acid production.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes
Question 21
A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after drinking antifreeze. He is drowsy but arousable. Pulse is 102/min. Serum anion gap and osmolar gap are high, and urine shows calcium oxalate crystals. He is given an antidote that prevents his body from making the toxin's harmful metabolites. Which of the following is the antidote and its mechanism?
A. Disulfiram, a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase
B. Disulfiram, an irreversible inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase
C. Fomepizole, an irreversible inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase
D. Hydroxocobalamin, an antidote for electron transport chain toxins
E. Fomepizole, a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase
Answer: E. Fomepizole, a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Disulfiram, fomepizole, and ALDH2 deficiency
Why this is correct:
Antifreeze contains ethylene glycol. Fomepizole competes for alcohol dehydrogenase, the first step in its breakdown, so the toxic downstream products aren't made. It's used for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Disulfiram doesn't inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase.
B. Disulfiram does irreversibly inhibit aldehyde dehydrogenase, but it treats alcoholism and doesn't block the first step of ethylene glycol metabolism.
C. Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase competitively, not aldehyde dehydrogenase.
D. Hydroxocobalamin is used for cyanide poisoning.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Amino Acids, Proteins & Enzymes
Question 22
A 40-year-old firefighter is brought to the emergency department after being trapped in a burning house full of plastic furniture. He is confused and has soot around his nose and mouth. Pulse is 124/min, blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 97%. Serum lactate is very high, and carboxyhemoglobin is only mildly high. Poisoning by a toxin that targets electron transport chain enzymes is suspected. Which of the following should be given?
A. Fomepizole
B. Beta-carotene
C. Hydroxocobalamin
D. Catalase
E. Disulfiram
Answer: C. Hydroxocobalamin
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Why this is correct:
Burning plastics can release cyanide, which targets enzymes in the electron transport chain and forces cells into anaerobic metabolism, raising lactate. Hydroxocobalamin is the course's antidote for cyanide poisoning.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Fomepizole treats methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning by blocking alcohol dehydrogenase.
B. Beta-carotene is used for erythropoietic protoporphyria.
D. Catalase is a peroxisomal enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide, not an antidote.

Question 23
A 21-year-old woman of East Asian descent comes to the clinic because her face and neck turn red, with palpitations and nausea, after only a few sips of alcohol. Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Disulfiram, fomepizole, and ALDH2 deficiency
Why this is correct:

Question 36
A 50-year-old woman with breast cancer is starting paclitaxel, which stabilizes microtubules so the mitotic spindle can't pull chromosomes apart. Her oncologist reviews the structure of the polymer the drug targets. Which of the following correctly describes microtubule structure?
A. Alpha-beta tubulin dimers form 9 protofilaments, with alpha tubulin at the plus end
B. Alpha-beta tubulin dimers form 13 protofilaments, with beta tubulin at the plus end
C. Alpha-beta tubulin dimers form 13 protofilaments, with alpha tubulin at the plus end
D. Gamma tubulin dimers form 13 protofilaments, with gamma tubulin at the plus end
E. Actin monomers form 13 protofilaments, with a formin cap at the plus end
Answer: B. Alpha-beta tubulin dimers form 13 protofilaments, with beta tubulin at the plus end
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Microtubule structure and dynamic instability
Why this is correct:
The basic unit of a microtubule is a dimer of alpha and beta tubulin. Beta tubulin is at the plus end and alpha at the minus end, and 13 protofilaments form each microtubule.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Microtubules have 13 protofilaments, and beta tubulin is at the plus end.
C. Alpha tubulin is at the minus end, not the plus end.
D. Gamma tubulin sits on the MTOC and starts microtubules; it isn't the building block.
E. Microtubules are made of tubulin, not actin.

Question 38
A 60-year-old man with lymphoma develops numbness in both feet after several cycles of vincristine, a microtubule inhibitor. He has decreased vibration sense and absent ankle reflexes. His physician explains that the drug interferes with normal microtubule dynamics. Which of the following normally determines whether a microtubule grows or shrinks?

Question 41
A 30-year-old man comes to the clinic because he and his wife haven't conceived after 2 years of trying. He has had chronic sinus infections and a productive cough since childhood. Question 44
A 38-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of flank pain and blood in her urine. Her mother started dialysis at 55. Blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg, and both kidneys are palpable. Ultrasound shows many cysts in both kidneys, and genetic testing confirms autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. Which of the following best explains how her cysts form?
A. Tau aggregates in the tubule cells, so the cells die and leave fluid-filled spaces
B. Dynein becomes hyperactive, so motile cilia push fluid into the tubules

Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Ciliopathies; Motile vs. nonmotile cilia

Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Tau aggregates are the neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer disease.
B. Hyperactive dynein comes from Bicaudal-D mutations in spinal muscular atrophy and ALS, and tubule primary cilia aren't motile.
C. SGLT2 overactivity isn't the cause of cysts.
E. Failure to clear debris is the problem with motile cilia in the airways, not the kidney.

Question 46
A 52-year-old man comes to the clinic because of slowness, stiffness, and a shuffling gait for 1 year, along with depression and an 8-kg (18-lb) weight loss. Question 48
A 78-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her daughter because of worsening memory over 3 years. She gets lost while driving and repeats questions. Serum vitamin B12 and TSH are normal, and MRI shows temporal lobe atrophy. Years later, autopsy shows neurofibrillary tangles in her neurons. Which of the following best describes the protein that forms these tangles?
A. Tau, which no longer binds microtubules and aggregates
B. Spectrin, which detaches from the membrane and aggregates
C. Dynactin, which is mutated so organelles pile up
D. Tau, which binds microtubules too tightly for them to depolymerize

Answer: A. Tau, which no longer binds microtubules and aggregates
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Tau and Alzheimer disease
Why this is correct:
Neurofibrillary tangles are aggregates of tau, a microtubule-associated protein. In Alzheimer disease, hyperphosphorylated tau no longer binds microtubules and forms aggregates. It's still debated whether disease comes from losing tau's normal function or from the toxic aggregates.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Spectrin forms the red cell membrane skeleton.
C. Dynactin mutations cause Perry syndrome.
D. In Alzheimer disease, tau detaches from microtubules rather than binding them too tightly.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Cytoskeleton & Microtubules
Question 49
A 34-year-old man with celiac disease has a duodenal biopsy that shows damaged microvilli. Each normal microvillus contains a core of parallel actin filaments, held in place by a stable cap at the plus end. Which of the following anchors the minus end of these filaments?
A. A basal body attached to the apical plasma membrane
B. Gamma tubulin at the microtubule-organizing center
C. Dystrophin attached to the extracellular matrix
D. The terminal web of the cortical actin cytoskeleton
E. Fascin bundles at the tip of each microvillus
Answer: D. The terminal web of the cortical actin cytoskeleton
Order: First
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Formins and Arp2/3: linear vs. branched actin
Why this is correct:
Microvilli are stable, uniform structures. Bundling proteins cross-link their parallel actin filaments, a stable cap at the plus end stops growth, and the minus end attaches to the terminal web of the cortical actin cytoskeleton.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Basal bodies anchor cilia, which are built from microtubules.
B. Gamma tubulin starts microtubules, not actin filaments.
C. Dystrophin anchors actin in muscle to the extracellular matrix.
E. Fascin cross-links filopodia, and the tip of a microvillus is its plus end.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Membrane Transport
Question 50
A researcher studies how intestinal epithelial cells move sugar from the gut lumen into the blood. She compares sugar transport across the apical membrane, which faces the external milieu, with sugar transport across the basolateral membrane, which faces the internal milieu. Which of the following best describes sugar transport at these two surfaces?
A. Active transport on the apical side and passive transport on the basolateral side
B. Endocytosis on the apical side and exocytosis on the basolateral side
C. Passive transport on both sides
D. Passive transport on the apical side and active transport on the basolateral side
E. Active transport on both sides
Answer: A. Active transport on the apical side and passive transport on the basolateral side
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: SGLT1 and SGLT2
Why this is correct:
The apical side faces the external milieu and uses active transport: the SGLT1 symporter brings sugar in along with sodium moving down its gradient. The basolateral side faces the internal milieu, where sugar leaves passively.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Intestinal sugar absorption uses transporters, not vesicle traffic.
C. Apical uptake is active, driven by the sodium gradient.
D. This reverses the two surfaces.
E. Basolateral sugar exit is passive.

Question 51
A 26-year-old woman with watery diarrhea for 2 days is given an oral rehydration solution containing glucose and sodium. Pulse is 104/min, and her mucous membranes are dry. Question 52
A 2-week-old girl is brought to the clinic because of severe watery diarrhea since her first feedings. She has lost 10% of her birth weight, and her fontanelle is sunken. Question 53
A 56-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is started on a drug that stops her kidneys from reabsorbing glucose. Three weeks later, she comes to the clinic because of vaginal itching and discharge, and she feels thirsty. Her blood glucose is lower than before, and her urine glucose is very high. Which of the following transporters does her new drug inhibit, and why did these side effects occur?
A. GLUT2; insulin release is blocked, so blood glucose stays high
B. GLUT5; fructose is lost in the urine and feeds bacteria
C. SGLT1; glucose isn't absorbed from the gut, so stools become loose
D. GLUT4; insulin can't move glucose into muscle, so levels rise

Answer: E. SGLT2; glucose left in the urine pulls water with it and feeds yeast
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: SGLT1 and SGLT2
Why this is correct:
SGLT2 inhibitors (phlorizin analogs such as Jardiance, Farxiga, and Invokana) block glucose reabsorption in the kidney. The glucose left in the urine takes water with it, causing dehydration and thirst, and it raises the chance of yeast infections.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. GLUT2 inactivation causes diabetes by blocking insulin release, and her glucose has fallen.
B. GLUT5 carries fructose in the gut and isn't the target of these drugs.
C. SGLT1 works in the intestine, and blocking it wouldn't raise urine glucose.
D. GLUT4 moves glucose into muscle and fat in response to insulin, and blocking it would raise blood glucose.

Question 55
A 62-year-old man with lung adenocarcinoma is scheduled for a PET scan to look for spread. He has fasted for 6 hours, and his blood glucose is normal. The protocol requires the radioactive glucose tracer 18F-FDG to be injected rather than taken by mouth. Which of the following best explains why FDG must be given intravenously?
A. FDG is a substrate of SGLT2 only, so the gut would absorb it too slowly
B. The gut absorbs glucose through SGLTs, while FDG is a substrate of GLUTs
C. FDG blocks insulin release, so oral dosing would cause hyperglycemia
D. FDG enters only tumor cells, so the gut lining can't absorb it

Answer: B. The gut absorbs glucose through SGLTs, while FDG is a substrate of GLUTs
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: GLUT transporter disorders; SGLT1 and SGLT2
Why this is correct:
18FDG is a substrate of all GLUTs and enters every cell in the body. It has to be injected because the GI tract absorbs glucose through SGLTs. GLUT1 is overexpressed in cancer cells, which is why tumors take up FDG.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. FDG is a substrate of all GLUTs, not SGLT2.
C. FDG doesn't block insulin release.
D. FDG enters all cells; tumors simply take up more because they overexpress GLUT1.

Question 59
A 2-day-old boy has repeated episodes of low blood glucose despite frequent feeds and needs IV dextrose. He weighed 4.5 kg (9.9 lb) at birth, and his mother doesn't have diabetes.
Laboratory studies show:
Glucose: very low
Insulin: high
Ketones: low
Genetic testing shows a mutation that restricts potassium exit from his pancreatic beta cells. Which of the following best explains why his beta cells release too much insulin?

A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of a scaly, red rash on his face and arms that worsens in sunlight and episodes of unsteady walking. He eats a normal diet. Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Pharmacodynamics
Question 65
A pharmacology lecture reviews the targets of small-molecule drugs, using metoprolol, which blocks a G protein-coupled receptor, and diltiazem, which blocks a voltage-gated calcium channel, as examples. Which of the following statements about small-molecule drug targets is correct?
A. Most drugs bind their targets irreversibly, so their effects outlast their levels
B. Most drugs target proteins such as GPCRs, enzymes, ion channels, nuclear receptors, and transporters
C. Most drugs target DNA directly, changing gene expression in target cells
D. Most drugs are monoclonal antibodies that bind surface receptors
E. Only GPCRs are drug targets, since other proteins can't bind small molecules
Answer: B. Most drugs target proteins such as GPCRs, enzymes, ion channels, nuclear receptors, and transporters
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Drug targets, occupancy, and KD
Why this is correct:
Small-molecule drugs act on GPCRs, enzymes, ligand- and voltage-gated ion channels, transcription factors, nuclear receptors, transport and structural proteins, and RNA. GPCRs account for about 12% of targets and ion channels about 19%.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Drugs work by occupying their targets, and that binding is reversible.
C. RNA is on the list of targets, but DNA isn't the main target of small-molecule drugs.
D. Monoclonal antibodies are biologics, not small molecules.
E. Ion channels, enzymes, and many other proteins are also targets.

Question 67
A 34-year-old woman with seasonal allergies enrolls in a trial of a new antihistamine. The investigators report the drug concentration at which half of her histamine receptors are occupied. Which of the following terms describes this value?

Answer: E. KD
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Drug targets, occupancy, and KD
Why this is correct:
Drugs work by reversibly occupying their targets. KD is the concentration of drug needed to bind half of the targets, and it reflects potency.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Bioavailability is the fraction of a dose that reaches systemic circulation.

Question 70
A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after an opioid overdose. His respirations are 6/min, his pupils are pinpoint, and he responds only to pain. After naloxone, his respirations rise to 14/min. B. A partial agonist
C. A positive allosteric modulator
D. A competitive antagonist
E. An irreversible enzyme inhibitor
Answer: D. A competitive antagonist
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Agonists, antagonists, and inverse agonists
Why this is correct:
A competitive antagonist occupies the binding site and competes with the agonist without activating the receptor. Because it competes, the agonist needs a higher concentration to occupy half of the receptors (a higher KD).
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A full agonist would activate the receptor and worsen the overdose.
B. A partial agonist produces some receptor activation.
C. A positive allosteric modulator binds a different site and increases the agonist's effect.

Question 72
A 58-year-old man with hypertension is choosing between two blood pressure drugs. Drug A occupies half of its target receptors at 1 nM, and Drug B needs 100 nM to do the same. At full doses, both lower blood pressure by the same maximum amount. Which of the following statements is correct?
A. The drugs have the same potency and the same efficacy
B. Drug B has greater efficacy, and the two are equally potent
C. Drug A is more potent, and the two drugs have equal efficacy
D. Drug B is more potent, and the two drugs have equal efficacy
E. Drug A has greater efficacy, and the two are equally potent
Answer: C. Drug A is more potent, and the two drugs have equal efficacy
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Agonists, antagonists, and inverse agonists; Drug targets, occupancy, and KD
Why this is correct:
Potency is the concentration of drug needed to bind the target (KD), and efficacy is the maximal physiological effect. Drug A needs less drug, so it's more potent, and both reach the same maximum, so their efficacy is equal.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Their KD values differ 100-fold, so their potency isn't the same.
B. Their maximal effects are equal, so neither has greater efficacy.
D. Drug B needs more drug, so it's less potent.
E. Equal maximal effects mean equal efficacy, and their potencies differ.

Why the other answers are wrong:

Question 76
A pharmacist compares two anticonvulsants for a 30-year-old woman with epilepsy who plans to become pregnant. Drug A has a TD50 of 200 mg and an ED50 of 20 mg. Drug B has a TD50 of 60 mg and an ED50 of 30 mg. Her liver and kidney function are normal. Which of the following drugs is safer, and why?
A. Drug A, because its ED50 of 20 mg is lower than Drug B's
B. Drug B, because its therapeutic index of 2 is larger
C. Drug A, because its therapeutic index of 10 is larger
D. Drug B, because its TD50 is lower than Drug A's
E. Neither, because their ED50 values are similar
Answer: C. Drug A, because its therapeutic index of 10 is larger
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Therapeutic index
Why this is correct:
The therapeutic index is TD50 divided by ED50, and a larger number is better because the effective and toxic doses are farther apart. Drug A's index is 200/20 = 10, and Drug B's is 60/30 = 2.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. A lower ED50 reflects how much drug is needed for effect, not how safe the drug is.
B. Drug B's index of 2 is smaller, not larger.
D. A lower TD50 means Drug B becomes toxic at a lower dose, which makes it less safe.
E. Safety depends on the ratio of toxic to effective dose, and the ratios differ five-fold.

Reference: Drug absorption and metabolism
Why this is correct:
Absorption is getting a drug into circulation. Permeation through the lipid bilayer depends on the drug's size, hydrophobicity, and lipid-water coefficient.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Therapeutic index, potency, and efficacy describe safety and drug action, not membrane permeation.
B. CYP metabolism and clearance describe how a drug is removed after absorption.
D. Clearance and volume of distribution describe what happens after a drug reaches the blood.
E. KD and efficacy describe binding to the target and the maximal effect.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Why the other answers are wrong:

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Pharmacokinetics
Question 90
A 55-year-old man in a study of a new antibiotic receives the drug intravenously one week and by mouth the next. The area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) is 60 mg·h/L after the IV dose and 30 mg·h/L after the oral dose. His kidney and liver function are normal. Which of the following is the oral bioavailability?
A. 30%
B. 25%
C. 200%
D. 100%
E. 50%
Answer: E. 50%
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bioavailability, volume of distribution, and clearance
Why this is correct:
Bioavailability (F) is how much drug reaches systemic circulation, calculated as AUC oral divided by AUC IV. Here it's 30/60 = 0.5, or 50%.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. This treats the oral AUC value itself as a percentage.
B. This doesn't follow from the ratio of the two AUCs.
C. This divides the IV AUC by the oral AUC, inverting the formula.
D. Only an IV dose has 100% bioavailability.

Question 91

Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bioavailability, volume of distribution, and clearance

Volume of distribution is the apparent volume in which a drug is distributed, calculated as amount divided by concentration: 500 mg / 10 mg/L = 50 L.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. This uses his body weight rather than the formula.
B. This divides the dose by 100 rather than by the measured concentration.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Pharmacokinetics
Question 92
A 68-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease takes an antiepileptic drug that is removed by the kidneys. Her creatinine has risen over the past year, and her drug level is now above the target range, with new drowsiness. The volume of plasma cleared of the drug each hour has fallen. Which of the following pharmacokinetic parameters has decreased?
A. Clearance
B. Bioavailability
C. KD
D. Therapeutic index
E. Volume of distribution
Answer: A. Clearance
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bioavailability, volume of distribution, and clearance
Why this is correct:
Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of a drug per unit of time. Worsening kidney function lowers clearance of a renally excreted drug, so its level rises.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Bioavailability describes how much of a dose reaches systemic circulation.
C. KD is the concentration that occupies half of the drug's targets.
D. The therapeutic index compares toxic and effective doses.
E. Volume of distribution describes how widely a drug spreads, not how fast it's removed.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Pharmacokinetics
Question 95
A 58-year-old man needs to be kept at a steady plasma concentration of a drug taken by mouth. The drug's clearance is 2 L/hour, the target concentration is 10 mg/L, and its oral bioavailability is 0.5. His kidney and liver function are normal. Which of the following maintenance dosing rates is needed?
A. 10 mg/hour
B. 40 mg/hour

D. 20 mg/hour

Answer: B. 40 mg/hour
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Loading and maintenance doses
Why this is correct:
The maintenance dose equals clearance times the target concentration, divided by bioavailability for an oral drug: (2 L/hour × 10 mg/L) / 0.5 = 40 mg/hour.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. This multiplies by bioavailability instead of dividing by it.
C. This doesn't follow from the maintenance dose formula.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Patterns of Inheritance
Question 96
A 28-year-old woman and her husband come to the clinic for preconception counseling. An autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 2,500 people in their population, and neither has a family history of it. Both are healthy, and the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Which of the following is the approximate carrier frequency in their population?
A. About 1 in 50
B. About 1 in 25
C. About 1 in 100
D. About 1 in 2,500
E. About 1 in 5
Answer: B. About 1 in 25
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
Why this is correct:
In Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, q² is the frequency of affected (aa) people. If q² = 1/2,500, then q = 1/50 and p is nearly 1. Carriers are 2pq, about 2 × 1/50 = 1/25.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. 1 in 50 is q, the allele frequency, not the carrier frequency.
C. This halves the carrier frequency instead of doubling q.
D. 1 in 2,500 is q², the frequency of affected people.
E. This is far too high for a disease affecting 1 in 2,500.
Objective: Illustrate the molecular basis of human genome instability and articulate the principles of inheritance of single gene mutations, cancer genetics, and genetic counseling (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Patterns of Inheritance
Question 97
A 30-year-old man is found to carry a recessive allele for a genetic disorder, and he and his partner are planning a pregnancy. In his population, the frequency of the recessive allele is 0.1, and the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Which of the following fractions of the population is expected to be affected homozygotes?
A. 1%
B. 18%
C. 20%
D. 10%
E. 81%
Answer: A. 1%
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
Why this is correct:
Under Hardy-Weinberg, p² is the frequency of AA, 2pq of Aa, and q² of aa. With q = 0.1, q² = 0.01, or 1%.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. 18% is 2pq, the carrier frequency.
C. 20% is 2q, which isn't a Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequency.
D. 10% is q, the allele frequency.
E. 81% is p², the frequency of unaffected homozygotes.
Objective: Illustrate the molecular basis of human genome instability and articulate the principles of inheritance of single gene mutations, cancer genetics, and genetic counseling (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Patterns of Inheritance
Question 98
A 26-year-old woman is referred for genetic counseling after her sister was diagnosed with an autosomal recessive condition. In their population, the recessive allele has a frequency of 0.2, and the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Which of the following fractions of the population is expected to be heterozygous carriers?
A. 20%
B. 16%
C. 64%
D. 32%
E. 4%
Answer: D. 32%
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
Why this is correct:
Under Hardy-Weinberg, 2pq is the frequency of heterozygotes. With q = 0.2 and p = 0.8, 2pq = 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32, or 32%.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. 20% is q, the allele frequency.
B. 16% is pq without the factor of 2.
C. 64% is p², the frequency of unaffected homozygotes.
E. 4% is q², the frequency of affected homozygotes.
Objective: Illustrate the molecular basis of human genome instability and articulate the principles of inheritance of single gene mutations, cancer genetics, and genetic counseling (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 3 / Cellular Energetics
Question 99
A 24-year-old man is enrolled in a study of muscle energy metabolism. He is healthy and runs 20 miles a week. A biopsy of his thigh muscle taken at rest shows ATP of 8 mM, ADP of 2 mM, and AMP of 0 mM. The investigators calculate his muscle's adenylate energy charge. Which of the following is his muscle's energy charge?
A. 0.9
B. 0.8
C. 0.5
D. 1.0
E. 0.2
Answer: A. 0.9
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Adenylate kinase and energy charge
Why this is correct:
Energy charge = ([ATP] + ½[ADP]) / ([ATP] + [ADP] + [AMP]). Here it's (8 + 1) / 10 = 0.9, the level cells aim to maintain.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. 0.8 is ATP divided by the total, which leaves out the half-weighting of ADP.
C. 0.5 doesn't follow from the formula.
D. An energy charge of 1.0 would require all of the adenylate pool to be ATP.
E. 0.2 is ADP divided by the total.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Why the other answers are wrong:

Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin: low
Reticulocyte count: high
Indirect bilirubin: high
Direct Coombs test: negative
G6PD activity: normal
A peripheral smear shows red cells with thorny projections, and enzyme testing shows a defect in the last step of glycolysis. Which of the following best explains the shape of his red cells?
A. Excess 2,3-BPG polymerizes hemoglobin
B. Low ATP causes the Na+/K+ pumps to fail
C. Antibodies coat the red cell membrane
D. Oxidized hemoglobin forms Heinz bodies
E. A defective spectrin skeleton deforms the cells
Answer: B. Low ATP causes the Na+/K+ pumps to fail
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Glycolytic enzyme deficiencies in red cells; Anaerobic glycolysis and lactic acidosis
Why this is correct:
Red cells have no mitochondria and depend on glycolysis for ATP. In pyruvate kinase deficiency, ATP isn't made fast enough, the Na+/K+ pumps fail, and the cells become echinocytes with thorny projections, causing hemolytic anemia. It's chronic and autosomal recessive.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. 2,3-BPG shifts oxygen affinity; it doesn't polymerize hemoglobin.
C. Antibody coating would give a positive Coombs test.
D. Heinz bodies form in G6PD deficiency, and his G6PD is normal.
E. Spectrin defects cause elliptocytes, not thorny cells.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 113
A 22-year-old woman eats a large pasta dinner, and her liver begins storing glucose as glycogen. A protein serves as the primer on which new glycogen chains are built, and the synthesizing enzyme is allosterically activated as glucose-6-phosphate rises. Which of the following correctly identifies the primer and the regulation of the synthesizing enzyme?
A. Glycogenin is the primer, and glycogen synthase is activated by glucagon
B. Glycogen phosphorylase is the primer, and glycogen synthase is activated by glucose-6-phosphate
C. The debranching enzyme is the primer, and glycogen synthase is activated by glucose-6-phosphate
D. Glycogenin is the primer, and glycogen synthase is activated by glucose-6-phosphate
E. Glycogenin is the primer, and glycogen synthase is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
Answer: D. Glycogenin is the primer, and glycogen synthase is activated by glucose-6-phosphate
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Glycogen synthesis and breakdown
Why this is correct:
Glycogenin is the primer for building glycogen from glucose. Glycogen synthase builds the chains, works with the branching enzyme, and is allosterically activated by glucose-6-phosphate.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Glucagon activates glycogen breakdown, not synthesis.
B. Glycogen phosphorylase breaks glycogen down; it isn't a primer.
C. The debranching enzyme works with phosphorylase during breakdown.
E. Glucose-6-phosphate activates glycogen synthase.

Question 114
A 34-year-old nurse becomes sweaty and shaky after skipping lunch during a busy shift. Her pulse is 104/min, and her blood glucose is low. A. It's inhibited by glucagon and epinephrine and activated by glucose
B. It's activated by glucagon and epinephrine and inhibited by glucose
C. It's activated by glucose-6-phosphate and inhibited by glucagon

Glycogen phosphorylase breaks down glycogen with the help of the debranching enzyme. Glucagon and epinephrine activate it, and glucose and glucose-6-phosphate allosterically inhibit it.
Why the other answers are wrong:

C. Glucose-6-phosphate inhibits phosphorylase and activates glycogen synthase.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 3 / Glucose Homeostasis
Question 116
A 35-year-old woman runs a half marathon, and her serum lactate is high at the finish line. Her muscles send lactate and alanine to her liver, which converts them to glucose and sends the glucose back to her muscles. Which of the following is this cycle called?
A. The citric acid cycle
B. The pentose phosphate pathway
C. The Cori cycle
D. The polyol pathway
E. The urea cycle
Answer: C. The Cori cycle
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Gluconeogenesis and the Cori cycle
Why this is correct:
In the Cori cycle, pyruvate from skeletal muscle becomes lactate and alanine, which travel to the liver. The liver makes glucose through gluconeogenesis and returns it to the muscle.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The citric acid cycle oxidizes acetyl-CoA in mitochondria.
B. The pentose phosphate pathway makes NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate.
D. The polyol pathway converts sugars to sugar alcohols such as sorbitol.
E. The urea cycle converts ammonia to urea.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 3 / Glucose Homeostasis
Question 117
A 5-month-old girl is brought to the clinic because she becomes sweaty, shaky, and irritable 2 to 3 hours after feeds. She has a doll-like face, a protuberant abdomen, and a liver palpable 7 cm below the costal margin. Her blood glucose during an episode is very low, and glucagon doesn't raise it. Ultrasound shows enlarged kidneys. Which of the following best explains why gluconeogenesis can't prevent her hypoglycemia?
A. Liver glycogen phosphorylase is deficient, so only gluconeogenesis can supply glucose
B. A lysosomal enzyme is deficient, so glycogen is trapped in lysosomes
C. The debranching enzyme is deficient, so only the outer branches can be broken down
D. The branching enzyme is deficient, so abnormal glycogen can't be broken down
E. Glucose-6-phosphatase is deficient, so neither glycogen breakdown nor gluconeogenesis can release glucose
Answer: E. Glucose-6-phosphatase is deficient, so neither glycogen breakdown nor gluconeogenesis can release glucose
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Glycogen storage diseases; Glycogen synthesis and breakdown
Why this is correct:
Von Gierke disease (type I) is a glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency in the liver and kidney, causing hepatomegaly and inter-meal hypoglycemia. Gluconeogenesis can't compensate because its glucose also has to be released by glucose-6-phosphatase.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. In Hers disease (liver phosphorylase), gluconeogenesis does keep glucose up, so the disease is milder.
B. Pompe disease (lysosomal) affects muscle and heart, not fasting glucose.
C. Cori disease (debranching enzyme) causes mild hypoglycemia that can improve.
D. Andersen disease (branching enzyme) leads to cirrhosis rather than this fasting picture.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Question 118
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because his grandmother noticed a protuberant abdomen. He is growing at the 20th percentile and meeting milestones. Question 119
A 22-year-old man comes to the clinic because of painful muscle cramps and dark urine within minutes of lifting weights. If he rests briefly, he can continue with less pain. A 2-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of vomiting, poor feeding, and yellow skin for several days. She is breastfed. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Question 133
A 7-month-old boy with hereditary fructose intolerance is brought to the emergency department after eating fruit at daycare. He is lethargic, vomiting, and mildly dehydrated, and his liver is enlarged.

Glucose: low
Lactate: high

Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Fructose metabolism disorders
Why this is correct:

Why the other answers are wrong:

C. Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose in the first step of glycolysis.

Question 135
A 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years comes to the clinic because of blurry vision and burning pain in her feet. Her hemoglobin A1c has been high for years. She has decreased vibration sense in both feet, early cataracts, and dot-blot hemorrhages on fundoscopy, and her urine shows microalbuminuria. Which of the following mechanisms contributes to her lens and nerve damage?

Difficulty: Easy

Why this is correct:

C. Galactitol causes cataracts in galactosemia, not in diabetes.

Question 137
A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted with confusion, abnormal eye movements, and a wide-based gait. He eats poorly, and thiamine deficiency is suspected. Which of the following red cell enzymes has its activity measured to estimate his thiamine stores?

Question 138
A 23-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of dark urine and back pain 2 days after starting a sulfa antibiotic for a urinary tract infection. He is pale and jaundiced. His brother had a similar episode.

Hemoglobin: low
Reticulocyte count: high
LDH: high
Direct Coombs test: negative

Question 140
A 30-year-old woman has a thigh abscess drained. Gram stain of the pus shows gram-positive cocci in clusters, and her white cell count is high with a neutrophilia. In her neutrophils, oxygen consumption rises sharply as a sequence of enzymes produces a potent bactericidal compound. Which of the following sequences produces hypochlorous acid?
A. Myeloperoxidase → catalase → NADPH oxidase
B. G6PD → transketolase → myeloperoxidase
C. Superoxide dismutase → NADPH oxidase → catalase
D. NADPH oxidase → superoxide dismutase → myeloperoxidase
E. Glutathione peroxidase → catalase → myeloperoxidase
Answer: D. NADPH oxidase → superoxide dismutase → myeloperoxidase
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Respiratory burst and chronic granulomatous disease
Why this is correct:
In the respiratory burst, activated phagocytes raise oxygen consumption to make hypochlorous acid (HOCl), which kills bacteria. The sequence is NADPH oxidase, then superoxide dismutase, then myeloperoxidase.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. This reverses the sequence and includes catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide rather than using it.
B. G6PD and transketolase belong to the pentose phosphate pathway.
C. NADPH oxidase comes first, and catalase isn't part of the burst.
E. Glutathione peroxidase and catalase break down hydrogen peroxide rather than turning it into HOCl.

Question 141
A 5-year-old boy is admitted with a liver abscess growing Staphylococcus aureus. He has had several skin abscesses and a Serratia pneumonia, and his maternal uncle had similar infections. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). His neutrophil count is normal, and serum immunoglobulins are high. A dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test of his neutrophils shows a low signal. Which of the following defects explains his infections with catalase-positive organisms?

B. It has no effect on the reductase, only on LDL receptors
C. It promotes kinase activity, phosphorylating and activating the reductase
D. It promotes kinase activity, phosphorylating and inactivating the reductase
E. It promotes phosphatase activity, dephosphorylating and activating the reductase
Answer: E. It promotes phosphatase activity, dephosphorylating and activating the reductase
Order: First
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: HMG-CoA reductase and statins
Why this is correct:
HMG-CoA reductase is active when it isn't phosphorylated. High insulin promotes phosphatase activity, activating the reductase, while high glucagon promotes kinase activity, inactivating it.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Insulin's short-term effect on the reductase is dephosphorylation, not degradation.
B. Insulin does act on the reductase.
C. Phosphorylation inactivates the reductase.
D. Kinase activity is promoted by glucagon, not insulin.

Question 157
A 50-year-old woman with hyperlipidemia starts atorvastatin, and her LDL falls. As her cells' cholesterol content drops, a regulatory complex moves from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi, and a signal reaches the nucleus. Which of the following is the effect of this signal?

Why this is correct:
The HMG-CoA reductase gene is regulated by cellular cholesterol. High cholesterol keeps the regulatory complex in the ER, and low cholesterol moves it to the Golgi, sending a signal to the nucleus to turn the gene on.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 3 / Cholesterol Metabolism
Question 158
A 44-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. Murphy sign is positive, and ultrasound shows gallstones made of cholesterol. Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Bile acids and cholelithiasis
Why this is correct:
Cholesterol is eliminated by conversion to bile acids, and 7-alpha-hydroxylase converts cholesterol to primary bile acids and salts. When it's deficient, cholesterol can't be broken down, and once cholesterol is more than 15% of bile it can aggregate into gallstones.
Why the other answers are wrong:

Question 163
A 50-year-old man with diabetes comes to the clinic because of chest pain on exertion. Serum triglycerides and cholesterol are both moderately high, and HDL is normal. Question 164
A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department with chest pain and is diagnosed with a myocardial infarction. He doesn't smoke or have diabetes, and his father died of a heart attack at 38. Serum LDL is very high, triglycerides are normal, and troponin is high. Which of the following best explains why macrophages in his arteries fill with cholesterol?

An LDL receptor defect (type II) keeps LDL in plasma longer, where it's more likely to be oxidized. Macrophage scavenger receptors take up oxidized LDL and aren't downregulated by cellular cholesterol, so macrophages become foam cells that contribute to plaques.

C. LDL receptor uptake is downregulated as cholesterol rises, which is why it isn't the route to foam cells.

Question 169
A 38-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of fatigue and right upper quadrant discomfort. She drinks two glasses of wine a night and often takes acetaminophen for headaches. A 45-year-old man with Lynch syndrome has his tumor DNA analyzed. The laboratory examines repeated sequences of 2 to 6 base pairs that commonly change length when replication errors go unrepaired. Which of the following are these regions?

Question 201
A laboratory wants to detect a single-base, disease-causing mutation, and a technician suggests hybridizing a probe under low-stringency conditions. Which of the following best explains why this is a poor choice?
A. Hybridization requires reverse transcriptase, so DNA probes fail
B. Low stringency prevents any hybridization, so no signal appears
C. Low stringency lets related sequences bind, so point mutations are missed
D. Hybridization works only with RNA, so genomic DNA gives no signal
E. Low stringency permanently denatures the probe, so it can't bind
Answer: C. Low stringency lets related sequences bind, so point mutations are missed
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: DNA hybridization and repeat sequences
Why this is correct:
Hybridization relies on complementary strands pairing. Under low stringency, closely related sequences also hybridize, so it can't tell apart disease-causing point mutations.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Hybridization doesn't require reverse transcriptase.
B. Low stringency allows more binding, not none.
D. DNA probes hybridize with DNA.
E. Denaturation is reversible, and strands can renature.

Question 248
A 30-year-old man has a point mutation in the third position of a codon, but his protein is completely normal. Which of the following properties of the genetic code explains why many mutations like this have no effect?

Difficulty: Easy

Question 281
A 58-year-old man has a myocardial infarction, and cardiac muscle cells die in the blocked region. Their membranes rupture early, and inflammation follows. Which of the following best describes how this form of cell death differs from apoptosis?

Question 289

Question 290
A 50-year-old woman with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer takes tamoxifen. The estrogen receptor binds DNA using a motif in which cysteine and histidine coordinate a metal ion. Which of the following identifies this motif and how tamoxifen works?

Question 310

Question 313
A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with cancer and found to carry a germline tumor suppressor mutation inherited from her father, who had cancer in his 30s. Her older sister, who doesn't carry the mutation, developed the same cancer at 68 after a lifetime of smoking. Which of the following best explains why the first woman developed cancer so much earlier?
A. She needed only one acquired hit to lose the gene's function
B. Germline mutations can't be repaired, so cancer always develops
C. Her mutation made the gene product hyperactive in every cell
D. Her mutation activated an oncogene that needs only one copy
E. Her sister's cancer needed three hits, while hers needed two
Answer: A. She needed only one acquired hit to lose the gene's function
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Tumor suppressor genes and the two-hit model
Why this is correct:
In the two-hit model, both copies of a tumor suppressor must be lost. Inheriting one defective copy means only one more hit is needed.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. A germline mutation raises risk but doesn't guarantee cancer.
C. Tumor suppressor mutations inactivate the gene.
D. The gene is a tumor suppressor, not an oncogene.
E. Sporadic tumor suppressor loss needs two hits, not three.

Reference: Chromosomal translocations in cancer
Why this is correct:
A translocation between non-homologous chromosomes makes two derivative (der) chromosomes, each named for the chromosome its centromere came from.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Telomeres don't determine the name.
B. Each derivative gets its own name.
C. Breakpoint genes don't name the chromosome.
D. Piece size doesn't determine the name.

Question 365
A 44-year-old man with an aggressive lymphoma containing about 10^9 tumor cells starts a regimen that kills 99% of the tumor cells present with each cycle. After the first cycle, about 10^7 cells remain. Which of the following would the next identical cycle be expected to kill?

Question 380
A 38-year-old man has a first-time seizure, and MRI shows a non-enhancing left frontal mass. The tumor is removed and is a slowly growing brain tumor with a mutation in isocitrate dehydrogenase. Which of the following does the mutant enzyme produce, and what's its effect?

Question 381
A 57-year-old man has a colon adenocarcinoma removed, and his tumor cells are grown in culture for a research study. They keep dividing well past the number of divisions normal cells can make, and their chromosome ends aren't shortening. Which of the following enzymes is most likely overexpressed?

Answer: D. Telomerase

Difficulty: Easy

Question 385
A 24-year-old man with relapsed B-cell ALL has his own T cells collected, engineered to recognize his cancer cells, and infused back. Reference: CAR-T and TIL therapy

Why the other answers are wrong:

B. CAR-T is used for liquid cancers.
D. His own cells don't cause graft-versus-host disease.
E. Tumor-derived lymphocytes describe TIL therapy.

Reference: TLR signaling and NF-kappa-B defects
Why this is correct:

Question 429
A 3-year-old boy is being evaluated for recurrent infections, and his immunologist reviews T cell maturation in the thymus. An immature double-positive T cell whose receptor recognizes self-peptide on MHC class I is selected to survive. Which of the following happens to that cell?
A. It keeps both CD4 and CD8
B. It loses CD4 and becomes a CD8 T cell
C. It becomes a B cell
D. It loses CD8 and becomes a CD4 T cell
E. It's eliminated by negative selection
Answer: B. It loses CD4 and becomes a CD8 T cell
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Lymphocyte development and selection
Why this is correct:
In positive selection, double-positive cells that recognize MHC class I lose CD4 and become CD8 T cells, while those recognizing MHC class II lose CD8 and become CD4 T cells.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Mature T cells are single positive.
C. T cells don't become B cells.
D. This happens with MHC class II recognition.
E. It was selected to survive.
Objective: Describe the cellular and molecular mechanisms that enable the immune system to recognize and produce specific effector responses to a diverse repertoire of pathogens (CBO 1.1)

Question 430
A 2-day-old boy has tetany and a seizure. He has a cleft palate, low-set ears, and an interrupted aortic arch. His serum calcium is very low, chest x-ray shows no thymic shadow, and flow cytometry shows no functional T cells. Which of the following treatments addresses his immune defect?
A. Thymus transplant
B. Eculizumab
C. Lifelong antifungals
D. Physical therapy
E. Antibody replacement
Answer: A. Thymus transplant
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: DiGeorge syndrome and APECED
Why this is correct:
DiGeorge anomaly comes from 22q11.2 deletions (CATCH-22). In complete DiGeorge, there's no thymus and no functional T cells, and treatment is thymus transplant.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Eculizumab treats PNH.
C. Antifungals don't restore T cells.
D. Physical therapy doesn't address immunity.
E. His problem is T cells, not antibody.

Question 431
A 60-year-old man with multiple myeloma has a serum electrophoresis showing a large amount of a single antibody. Each antibody has two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds. Which of the following identifies the part that binds antigen and what determines the antibody's class?
A. The N-terminal variable region binds antigen, and the heavy chain type determines class
B. The Fc region binds antigen, and kappa versus lambda determines class
C. The N-terminal variable region binds antigen, and the light chain determines class
D. The hinge region binds antigen, and the J chain determines class
E. The C-terminal constant region binds antigen, and the light chain determines class
Answer: A. The N-terminal variable region binds antigen, and the heavy chain type determines class
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Antibody structure
Why this is correct:
The antigen-binding site is the variable region at the N terminus of the heavy and light chains, and the heavy chain (gamma, alpha, mu, epsilon, delta) determines class.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The Fc region binds receptors, not antigen.
C. The light chain doesn't set class.
D. The hinge gives flexibility, and the J chain links polymers.
E. The constant region doesn't bind antigen.

Question 432
A laboratory preparing an antivenom digests IgG antibodies with papain, wanting fragments that can bind the venom but lack the Fc region. Which of the following does papain digestion produce?
A. Two heavy chains and two light chains
B. One Fab and two Fc fragments
C. One F(ab')2 fragment and a degraded Fc
D. Four identical Fab fragments
E. Two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment
Answer: E. Two Fab fragments and one Fc fragment
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Papain and pepsin antibody fragments
Why this is correct:
Papain cuts above the disulfide link between heavy chains, giving two antigen-binding Fab fragments and one Fc fragment. Pepsin cuts below it, giving one F(ab')2 and a degraded Fc.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Papain cleaves rather than just separating chains.
B. There are two Fab fragments and one Fc.
C. This is the pepsin result.
D. Each IgG has only two Fab arms.

Question 433

Question 434
A researcher explains that the T cell receptor resembles the antigen-binding arm of an antibody, with two chains that each have one variable and one constant region. Which of the following T cell receptor chains corresponds to the antibody heavy chain?

B. The alpha chain
C. The beta chain

Answer: C. The beta chain
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: T cell receptor structure
Why this is correct:
TCRs are alpha-beta (or gamma-delta) dimers; the alpha chain is analogous to the light chain and the beta chain to the heavy chain.
Why the other answers are wrong:

B. The alpha chain corresponds to the light chain.
D. Kappa is an antibody light chain.
E. CD3 transduces the signal but isn't a TCR chain.

Question 436
A 5-month-old girl has recurrent thrush, chronic diarrhea, and Pneumocystis pneumonia. Flow cytometry shows no T or B cells, but NK cells are present.
