Question 437
A 3-month-old boy is admitted with a red, scaly rash over his whole body, diarrhea, and poor weight gain. He has hair loss, enlarged nodes, and hepatosplenomegaly, and his CBC shows marked eosinophilia. His parents are first cousins, and testing shows partial RAG function. B. Chediak-Higashi syndrome

E. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Answer: C. Omenn syndrome

Difficulty: Easy

Question 438
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because she has become increasingly unsteady over 2 years. Question 440
A 14-year-old boy with seasonal allergies has a high serum IgE and positive skin tests for pollen. His B cells first made IgM and IgD, but under cytokine direction they began making IgE with the same antigen specificity. Which of the following explains how this happens?
A. VDJ is joined to a new heavy chain constant gene, and the DNA between is looped out
B. The heavy chain transcript is alternatively spliced
C. The light chain switches from kappa to lambda
D. A new V(D)J recombination creates a new variable region
E. The constant gene is mutated and the VDJ is replaced
Answer: A. VDJ is joined to a new heavy chain constant gene, and the DNA between is looped out
Order: First
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Class switching
Why this is correct:
In class switching, cytokines direct the B cell to join its VDJ to a different heavy chain constant gene after the intervening DNA is looped out, so specificity stays the same.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Alternative splicing makes IgM and IgD together, not IgE.
C. Light chain type doesn't set class.
D. A new variable region would change specificity.
E. The VDJ stays the same.

Question 441
A 6-month-old breastfed girl is brought for a well visit and has never had a diarrheal illness. An antibody in her mother's milk coats her gut lining and keeps bacteria and viruses from attaching to intestinal cells. Which of the following antibodies does this?

D. IgE

Answer: C. Dimeric IgA
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy

Blocking pathogens from attaching to their receptors is a function unique to IgA, and dimeric IgA joined by the J chain protects mucosal surfaces.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 6 / Antibody Function
Question 443
A healthy 3-day-old boy born at 39 weeks has a serum IgG level higher than his mother's. Which of the following receptors explains this?
A. FcRn, which transports maternal IgG across the placenta
B. CR1 on red cells, which carries IgG to the fetus
C. FcεRI, which transports IgE and IgG to the fetus
D. The J chain, which transports IgA and IgG to the fetus

Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Opsonization, Fc receptors, and FcRn

FcRn (the Brambell receptor) protects IgG from degradation and actively transports maternal IgG across the placenta, so a baby's IgG can exceed the mother's.
Why the other answers are wrong:

C. FcεRI binds IgE on mast cells.
D. The J chain links IgA and IgM.
E. The newborn's own IgG production is minimal.

Question 444
A 60-year-old woman with lymphoma is treated with a monoclonal antibody that binds a protein on her tumor cells. NK cells recognize the bound antibody through their Fc receptors, and crosslinking of these receptors kills the tumor cells by apoptosis. Which of the following names this mechanism and the antibody subclasses that best support it?

B. Neutralization, supported by IgA

Difficulty: Easy

Question 445
A 29-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of joint pain, a facial rash, and foamy urine. Her urine shows protein and red cell casts, her ANA is positive, and C3 and C4 are low. Normally, circulating immune complexes are tagged with complement, bind a receptor on red cells, and are cleared in the spleen and liver. Question 451

Foundations of Medicine / Week 6 / T Cell Receptors & the MHC
Question 453
A 48-year-old man receives a deceased-donor kidney. Minutes after the vessels are connected, the kidney turns mottled and dark, and biopsy shows widespread thrombosis. A clerical error is found: the kidney was ABO incompatible. Which of the following types of rejection is this?
A. Chronic rejection
B. Hyperacute rejection
C. Graft-versus-host disease
D. Acute rejection
E. Type IV hypersensitivity
Answer: B. Hyperacute rejection
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Transplant matching and rejection
Why this is correct:
Hyperacute rejection is antibody mediated, happens within minutes, and causes massive thrombosis from ABO mismatches or other preformed antibodies; ABO antigens are on graft endothelium.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Chronic rejection develops over months to years.
C. GVHD comes from donor T cells.
D. Acute rejection develops over days to months.
E. Type IV reactions are delayed.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 6 / T Cell Receptors & the MHC
Question 454
A 58-year-old woman who received a kidney transplant 6 years ago has a creatinine that has risen slowly over 2 years. She has no fever or graft pain, and biopsy shows thickened, narrowed arteries in the graft. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Chronic rejection
B. Type I hypersensitivity
C. Graft-versus-host disease
D. Hyperacute rejection
E. Acute rejection
Answer: A. Chronic rejection
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Transplant matching and rejection
Why this is correct:
Chronic rejection develops over months to years and is marked by arteriosclerosis in the graft.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Type I reactions are immediate and IgE-mediated.
C. GVHD attacks the host, not the graft.

Question 468
A healthy 2-month-old girl receives a vaccine against Haemophilus influenzae type b in which the bacterial capsule sugar is linked to a protein. Which of the following best explains why the sugar is linked to a protein?

Difficulty: Medium

Why the other answers are wrong:

D. MHC molecules present peptides, not sugars.

Question 481
A 3-month-old boy with a known 22q11 deletion has a lymph node biopsy during evaluation for recurrent infections. He had heart surgery at 2 weeks and takes calcium supplements. The node's follicles look normal, but the zone between the follicles and the medulla is nearly empty. Which of the following identifies the depleted zone and the reason?
A. The paracortex, because T cells are absent
B. The cortex, because B cells are absent
C. The germinal centers, because B cells can't class switch
D. The subcapsular sinus, because lymph can't enter
E. The medulla, because plasma cells are absent
Answer: A. The paracortex, because T cells are absent
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Lymph node structure and circulation; DiGeorge syndrome and APECED
Why this is correct:
The paracortex is the T cell zone with high endothelial venules, and in DiGeorge syndrome T cells are absent, so it looks empty.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The cortical B cell follicles look normal.
C. Class switching isn't the defect here.
D. Lymph entry isn't impaired.
E. The medulla holds plasma cells, which aren't the missing cells.

Question 482
A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, anxiety, and tingling in her hands 2 days after starting phenobarbital for seizures, and she has been dieting heavily. Pulse is 118/min, blood pressure is 152/96 mm Hg, her abdomen is soft, and her urine turns dark red in light. Which of the following most directly addresses the cause of her attack?
A. Iron supplementation
B. Phlebotomy
C. Low-dose chloroquine
D. IV hemin and glucose to suppress ALA synthase
E. Beta-carotene
Answer: D. IV hemin and glucose to suppress ALA synthase
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Acute intermittent porphyria; Regulation of heme synthesis: ALAS1 vs. ALAS2
Why this is correct:
Acute intermittent porphyria is a PBG deaminase deficiency. Barbiturates use up heme and release feedback on ALAS1, so ALA and PBG build up. IV hemin restores feedback, glucose also inhibits ALAS, and the trigger should be stopped.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Iron doesn't suppress ALAS1.
B. Phlebotomy treats porphyria cutanea tarda.
C. Chloroquine treats porphyria cutanea tarda.
E. Beta-carotene treats erythropoietic protoporphyria.

Question 483

Question 485

Question 486
A 30-year-old man who has lived at high altitude for 6 months has a high hemoglobin and a high erythropoietin level. His marrow is making more heme, while his liver's heme production is unchanged. Which of the following explains the difference in heme regulation in the two tissues?
A. Marrow ALAS2 is driven by erythropoietin and controlled by iron through an IRE, while liver ALAS1 is inhibited by heme
B. Both are inhibited by heme
C. Marrow ALAS2 is induced by barbiturates
D. Both are controlled only by vitamin B6
E. Liver ALAS1 is driven by erythropoietin
Answer: A. Marrow ALAS2 is driven by erythropoietin and controlled by iron through an IRE, while liver ALAS1 is inhibited by heme
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Regulation of heme synthesis: ALAS1 vs. ALAS2
Why this is correct:
Hepatic ALAS1 is regulated by heme feedback so it can meet drug demands on P450. Erythroid ALAS2 isn't regulated by heme; EPO stimulates it, and iron controls its translation through an IRE.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. ALAS2 isn't regulated by heme feedback.
C. Barbiturates act on liver ALAS1.
D. B6 is a cofactor, not the regulator.
E. EPO acts on erythroid ALAS2.

Question 487
A 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis for 12 years comes to the clinic because of fatigue. Her joints have been flaring, and she has no bleeding. She has a mildly microcytic anemia; ferritin is high, TIBC is low, and serum iron is low. Oral iron hasn't helped. Which of the following explains why iron isn't reaching her red cell precursors?

B. High hepcidin closes ferroportin and traps iron in cells
C. She lacks intrinsic factor
D. She has a globin chain deletion
E. Low hepcidin increases iron absorption
Answer: B. High hepcidin closes ferroportin and traps iron in cells

Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Anemia of chronic disease; Iron studies in microcytic anemia

Why the other answers are wrong:

C. Intrinsic factor affects B12, not iron.
D. Thalassemia wouldn't cause this inflammatory iron pattern.
E. Hepcidin is high in inflammation.

Question 488
A 22-year-old man of Mediterranean descent has a CBC at a pre-employment physical. He feels well, and his father has a mild anemia that never responded to iron. B. These point to immune hemolysis.
C. These point to iron deficiency.

Question 490
A 58-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis comes to the clinic because of fatigue, numbness and tingling in both feet, and poor balance in the dark. A 27-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation who drinks several glasses of wine a day and hasn't taken her prenatal vitamin is tired but has no numbness or balance problems. Question 494
A 16-year-old girl comes to the emergency department with dark red urine and back pain 3 days after a sore throat and fever. She is pale and mildly jaundiced. Hemoglobin is low, LDH is very high, haptoglobin is undetectable, her urine contains free hemoglobin, and a week later her urine tubular cells stain for iron. A. Iron deficiency
B. A production failure
C. Intravascular hemolysis
D. Anemia of chronic disease
E. Extravascular hemolysis
Answer: C. Intravascular hemolysis
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy

Why this is correct:
In intravascular hemolysis, cells burst in vessels, causing hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and later hemosiderinuria, and haptoglobin falls to near zero.

B. Production failure doesn't raise LDH.
D. Chronic disease doesn't cause hemolysis.
E. Extravascular hemolysis causes spherocytes without hemoglobinuria.

Question 495
A 12-year-old boy comes to the clinic because of intermittent yellow eyes and right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals. His father had his spleen removed as a teenager. Question 501
A 28-year-old woman of Southeast Asian descent and her husband come for preconception counseling. She has a mild microcytic anemia with normal ferritin, and genetic testing shows two alpha-globin genes deleted on the same chromosome (--/αα). Her husband has the same finding. Which of the following explains why this genotype is more concerning for their children than deletions on opposite chromosomes?
A. Trans deletions carry the higher risk
B. A cis deletion plus her husband's could leave a child with no alpha genes
C. A cis deletion causes sickle cell disease
D. A cis deletion always causes HbH disease in the carrier

Answer: B. A cis deletion plus her husband's could leave a child with no alpha genes
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Alpha-thalassemia
Why this is correct:
Cis deletions (common in Asians) are inherited as a unit, so a child can get two empty chromosomes (--/--), producing Hb Barts and hydrops fetalis. Trans deletions (-α/-α) can't do this.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Trans deletions can't produce --/--.
C. Sickle cell is a beta-globin mutation.

A. Glutamic acid to valine at position 6
B. Glutamic acid to lysine at position 26
C. Glutamic acid to lysine at position 6 of beta-globin
D. Deletion of three alpha genes
E. A point mutation reducing beta-globin production
Answer: C. Glutamic acid to lysine at position 6 of beta-globin
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: HbS, HbC, and HbE variants
Why this is correct:
HbC is a glutamic acid to lysine substitution at position 6 of beta-globin ("HbC = LyCine"), causing mild anemia, splenomegaly, and rectangular crystals.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Glu6Val is HbS.
B. Glu26Lys is HbE.
D. Three alpha deletions cause HbH.
E. Reduced production is beta-thalassemia.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 7 / Hemoglobinopathies
Question 506
An 8-month-old boy whose family recently moved from Nigeria is brought to the clinic because his hands and feet have been swollen and painful for 2 days. He didn't have a newborn screen and was healthy until recently. He's pale with a temperature of 38.0°C (100.4°F), and electrophoresis shows HbS and HbF with no HbA. Which of the following explains why he was well until now?
A. Maternal antibodies prevented sickling
B. The mutation was acquired after birth
C. Fetal hemoglobin, which has no beta chains, protected him until it declined
D. HbA2 protected him in infancy
E. His spleen protected him until it infarcted
Answer: C. Fetal hemoglobin, which has no beta chains, protected him until it declined
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Hemoglobin switching; Sickle cell disease
Why this is correct:
HbF has no beta chains and inhibits polymerization, so beta-chain disorders don't cause symptoms until HbF falls around 6 months; dactylitis is a common first sign.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Antibodies don't prevent sickling.
B. The mutation is inherited.
D. HbA2 is a minor adult hemoglobin.
E. The spleen doesn't prevent sickling.

Question 507
A 10-year-old girl with sickle cell disease comes to the emergency department with fatigue and pallor. A week ago she had fever and a runny nose, and her brother now has bright red cheeks. Question 511
A 7-year-old boy of Italian descent has needed monthly transfusions since 6 months of age. His skull x-ray has a hair-on-end appearance, and he has prominent cheekbones and upper jaw with hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following causes his bone changes?

Question 512
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of frequent nosebleeds and bruising since he started walking. His parents are first cousins. Question 514
A 17-year-old girl comes to the clinic because of periods heavy enough to soak a pad every hour and frequent nosebleeds, and she bled for 2 days after wisdom tooth removal. Question 516
A 64-year-old man has a coronary stent placed after a myocardial infarction. He's discharged on aspirin and a second antiplatelet drug that blocks the receptor platelets use to respond to released ADP. Which of the following drugs is this?

Question 523
A 67-year-old man hospitalized after a hip replacement is started on IV heparin for a DVT. On day 7, his platelet count has fallen by more than half, and his other leg is swollen with a new clot. A 48-year-old woman whose mother had recurrent clots is started on warfarin for a pulmonary embolism without heparin bridging. Question 560

Question 564
A 35-year-old woman returning from 3 weeks in Haiti without prophylaxis has uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria with 1% parasitemia. She's alert and can take oral medication, and because chloroquine sensitivity persists in the Caribbean, she's treated with chloroquine. Which of the following best explains how this drug kills the parasite?
A. It binds free heme and blocks heme polymerase, so toxic heme accumulates
B. It inhibits parasite dihydrofolate reductase
C. It kills hepatic hypnozoites
D. It generates reactive oxygen species through an endoperoxide bridge
E. It collapses the parasite's mitochondrial electron transport
Answer: A. It binds free heme and blocks heme polymerase, so toxic heme accumulates
Order: First
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Antimalarial drugs
Why this is correct:
The parasite turns toxic heme from digested hemoglobin into inert hemozoin. Chloroquine, quinine, mefloquine, and amodiaquine bind free heme and block that step, which also explains their cross-resistance.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Antifolates such as proguanil inhibit parasite DHFR.
C. Primaquine and tafenoquine kill hypnozoites.
D. Artemisinins work through an endoperoxide bridge.
E. Atovaquone collapses mitochondrial electron transport.

Question 568
A 27-year-old man who had his spleen removed after a motorcycle crash 3 years ago and never received the recommended vaccines comes to the emergency department with fever and chills for 8 hours. He's confused, his temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), his blood pressure is 80/44 mm Hg, and his white count is high. His peripheral smear is shown. A 60-year-old man on IV penicillin for endocarditis develops fatigue and dark urine on day 10. His hemoglobin has fallen, LDH and bilirubin are high, haptoglobin is low, and his platelets, PT, and PTT are normal. His smear is shown. Which of the following tests is needed to confirm the cause?
![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/52/Warm_autoimmune_hemolytic_anemia_blood_smear.jpg)
A. ADAMTS13 level
B. Direct Coombs test
C. G6PD level
D. Osmotic fragility
E. Indirect Coombs test
Answer: B. Direct Coombs test
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Direct and indirect Coombs tests; Warm vs. cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia
Why this is correct:
Penicillin can cause warm AIHA with spherocytes, and the direct Coombs test detects antibody on the red cells; the indirect test checks serum before transfusion.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. ADAMTS13 is tested in TTP.
C. G6PD testing looks for oxidative hemolysis.
D. Osmotic fragility can't separate AIHA from spherocytosis.
E. The indirect test checks serum.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of diagnostic radiology and be able to interpret the results of imaging studies, histopathologic exams and routine laboratory tests (CBO 2.4)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 7 / Hemolytic Anemias
Question 597
A 19-year-old college student with 2 weeks of sore throat, fever, swollen neck nodes, a palpable spleen, and a positive heterophile test now has fatigue and dark urine. His hemoglobin is low, bilirubin is high, haptoglobin is low, and his blood clumps on the slide at room temperature, as shown. Which of the following antibody classes is responsible?
![Blood smear on slide](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Cold_agglutinin_disease_-_macroscopic_agglutination_on_blood_smear.jpg)
A. IgG
B. IgA
C. No antibody is involved
D. IgE
E. IgM
Answer: E. IgM
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Warm vs. cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia
Why this is correct:
Cold AIHA is IgM that binds red cells in the cold, fixes complement, and causes agglutination; it's linked to Mycoplasma and mononucleosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. IgG causes warm AIHA.
B. IgA isn't the cause.
C. The agglutination is antibody-mediated.
D. IgE causes allergy.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 599
A 22-year-old man of Mediterranean descent has a routine CBC at a pre-employment physical. He feels well. Question 600
A 9-month-old boy whose family recently moved from Ghana, and who had no newborn screen, is brought to the clinic because his hands and feet have been swollen and painful for 2 days. Both parents have sickle cell trait. He's pale and febrile, with a high reticulocyte count and bilirubin. His smear is shown. Which of the following molecular changes explains these cells?

A. A spectrin mutation
B. Glutamic acid replaced by lysine at position 6
C. Deletion of three alpha-globin genes
D. Glutamic acid replaced by lysine at position 26
E. Glutamic acid replaced by valine at position 6 of beta-globin
Answer: E. Glutamic acid replaced by valine at position 6 of beta-globin
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Sickle cell disease; HbS, HbC, and HbE variants

Sickle cell disease comes from a GAG-to-GTG mutation replacing glutamic acid with valine at position 6 of beta-globin, and deoxygenated HbS polymerizes and distorts the cells.

Question 601
A 26-year-old woman of Southeast Asian descent has a mild microcytic anemia on prenatal screening, with normal ferritin and a normal HbA2. Her partner has similar blood counts, and they're counseled that their fetus could inherit a severe form. Her smear is shown. Which of the following is the genetic basis of her condition?

Difficulty: Hard

Question 603
A 16-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has had three admissions for pain crises this year and one episode of acute chest syndrome. His smear is shown, and he's started on a daily oral drug to reduce crises. Which of the following best explains how it helps?

Question 604
A 22-year-old man with sickle cell disease comes to the emergency department with a painful erection lasting 5 hours. Question 605
A 4-year-old girl with sickle cell disease who missed several doses of her penicillin prophylaxis this week is brought to the emergency department with a temperature of 39.5°C (103.1°F), a pulse of 150/min, and a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg. Her white count is high, her spleen isn't palpable, and her smear shows small nuclear remnants in some red cells. Which of the following explains why her fever is an emergency?
![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Sickle_Cell_Anemia_%285610746554%29.jpg)
A. Fever releases lead from bone
B. Functional asplenia puts her at risk from encapsulated organisms
C. Fever is never an emergency in children
D. She's at risk of malaria
E. Fever triggers TTP
Answer: B. Functional asplenia puts her at risk from encapsulated organisms
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Asplenia and Howell-Jolly bodies; Sickle cell disease
Why this is correct:
Repeated splenic infarction causes functional autosplenectomy, with Howell-Jolly bodies and the same infection risk as surgical asplenia, so fever is an emergency.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. She has no lead exposure.
C. Fever in asplenia is an emergency.
D. She has no malaria exposure.
E. Fever doesn't trigger TTP in sickle cell disease.

Question 606
A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of fever, confusion, and abdominal pain, and she has petechiae on her legs.
Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin: low
Platelets: very low
Creatinine: mildly high
Haptoglobin: undetectable
PT and PTT: normal
Her pregnancy test is negative, and her smear is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ee/Micrograph_of_schistocytes.jpg)
A. Transfuse platelets
B. Give FFP and cryoprecipitate for DIC
C. Start plasma exchange immediately
D. Wait for ADAMTS13 results
E. Start steroids alone for warm AIHA
Answer: C. Start plasma exchange immediately
Order: Third
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: TTP, HUS, and DIC; Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Why this is correct:
Schistocytes with low platelets, confusion, mild renal failure, and normal PT and PTT point to TTP. Plasma exchange should start without waiting for ADAMTS13, and platelets shouldn't be transfused.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Platelet transfusion can worsen TTP.
B. Her PT and PTT are normal.
D. Waiting delays life-saving treatment.
E. This isn't warm AIHA.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 7 / Hemostasis, Thrombosis & Bleeding Disorders
Question 607
A 34-year-old woman is diagnosed with TTP after presenting with fever, confusion, and low platelets, and her PT and PTT are normal. Her smear is shown, and her ADAMTS13 activity comes back very low. Which of the following explains how this deficiency causes her disease?
![Peripheral blood smear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ee/Micrograph_of_schistocytes.jpg)
A. Uncleaved vWF multimers form platelet microthrombi that shear red cells
B. Clotting factors are consumed and fibrin strands shear red cells
C. Red cells lack spectrin
D. Antibodies coat red cells
E. Platelets lack GpIb
Answer: A. Uncleaved vWF multimers form platelet microthrombi that shear red cells
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Why this is correct:
Without ADAMTS13, large vWF multimers aren't cleaved, platelets clump into microthrombi in small vessels, and passing red cells are sheared into schistocytes.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Factor consumption is DIC.
C. Spectrin defects cause spherocytosis.
D. Antibody coating is AIHA.
E. GpIb deficiency is Bernard-Soulier.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 608
A 62-year-old man admitted with sepsis from pneumonia is on norepinephrine and oozes from his IV sites on day 2. His hemoglobin and platelets are low, his creatinine is high, and his smear is shown. Which of the following findings separates his condition from TTP?

B. A positive Coombs test

D. Normal haptoglobin
E. Schistocytes

Difficulty: Easy
Reference: TTP, HUS, and DIC

Schistocytes appear in TTP, HUS, and DIC, but DIC consumes clotting factors, raising the PT, PTT, and D-dimer, while TTP has a normal PT and PTT.

C. Both lower platelets.
D. Haptoglobin is low in both.
E. Both show schistocytes.

C. Hairy cell leukemia is a separate disease.
E. This pace isn't typical of CLL.
Objective: Identify the etiology, pathophysiology, and pathology of specific hematological, problems and correlate them with clinical signs and symptoms (CBO 1.2)

Question 659
A 35-year-old man with falciparum malaria after a trip to Mozambique is alert with 1.5% parasitemia and normal creatinine and glucose. His smear is shown, and he starts artemether combined with lumefantrine. Which of the following explains why artemether is paired with a second drug?

Why the other answers are wrong:

A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV and a CD4 count of 130/μL has raised, violaceous plaques on his legs, trunk, and hard palate that have enlarged over 3 months, as shown. Biopsy shows sheets of proliferating endothelial spindle cells. Which of the following viruses is responsible?
![Clinical photo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3c/Kaposi%27s_Sarcoma.jpg)
A. EBV
B. HPV 6
C. CMV
D. HHV-6
E. HHV-8 (KSHV)
Answer: E. HHV-8 (KSHV)
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (HHV-8)
Why this is correct:
Kaposi sarcoma is a multicentric vascular tumor of endothelial spindle cells caused by HHV-8.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. EBV causes lymphomas.
B. HPV 6 causes warts.
C. CMV causes retinitis and colitis.
D. HHV-6 causes roseola.
Objective: Explain the molecular and genetic basis of oncogenesis and susceptibility to cancer (CBO 1.2)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 8 / HIV Treatment & Resistance
Question 760
A 34-year-old man with multidrug-resistant HIV for 15 years starts an injectable drug that resembles the C-helix of gp41 and blocks the conformational change needed for fusion. After a week he has red, itchy nodules at the injection sites. Which of the following drugs is this?
A. Ritonavir
B. Abacavir
C. Dolutegravir
D. Maraviroc
E. Enfuvirtide
Answer: E. Enfuvirtide
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: HIV entry inhibitors: maraviroc and enfuvirtide
Why this is correct:
Enfuvirtide is a fusion inhibitor that mimics the gp41 C-helix, is used in multidrug-resistant HIV, and causes injection-site reactions.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Ritonavir is a protease inhibitor.
B. Abacavir is an oral NRTI.
C. Dolutegravir is an integrase inhibitor.
D. Maraviroc blocks CCR5.
Objective: Describe the mechanisms of action of major classes of antimicrobial drugs and recommend appropriate antibiotic treatments for infectious diseases based on patient factors, pathogens involved, and pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drugs (CBO 1.4)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 8 / HIV Treatment & Resistance
Question 762
A 30-year-old man with HIV and hepatitis C starts a regimen that includes zidovudine. A month later he has fatigue, his hemoglobin has fallen with a high MCV, and his neutrophil count has dropped well below normal. Which of the following toxicities is this?
A. Bone marrow suppression
B. Bone density loss
C. Injection-site reactions
D. Stevens-Johnson syndrome
E. Hypersensitivity
Answer: A. Bone marrow suppression
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: NRTIs and NNRTIs
Why this is correct:
NRTIs are chain terminators, and zidovudine, a thymidine analog lacking the 3' OH, causes bone marrow suppression.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. Tenofovir (TDF) causes bone loss.
C. Enfuvirtide causes injection-site reactions.
D. SJS isn't zidovudine's main toxicity.
E. Abacavir causes hypersensitivity.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 8 / Pathology of Cell Injury & Death
Question 766
A 70-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension dies 3 days after a large myocardial infarction. At autopsy, some heart muscle cells have small, dense, shrunken nuclei, others have fragmented nuclei, and some have none. Which of the following is the correct order of these nuclear changes?
A. Karyorrhexis, then pyknosis, then karyolysis
B. Koilocytosis, then syncytium
C. Pyknosis, then karyorrhexis, then karyolysis
D. Karyolysis, then pyknosis, then karyorrhexis
E. Hydropic degeneration, then fatty change
Answer: C. Pyknosis, then karyorrhexis, then karyolysis
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Reversible vs. irreversible cell injury
Why this is correct:
Irreversible injury shows pyknosis (shrinkage), then karyorrhexis (fragmentation), then karyolysis (dissolution), while the cytoplasm turns deep pink.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Pyknosis comes first.
B. These are viral cytopathic effects.
D. Karyolysis comes last.
E. These are reversible changes.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 8 / Pathology of Cell Injury & Death
Question 767
A 58-year-old man from Haiti who lived in the United States for 20 years, with a small calcified nodule on an old chest x-ray, dies of an unrelated cause. At autopsy, the lung has the subpleural lesion shown, with soft, white, cheese-like dead tissue and, on histology, amorphous pink debris surrounded by granulomas. Which of the following conditions is classically associated with this type of necrosis?
![Gross specimen](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b5/Tuberculosis_-_Sub-pleural_primary_%28Ghon%29_focus_%286596011395%29.jpg)
A. Stroke
B. Pancreatitis
C. Hypertension
D. Myocardial infarction
E. Tuberculosis
Answer: E. Tuberculosis
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Types of necrosis
Why this is correct:
Caseous necrosis produces soft, white, cheese-like material without tissue architecture, surrounded by granulomas, and it's classically seen in tuberculosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Stroke causes liquefactive necrosis.
B. Pancreatitis causes fat necrosis.
C. Hypertension causes fibrinoid necrosis.
D. Infarction causes coagulative necrosis.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of diagnostic radiology and be able to interpret the results of imaging studies, histopathologic exams and routine laboratory tests (CBO 2.4)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 8 / Pathology of Cell Injury & Death
Question 768
A 64-year-old man who smoked dies 2 days after a large myocardial infarction from an LAD occlusion. A section of his heart shows deeply eosinophilic muscle fibers that have lost their nuclei but keep their outlines. Which of the following types of necrosis is this?
![Histology section](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/48/Histopathology_of_coagulative_necrosis_of_cardiomyocytes.jpg)
A. Liquefactive necrosis
B. Fat necrosis
C. Coagulative necrosis
D. Fibrinoid necrosis
E. Caseous necrosis
Answer: C. Coagulative necrosis
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Types of necrosis
Why this is correct:
Coagulative necrosis keeps cell outlines early because acidosis denatures proteins, and it follows arterial occlusion in the heart, kidney, liver, and spleen.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Liquefactive necrosis occurs in the brain.
B. Fat necrosis occurs in pancreatitis.
D. Fibrinoid necrosis occurs in vessel walls.
E. Caseous necrosis occurs in TB.
Objective: Explain principles and rationales for use of diagnostic radiology and be able to interpret the results of imaging studies, histopathologic exams and routine laboratory tests (CBO 2.4)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Cocci
Question 769
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with fever, vomiting, and a diffuse red rash that started yesterday. She is on the third day of her period and has been using high-absorbency tampons. She takes an oral contraceptive. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 132/min, and blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg. She has a sunburn-like rash over her trunk and palms. Blood cultures are negative, but a vaginal swab grows the organism shown in the Gram stain below, which is coagulase positive. How does this organism's toxin cause her shock? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/24/Gram_Positive_Cocci_in_singles%2C_pairs_and_clusters.jpg" alt="Gram stain">
A. The toxin inactivates elongation factor 2
B. The toxin raises cGMP in the gut
C. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release
D. The toxin is lipooligosaccharide from the outer membrane
E. The toxin is a superantigen that binds MHC II and raises IL-2
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by TSST-1, a superantigen toxin of Staphylococcus aureus, a coagulase-positive gram-positive coccus in clusters. The toxin binds MHC II and increases IL-2.

Why this is correct: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A strep) is a gram-positive coccus in chains that causes pharyngitis, erysipelas, cellulitis, and scarlet fever. M protein is its major virulence factor.

Question 772
A 3-day-old boy develops fever, poor feeding, and lethargy. He was born at 38 weeks by vaginal delivery after 20 hours of ruptured membranes. His mother had no prenatal care in the third trimester. Question 779
A 42-year-old rancher comes to the physician because of a sore on his forearm that started as a small bump 6 days ago. He recently skinned a cow that had died suddenly. He takes no medications. C. Pneumolysin

E. TSST-1

Why this is correct: Cutaneous anthrax comes from contact with infected animal tissue and causes a malignant pustule with painful adenopathy. Question 780
A 20-year-old college student comes to the emergency department with intense vomiting that started 2 hours after eating leftover fried rice from a restaurant. B. A toxin inactivates elongation factor 2

Why this is correct: Bacillus cereus causes food poisoning linked to fried rice. Its heat-stable toxin causes vomiting and raises cGMP, and its heat-labile toxin causes diarrhea and raises cAMP.

Question 781

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 785
A 62-year-old man is admitted with fever and hypotension from a urinary source. He has diabetes and takes insulin. Temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), and blood pressure is 80/44 mm Hg. Blood cultures grow a gram-negative rod that ferments glucose, reduces nitrate to nitrite, and is oxidase negative. His lactate is 5.4 mmol/L, and his WBC is 21,000/mm³. Urinalysis shows many white cells. Which component of this organism mainly drives his shock?
A. M protein
B. Pneumolysin
C. TSST-1
D. Exotoxin A
E. Endotoxin
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Enterobacteriaceae (including E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Serratia, Enterobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia) are facultative anaerobes that ferment glucose, reduce nitrate, and lack cytochrome c oxidase. Endotoxin, released more during rapid growth and lysis, is the major cause of septic shock.

Question 787
A 58-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted with high fever, cough, and thick, bloody sputum. He drinks a liter of vodka daily. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), and he has crackles over the right upper lobe. Sputum grows a non-motile gram-negative rod that ferments glucose and is oxidase negative, with large mucoid colonies from a thick capsule. His WBC is 19,400/mm³. Chest x-ray shows right upper lobe consolidation with a bulging fissure. Which organism is most likely?
A. Proteus mirabilis
B. Haemophilus influenzae
C. Pseudomonas aeruginosa
D. Streptococcus pneumoniae
E. Klebsiella pneumoniae
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Klebsiella pneumoniae is an Enterobacteriaceae member that is non-motile with a thick capsule.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 788
A 40-year-old man is admitted with burns over 35% of his body after a house fire. On day 8, his burn wounds develop a blue-green exudate with a sweet, grape-like odor. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). Culture grows an aerobic gram-negative rod that is oxidase positive. He is on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Which toxin from this organism inactivates elongation factor 2?
A. Elastase
B. Exoenzyme S
C. TSST-1
D. Heat-stable toxin
E. Exotoxin A
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod from soil and water with a blue-green pigment and grape-like odor. Exotoxin A inactivates EF-2, elastase and alkaline protease destroy the cornea, and exoenzyme S impairs phagocytosis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 789
A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of burning with urination and a thick yellow discharge from his penis for 3 days. He had a new sexual partner 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). A Gram stain of the discharge looks like the image below, and the organism ferments glucose but not maltose. He has no rash or joint pain, and HIV testing is negative. His urinalysis shows many white cells. Which treatment is recommended? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/87/Neisseria_gonorrhoeae_PHIL_3693_lores.jpg" alt="Gram stain of urethral discharge">

D. Oral ciprofloxacin

Answer: A
Why this is correct: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus that ferments glucose only and has LOS and pili but no capsule. It's treated with parenteral ceftriaxone, and it has chromosomal resistance to other drugs.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 790
An 18-year-old college freshman is brought to the emergency department with fever, headache, and a spreading purple rash that began this morning. He lives in a dormitory. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 136/min, and blood pressure is 74/40 mm Hg. He has neck stiffness and oozing from IV sites. CSF shows gram-negative diplococci that ferment both glucose and maltose. He dies of shock, and autopsy shows adrenal hemorrhage. What is the name of this complication?
A. Hemolytic uremic syndrome
B. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
C. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
D. Weil disease
E. Toxic shock syndrome
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Neisseria meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus that ferments glucose and maltose and has a capsule, LOS (lipid A is the toxic part), and pili. Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is DIC and shock.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 791
An unvaccinated 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with high fever, drooling, a muffled voice, trouble swallowing, and breathing distress. A. Serogroup B vaccine
B. Quadrivalent meningococcal vaccine
C. Pneumococcal vaccine
D. Tdap
E. Hib vaccine
Answer: E
Why this is correct: H. influenzae causes epiglottitis (the 4 Ds: dysphagia, dysphonia, drooling, and distress), and it's prevented by the Hib vaccine.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 792
A 20-month-old boy is brought to the physician because he refuses to walk and his right knee is swollen and warm. He had a cold with mouth sores last week. He attends daycare. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), and he holds his knee flexed. Joint fluid has many neutrophils, but routine cultures are negative. His WBC is 14,800/mm³, and his ESR is elevated. How is the most likely organism usually identified?
A. Darkfield microscopy
B. Regan-Lowe medium
C. PCR-based assays
D. India ink stain
E. Culture with X and V factors
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Kingella kingae is an oxidase-positive gram-negative coccobacillus that causes septic arthritis in toddlers, endocarditis, and osteoarticular infection. It has pili, a capsule, and a toxin, and PCR-based assays are used for diagnosis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 793
A 36-year-old man with AIDS comes to the physician because of fever, night sweats, diarrhea, and a 9-kg weight loss. He stopped his antiretrovirals a year ago. His CD4 count is 30/μL. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), and he has an enlarged liver and spleen and anemia. Blood cultures grow slow-growing organisms that are non-chromogens. A stain of the organisms is shown below. A. Clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol
B. Dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine
C. Amphotericin B and flucytosine
D. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone
E. Doxycycline alone
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Mycobacterium avium complex causes disseminated infection in AIDS with CD4 under 50, with fever, night sweats, diarrhea, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia. It's a slow-growing non-chromogen. Treatment is clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol, adding rifabutin if severe.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 794
A 55-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 2 years ago develops cough and fever for 3 weeks, followed by headache and new weakness in his right arm. He takes tacrolimus and prednisone. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Chest CT shows a lung nodule, and brain MRI shows an abscess. Sputum shows weakly acid-fast, filamentous branching organisms, shown below. Biopsy shows no granulomas. A. Toxoplasma gondii
B. Mycobacterium avium complex
C. Nocardia asteroides
D. Mycobacterium kansasii
E. Cryptococcus neoformans
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Nocardia is a gram-positive, weakly acid-fast organism with branching filaments. N. asteroides causes lung infections in immunocompromised patients and can spread to the brain as an abscess. It prevents phagosome acidification and fusion and doesn't form granulomas.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 795
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a painless, enlarging lump in her neck for 6 weeks. She is healthy otherwise, and her vaccines are up to date. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), and there's a firm 3-cm node in her neck. Culture of the node grows a slow-growing mycobacterium that makes yellow pigment even when grown in the dark. She has no fever, cough, or TB exposure. Her chest x-ray is normal. How is this organism classified?
A. A non-grower
B. A scotochromogen
C. A rapid grower
D. A photochromogen
E. A non-chromogen
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Scotochromogens, like M. scrofulaceum and M. gordonae, make pigment in the dark and are slow growers. Photochromogens, like M. kansasii and M. marinum, make pigment only with light.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 796
A 22-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis has worsening cough and weight loss despite her usual treatments. Her FEV1 has fallen to 48% of predicted. Chest CT shows nodules and bronchiectasis that resemble MAC disease. Sputum grows a mycobacterium that forms non-pigmented colonies within a week. She takes inhaled antibiotics and pancreatic enzymes. Her BMI is 17.8. Which organism is most likely?
A. Mycobacterium avium complex
B. Mycobacterium abscessus
C. Mycobacterium marinum
D. Mycobacterium kansasii
E. Mycobacterium leprae
Answer: B
Why this is correct: M. abscessus resembles MAC disease, comes from soil, dust, water, and animals, and is a non-pigmented rapid grower. Rapid growers also include M. chelonae and M. fortuitum.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 797
A 38-year-old man from Brazil comes to the physician because of a few pale, numb skin patches on his arm and trunk. He burned his hand on a stove without feeling it. He has thickened nerves at his elbow. Biopsy shows granulomas with very few acid-fast bacilli. His family has lived for generations in a rural area where armadillos are common. He has no fever. Which immune response explains this form of his disease?
A. An IgE-mediated response
B. No immune response
C. A weak TH1 and strong TH2 response
D. A complement deficiency
E. A strong TH1 response with IL-2 and IFN-γ
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Tuberculoid (paucibacillary) leprosy reflects a strong TH1 response with IL-2 and IFN-γ, causing granulomatous infection, nerve damage, and autoamputation. It's treated with dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 798
A 52-year-old man from rural India comes to the physician because of numb hands and feet and many skin nodules on his face and ears. He has lost his eyebrows, and his face looks thickened. Biopsy shows many acid-fast bacilli clustered in globi. He has no fever, and his CBC is normal. He has lost sensation in several fingers. Which immune response and treatment fit this form?
A. A strong TH2 response; amphotericin B
B. A strong TH1 response; clarithromycin and ethambutol
C. A strong TH1 response; dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine
D. A strong TH2 response; doxycycline alone
E. A strong TH2 response; dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Lepromatous (multibacillary) leprosy reflects a weak TH1 and strong TH2 response, with globi of acid-fast bacilli. It's treated with the triple regimen of dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine. M. leprae is found in armadillos.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 799

Why this is correct: Disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection occurs in patients with AIDS and CD4 under 50, or with genetic mutations in IFN-γ and IL-12.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 800
A 6-year-old girl from North Carolina is brought to the emergency department in June because of fever, headache, and a rash for 3 days. Her family went camping 10 days ago, and her mother removed a tick from her scalp. Temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F). The rash began on her wrists and ankles and spread to her trunk, as shown below. Platelets are 82,000/mm³, and ALT and AST are elevated. What is the most appropriate treatment? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d2/Rocky_Mountain_spotted_fever_PHIL_1962_lores.jpg" alt="Clinical photo">
A. Penicillin
B. Doxycycline
C. Supportive care only
D. Vancomycin
E. Ceftriaxone
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is caused by Rickettsia, obligate intracellular bacteria spread by ticks in spring and summer. The rash starts at the wrists and ankles and moves to the trunk, with thrombocytopenia and raised liver enzymes. Delay raises fatality, and treatment is doxycycline.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 801
A 45-year-old man who raises goats and drinks unpasteurized milk comes to the physician because of fevers that come and go over 6 weeks, drenching foul-smelling sweats, and lower back pain. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), and his liver and spleen are enlarged. He has tenderness over his sacroiliac joints. Blood and marrow cultures grow a gram-negative coccobacillus, and a Rose Bengal test is positive. His WBC is normal, and his ALT is mildly elevated. What is the treatment?
A. Doxycycline plus gentamicin
B. Penicillin G
C. Dapsone, rifampin, and clofazimine
D. Supportive care only
E. Doxycycline alone
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Brucellosis comes from infected animals, animal-derived food, inhalation, or skin abrasions. It causes undulating fever, night sweats, malodorous sweat, hepatosplenomegaly, sacroiliitis, and spondylitis. It's diagnosed by blood and marrow culture and the Rose Bengal test and treated with doxycycline plus gentamicin or doxycycline, rifampin, and ceftriaxone.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 802
A 50-year-old dairy farmer with untreated brucellosis for several months is brought in by his wife because he has become depressed and his personality has changed. He also has double vision. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F). He has a sixth nerve palsy. MRI shows meningeal enhancement and a small abscess. His CSF shows lymphocytes and a high protein. What is the diagnosis?
A. Toxoplasmosis
B. Neurobrucellosis
C. Rocky Mountain spotted fever
D. PML
E. Tetanus
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Neurobrucellosis causes cranial nerve palsies, personality change, depression, meningoencephalitis, brain abscess, and granuloma.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 803
A 55-year-old man from Missouri comes to the physician because of fever, headache, and muscle aches for 5 days. He removed a tick after hiking 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). He has a faint petechial rash on his trunk. WBC is 2,800/mm³, platelets are 90,000/mm³, and liver enzymes are elevated. A blood smear shows clusters of organisms inside vacuoles of monocytes. He has no joint pain. His CSF is normal. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
A. Q fever; hydroxychloroquine alone
B. Human granulocytic anaplasmosis; doxycycline
C. Brucellosis; doxycycline and gentamicin
D. Rocky Mountain spotted fever; penicillin
E. Human monocytic ehrlichiosis; doxycycline
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Ehrlichia chaffeensis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that replicates in host cell vacuoles (Anaplasmataceae). It causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis with nonspecific symptoms, rare vasculitis, and a rash in about a third. It's treated with doxycycline.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 804
A 62-year-old woman from Wisconsin comes to the physician because of fever, chills, and muscle aches for 4 days after a tick bite. She has fewer GI symptoms and no rash. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). She has mild anemia, leukopenia with increased bands, and a platelet count of 88,000/mm³. A smear shows clusters of organisms inside neutrophil vacuoles. A. Ehrlichia chaffeensis
B. Anaplasma phagocytophilum
C. Coxiella burnetii
D. Brucella
E. Rickettsia
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Anaplasma phagocytophilum causes human granulocytic anaplasmosis, with nonspecific symptoms, fewer GI symptoms, a rash in about 10%, mild anemia, leukopenia with bands, and low platelets. It's treated with doxycycline.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 805
A 40-year-old man who works in a slaughterhouse comes to the physician because of fever, headache, dry cough, and shortness of breath. Temperature is 39.4°C (103°F), but his pulse is only 72/min. He has crackles at both bases, and CT shows rounded densities with halo signs. WBC is low, and CRP, ALT, and AST are elevated. Echocardiogram shows a bicuspid aortic valve. He has no rash. His blood cultures are negative. What is the treatment?
A. Doxycycline alone
B. Ceftriaxone
C. Doxycycline plus gentamicin
D. Doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine
E. Supportive care only
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever in abattoir workers, spread by infected aerosols, raw milk, or ticks. It causes flu-like illness, pneumonia with rounded densities and halo signs, and relative bradycardia, and chronic infection can cause endocarditis. Without heart disease it's treated with doxycycline; with heart disease, doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 806
A 30-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, headache, and calf pain after a trip to Southeast Asia, where he waded through floodwater. He improved for a few days and then got worse. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). His eyes are red without discharge, and he is jaundiced. He coughs up blood. Darkfield microscopy of his blood shows highly motile spirochetes. His creatinine is elevated, and his platelets are 80,000/mm³. What is the treatment for his severe illness?
A. Dapsone
B. Supportive care only
C. Penicillin G or ceftriaxone
D. Doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine
E. Vancomycin
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Leptospirosis comes from rats and contaminated food, soil, or water, with organisms entering through skin defects. Weil disease is often biphasic, with jaundice, conjunctival suffusion, and pulmonary hemorrhage. Severe illness is treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone, and mild illness with doxycycline.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 807
A 28-year-old woman who works at a pet store comes to the physician because of fever, chills, headache, dry cough, and diarrhea for 5 days. Several birds at the store recently died. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). She has faint pink spots on her face, and chest x-ray shows lobar pneumonia. Sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils. Her WBC is normal, and her liver enzymes are mildly elevated. What is the treatment?
A. Penicillin G
B. Amphotericin B
C. Doxycycline
D. Doxycycline plus gentamicin
E. Supportive care
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Psittacosis is caused by Chlamydophila psittaci from parrots and other birds. Poultry workers, veterinarians, pet store workers, and bird owners are at risk. It causes fever, dry cough, diarrhea, facial rash (Horder spots), and lobar pneumonia, and it's treated with doxycycline, or azithromycin in children.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 808
A 35-year-old man from New Mexico is admitted with fever, muscle aches, and sudden cough and shortness of breath. Last week he cleaned out a cabin full of mouse droppings. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 80%. Platelets are 60,000/mm³, and chest x-ray shows bilateral pulmonary edema. His creatinine is normal. He has no rash. What is the treatment?
A. Supportive care
B. Amphotericin B
C. Ceftriaxone
D. TMP-SMX
E. Doxycycline
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas (Four Corners states) is spread by inhaling saliva, urine, or feces from white-footed mice. It causes fever, low blood pressure, cough, low platelets, pulmonary edema, and shock. Treatment is supportive.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 809
A 40-year-old man with HIV comes to the physician because of purple skin lesions on his legs that have grown over 3 months. He stopped his antiretrovirals a year ago. His CD4 count is 150/μL. He has several raised, violet plaques on his legs, as shown below, and similar lesions on his palate. He has no other symptoms. He has no fever or weight loss. His lymph nodes aren't enlarged, and he has no GI bleeding. C. Hantavirus
D. JC virus
E. Human herpesvirus 8

Why this is correct: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and involves skin, oral mucosa, and lymph nodes, with visceral involvement in about half. Stage T0 is treated with antiretrovirals alone, and stage T1 with antiretrovirals plus liposomal doxorubicin.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 810
A 36-year-old man with HIV who isn't taking antiretrovirals comes to the emergency department with a dry cough and shortness of breath on exertion for 3 weeks. His CD4 count is 110/μL, and he isn't on any prophylaxis. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), and oxygen saturation falls to 86% when he walks. Room air PaO2 is 62 mm Hg. B. TMP-SMX alone

E. TMP-SMX plus corticosteroids

Why this is correct: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia occurs with CD4 below 200 and shows ground-glass opacities. Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 811
A 45-year-old man with AIDS has headaches, a seizure, and new weakness in his left leg. He has been on toxoplasmosis treatment for 2 weeks without improvement. His CD4 count is 30/μL. E. Amphotericin B plus flucytosine
Answer: B
Why this is correct: CNS lymphoma causes headaches, seizures, and focal deficits with enhancing lesions and edema. It's associated with EBV, diagnosed by EBV PCR in CSF, and treated with radiation.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Beta-Lactam Antibiotics

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Other Cell Wall & Membrane Antibiotics
Question 814
A 52-year-old man with MRSA endocarditis is on daptomycin. He has type 2 diabetes and takes a statin. After 2 weeks he has muscle pain and weakness, and his CK is 8,400 U/L. He has no dark urine. His creatinine is normal. Which adverse effect of daptomycin is this?
A. Thrombocytopenia
B. Body fluid discoloration
C. Ototoxicity
D. Tooth discoloration
E. Rhabdomyolysis
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Daptomycin's main adverse effect is rhabdomyolysis. It works by forming cation channels that release potassium and cause rapid depolarization.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / DNA & RNA Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 815
A 40-year-old woman with a prosthetic joint infection is started on rifampin along with another antibiotic. She takes an oral contraceptive and warfarin. A week later her urine and tears are orange, and her INR has dropped. Her prosthetic joint was placed 2 years ago. Her liver enzymes are mildly elevated. Why is rifampin never used alone, and why did her INR drop?
A. Resistance develops with monotherapy, and rifampin induces CYP enzymes
B. It only works in urine, and it chelates warfarin
C. It's inactivated by surfactant, and it inhibits CYP enzymes
D. It causes tendon rupture, and it prolongs QT
E. It's too nephrotoxic, and it binds vitamin K
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Rifamycins inhibit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Rifampin has broad activity and penetrates biofilms but isn't used as monotherapy. Rifamycins induce CYP enzymes, causing drug interactions, and cause body fluid discoloration, hepatotoxicity, and flu-like symptoms.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / DNA & RNA Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 816

C. It covers only gram-positive organisms
D. It covers MRSA and anaerobes
E. It covers Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas but has poor gram-positive coverage
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Ciprofloxacin covers Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas but has poor gram-positive coverage. Levofloxacin adds strep coverage and has a long half-life.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Protein Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 818
A 62-year-old man with a VRE infection is on linezolid. He also takes sertraline for depression. After 2 weeks his platelets have fallen to 64,000/mm³, and he now has agitation, tremor, fever, and muscle rigidity. His VRE bacteremia has cleared. His creatinine is normal, and his lactate is mildly elevated. Which drug class is linezolid, and what explains his new symptoms?
A. A tetracycline; photosensitivity
B. A glycopeptide; infusion syndrome
C. An oxazolidinone; serotonin syndrome
D. A rifamycin; hepatotoxicity
E. A lincosamide; C. difficile infection
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Linezolid is an oxazolidinone that binds the 50S subunit to prevent translation. It covers staph, strep, Enterococcus, mycobacteria, and Nocardia. Toxicities include thrombocytopenia (around 2 weeks), neuropathy (around 4 weeks), lactic acidosis, serotonin syndrome, and rhabdomyolysis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 819
A 34-year-old man and his 32-year-old wife are evaluated for infertility after 18 months of trying to conceive. His semen analysis shows a normal count and motility, but electron microscopy shows that most sperm lack the cap-like sac over the front of the head. His wife's evaluation is normal. He takes no medications and doesn't smoke. His sperm swim toward the egg in vitro but can't penetrate its outer layer. Which structure is defective?
A. The acrosome
B. The zona pellucida
C. The mitochondrial sheath
D. The nucleus
E. The flagellum
Answer: A
Why this is correct: The acrosome is a sac of digestive enzymes needed to get through the zona pellucida. During the acrosome reaction, ZP-degrading enzymes are released and the sperm pushes through.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 820
A 30-year-old woman undergoes IVF after 2 years of infertility. She has endometriosis and takes no other medications. In the lab, freshly collected sperm are washed and incubated in a medium that removes cholesterol from their plasma membrane before being placed with her eggs. This step mimics what happens naturally in the female reproductive tract. Her husband's semen analysis is normal. Her AMH is normal, and her BMI is 23. What change follows cholesterol removal?
A. Motility decreases as the membrane stiffens
B. The cortical reaction occurs and blocks polyspermy
C. Calcium influx causes hyperactivated motility
D. The sperm nucleus decondenses and forms a pronucleus
E. The acrosome is lost immediately and the sperm dies
Answer: C
Why this is correct: During capacitation, secretions of the cervix and uterus remove cholesterol from the sperm membrane, which had inhibited motility and ZP3 receptor activation. Calcium then enters the sperm and hyperactivates motility.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 821
A 36-year-old woman undergoes IVF. She has one ovary after a cyst removal and takes no medications. After insemination, the embryologist sees that one sperm has fused with the egg membrane and that granules just under the egg surface have released their contents, making the outer layer impermeable to other sperm. Her husband's semen analysis is normal. Fifteen eggs were retrieved, and 12 were mature. What is the purpose of this response?
A. It triggers capacitation
B. It causes implantation
C. It starts compaction
D. It releases hCG
E. It blocks polyspermy
Answer: E
Why this is correct: In the cortical reaction, cortical granules are released and cross-link the zona pellucida so it becomes impermeable to more sperm, blocking polyspermy.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 822
A 33-year-old woman is undergoing egg retrieval for IVF. She has regular periods and no medical problems. The retrieved eggs are paused partway through a cell division that they finish only if a sperm fuses with them. Her AMH is normal, and her husband's semen analysis is normal. She has been taking injectable gonadotropins for 10 days. At which stage are they arrested, and what happens after fusion?
A. Metaphase II; the oocyte begins mitosis before the pronuclei form
B. Metaphase II; the oocyte completes meiosis II and the pronuclei fuse
C. Prophase I; the oocyte completes meiosis I and releases a polar body
D. Anaphase I; cleavage begins as soon as the membranes fuse
E. Telophase II; the zona dissolves and the pronuclei form
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Oocytes are arrested at metaphase II. After fusion with a sperm, the oocyte completes meiosis II, the male and female pronuclei decondense and fuse, and the first zygotic mitosis follows.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 823
A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with lower abdominal pain and vaginal spotting. Her last period was 7 weeks ago. She had pelvic inflammatory disease 3 years ago. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Her β-hCG is positive, and ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a mass in the left fallopian tube. Her pulse is 96/min, and her abdomen is mildly tender on the left. Normally, which structure keeps the zygote from implanting before it reaches the uterus?
A. The amnion
B. The chorion frondosum
C. The decidua capsularis
D. The zona pellucida
E. The acrosome
Answer: D
Why this is correct: The zona pellucida is the thick extracellular layer around the oocyte. It contains sperm receptors, cross-links to block polyspermy, and prevents premature implantation (ectopic pregnancy) as the zygote moves through the uterine tube. The trophoblast breaks down the ZP at about 5 to 6 days.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 824
A 35-year-old woman undergoing IVF is updated by the embryologist on day 3 after fertilization. She has diminished ovarian reserve and takes no other medications. Her embryo has divided into a loose cluster of small cells, which will soon form a smooth ball as cells form junctions with each other. Her husband is 38 and healthy. Six embryos were created, and four are developing normally. What is the smooth-ball stage called, and which junctions form?
A. A gastrula; desmosomes
B. A blastocyst; tight junctions only
C. A zygote; gap junctions
D. A compacted morula; adherens junctions
E. A bilaminar disc; adherens junctions
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Cleavage divisions divide the zygote into smaller blastomeres. The morula forms by about day 3 and undergoes compaction into a smooth ball as adherens junctions form between cells.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 825
A 31-year-old woman has a day-5 embryo transferred during IVF. She has tubal factor infertility. The embryo now has a fluid-filled cavity, an outer cell layer, and an inner ball of cells that will split into two populations. She had a laparoscopy that showed blocked tubes. Her husband's semen analysis is normal. She takes vaginal progesterone. Which population of the inner cells will form the embryo proper and the amniotic sac?
A. Hypoblast
B. Epiblast
C. Extraembryonic mesoderm
D. Trophoblast
E. Syncytiotrophoblast
Answer: B
Why this is correct: In the blastocyst, the inner cell mass splits into the epiblast, which forms the embryo proper and amniotic sac, and the hypoblast, which lies closest to the cavity and becomes the primary yolk sac. The trophoblast forms the fetal chorion.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 826
A 27-year-old woman takes a home pregnancy test 2 weeks after a missed period, and it's positive. She has regular cycles and takes no medications. Her physician confirms a serum β-hCG of 2,400 mIU/mL. Her pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. She has mild nausea in the mornings. Her BMI is 22. Which cells make the hormone this test detects, and what does the hormone do?
A. The epiblast; it forms the amnion and maintains the corpus luteum
B. The corpus luteum; it triggers ovulation and stimulates progesterone
C. The cytotrophoblast; it degrades the zona pellucida for implantation
D. The decidua basalis; it provides nutrients to the implanting embryo
E. The syncytiotrophoblast; it maintains the corpus luteum and its progesterone
Answer: E
Why this is correct: hCG is secreted by the multinucleated syncytiotrophoblast, is essential for pregnancy maintenance, and is the basis of pregnancy tests. It maintains the corpus luteum and stimulates progesterone. Implantation must have occurred for it to be measured.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 827
A 25-year-old woman is 3 weeks past conception. She is healthy and takes a prenatal vitamin. During the second week, channels form inside the invading outer trophoblast and fill with maternal blood and uterine gland secretions, allowing early exchange. Her vital signs are normal, and she has mild breast tenderness. What are these channels, and what circulation do they create?
A. The intervillous space; the umbilical circulation
B. The chorionic cavity; the amniotic circulation
C. Lacunae; the primitive uteroplacental circulation
D. Tertiary villi; the fetal circulation
E. Somites; the vitelline circulation
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Lacunar spaces form inside the syncytiotrophoblast and fill with maternal blood and glandular secretions as it erodes maternal vessels, creating the primitive uteroplacental circulation. The embryo initially gets nutrients by diffusion from this circulation.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 828
A 34-year-old woman is undergoing IVF for unexplained infertility. She takes no medications. Her husband's semen analysis is normal. Ten eggs were retrieved. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. About 18 hours after insemination, the embryologist photographs one of her eggs, shown, with two round structures in the center and a small cell pinched off at the edge. Fertilization has taken place. What happens next inside this cell? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1e/Zygote1.jpg" alt="Light micrograph of an egg">
A. The two pronuclei fuse, and the first mitosis follows
B. The acrosome reaction occurs, and the zona hardens
C. Capacitation begins, and cholesterol leaves the sperm
D. The embryo implants, and hCG production begins
E. The cells compact, and a morula forms
Answer: A
Why this is correct: After fusion, the oocyte completes meiosis II (releasing a polar body), and the male and female pronuclei decondense and fuse. The first zygotic mitosis follows.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 829
A 31-year-old woman undergoing IVF receives a photo of her embryo on day 3 after fertilization, shown. She has polycystic ovary syndrome and takes metformin. Her embryos were created by ICSI. Four of eight embryos reached this stage. She is 31 and has no other medical problems. Her husband's semen analysis is normal. What is the answer? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6b/Embryo%2C_8_cells.jpg" alt="Light micrograph of an embryo">
A. Trophoblast cells produced by gastrulation
B. Epiblast cells produced by meiosis
C. Blastomeres produced by cleavage divisions
D. Syncytiotrophoblast produced by fusion
E. Neural crest cells produced by delamination
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Cleavage divisions after fertilization are mitotic divisions that partition the zygote into increasingly smaller blastomeres. By about day 3 a loose cluster forms the morula, which then compacts.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 830
A 28-year-old woman has a frozen day-5 embryo, like the one illustrated, thawed and transferred. She has had one prior IVF cycle. The embryo must escape its protective shell before it can attach to the uterine wall, and its outer cells help it do this. Her endometrial lining is 11 mm. She takes vaginal progesterone and estradiol. She is 28 and healthy. What do the outer cells produce? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b7/Human_Blastocyst_%28NIH_BioArt_209_-_630577%29.png" alt="Illustration of an embryo">
A. Surfactant that lubricates the shell so the embryo slips out
B. Cortical granules that harden the shell so it cracks open
C. Sonic hedgehog that signals the shell to dissolve
D. Proteolytic enzymes that break down the zona pellucida
E. hCG that maintains the corpus luteum and softens the shell
Answer: D
Why this is correct: At about 5 to 6 days, the trophoblast begins producing proteolytic enzymes that break down the zona pellucida, which had prevented premature implantation in the uterine tube.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Germ Layers & Body Plan
Question 831
A 26-year-old woman is 3 weeks after conception. She takes a prenatal vitamin. During this week, epiblast cells migrate through a groove in a midline structure to create the three germ layers. Her vital signs are normal, and she has no bleeding. She works as an accountant. Which cells are the first to migrate through the groove, and what do they become?
A. They become endoderm, replacing the hypoblast
B. They become trophoblast, replacing the outer cell layer
C. They become ectoderm, replacing the epiblast
D. They become mesoderm, filling the space between the layers
E. They become the amnion, lining the amniotic cavity
Answer: A
Why this is correct: During gastrulation, epiblast cells migrate through the primitive groove. The first cells become endoderm and replace the hypoblast, the second become mesoderm, and cells that don't ingress become ectoderm.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Germ Layers & Body Plan
Question 832
A 4-year-old boy is evaluated for short stature and blurry vision. He has no other medical problems. MRI shows a mass arising from tissue that originally came from the roof of the mouth. This gland and his eye lens share the same germ layer. He has headaches, and his visual fields show a defect. His growth has slowed over the past year. His vaccines are up to date. Which germ layer is it?
A. Neural crest
B. Neural tube
C. Surface ectoderm
D. Endoderm
E. Paraxial mesoderm
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Surface (non-neural) ectoderm forms the epidermis, nails, hair, glands, the anterior pituitary, tooth enamel, and the lens and cornea.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Germ Layers & Body Plan
Question 833
A 3-day-old girl has a single central incisor, a narrow nasal bridge, and close-set eyes. MRI shows the forebrain didn't divide into two hemispheres. Her father has a single central incisor too. Genetic testing shows an inherited mutation in a signaling ligand normally secreted by the notochord. She was born at term to healthy parents. Her glucose is 42 mg/dL, and she has poor feeding. Her parents are 30 and 32. Which ligand is affected?
A. IDO1
B. Retinoic acid
C. Alpha-fetoprotein
D. hCG
E. Sonic hedgehog
Answer: E
Why this is correct: The notochord, derived from chordamesoderm, secretes sonic hedgehog, which helps specify the neural plate. Inherited mutations in sonic hedgehog can cause holoprosencephaly.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Germ Layers & Body Plan
Question 834
A 6-month-old boy is evaluated for chronic constipation and an absence of sweating on one side of his face. His parents are healthy. His sympathetic ganglia and the pigment cells of his dermis come from the same embryonic cell population, which migrates from the edges of the neural plate. He was born at term and is growing well. He has a drooping right eyelid and a small right pupil. Which population is it?
A. Intermediate mesoderm
B. Neural crest cells
C. Endoderm
D. Surface ectoderm
E. Neural tube
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Neural crest cells form at the lateral borders of the neural plate and migrate widely, forming sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, dermal pigment cells, and muscle and connective tissues.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Germ Layers & Body Plan
Question 835
A 29-year-old woman at 16 weeks' gestation has a maternal serum screen showing a markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein. She didn't take folic acid before conception. Ultrasound shows the fetus has no cranial vault above the orbits. She has no family history of birth defects and takes no medications. Her BMI is 32. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Failure of which structure to close caused this defect, and what is the prognosis?
A. The caudal neuropore; the condition is viable
B. The rostral neuropore; the brain is normal but outside the skull
C. The notochord; the condition is mild
D. The rostral neuropore; the condition is nonviable
E. The primitive streak; the condition is viable
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Neural tube defects come from incomplete neuropore closure and can be detected with ultrasound or AFP. Failure of the rostral neuropore causes anencephaly (absence of a major portion of brain and skull, nonviable), exencephaly, or encephalocele.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Germ Layers & Body Plan
Question 836
A 7-year-old girl is seen for a sports physical. She is healthy and takes no medications. On exam, there is a small tuft of dark hair over her lower back with no underlying mass. X-ray shows a gap in the posterior arch of L5, but skin fully covers it. Her neurologic exam is normal. Her reflexes and strength are normal, and she has no bladder or bowel problems. What is the diagnosis?
A. Anencephaly
B. Meningocele
C. Encephalocele
D. Spina bifida occulta
E. Myelomeningocele
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Spina bifida comes from failure of the caudal neuropore to close. In spina bifida occulta, skin covers the vertebral defect, and a tuft of hair is often present. A meningocele contains meninges and CSF, and a myelomeningocele contains spinal cord and nerves.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Germ Layers & Body Plan
Question 837
A 20-year-old man is evaluated for back pain after a fall. X-rays show normal vertebrae and ribs. These bones, along with the muscles and dermis of his back, came from blocks of mesoderm on either side of the notochord. He plays college football and takes no medications. He has mild tenderness over his lower back muscles. His neurologic exam is normal. Which mesoderm forms these blocks?
A. Intermediate mesoderm
B. Paraxial mesoderm
C. Visceral lateral plate mesoderm
D. Axial mesoderm
E. Somatic lateral plate mesoderm
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Paraxial mesoderm is organized into somites, which divide into sclerotome and dermomyotome. In the trunk it forms vertebrae, ribs, rib cartilage, back muscles, and back dermis; in the head it forms striated muscles of the face, jaw, and throat.

Why this is correct: Intermediate mesoderm differentiates into urogenital structures.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Germ Layers & Body Plan
Question 839

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Germ Layers & Body Plan
Question 840
A newborn girl is delivered at 38 weeks. Her intestines are outside her body through an opening to the right of a normal umbilical cord, with no covering membrane. Question 841
