Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 845
A 38-year-old woman is carrying a pregnancy as a gestational surrogate for a couple who used their own egg and sperm. She has had two healthy pregnancies of her own and takes a prenatal vitamin. The embryo transfer was done 10 weeks ago, and her ultrasound is normal. Her vital signs are normal. Which statement is correct?
A. Pregnancy causes global immunosuppression, so the antigens don't matter
B. Her own babies had two sets of foreign antigens, while this fetus has one
C. The fetus expresses no foreign antigens, so it is ignored like self
D. The fetus is handled like a transplanted organ, with the same rejection risk
E. The fetus has two foreign antigen sets; her own babies had one
Answer: E
Why this is correct: An embryo expresses maternal and paternal antigens, making it a semi-allograft. In surrogate pregnancy, the fetus expresses two sets of foreign antigens. The mother's immune system must not treat these as danger signals.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 846
A 34-year-old woman with recurrent early pregnancy loss is started on progesterone supplementation after ovulation. She has regular cycles and no other medical problems. Her progesterone prepares the uterus and also affects her immune cells. She has had three losses before 10 weeks. Her karyotype and her husband's are normal, and her thyroid tests are normal. B. It shifts the immune response from Th2 to Th1
C. It activates cytotoxic T cells against the placenta
D. It promotes the expansion and function of regulatory T cells
E. It transports IgG across the placenta to the fetus
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Progesterone rises with ovulation, prepares the uterus for implantation, and promotes the expansion and function of regulatory T cells.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 847
A 58-year-old man with metastatic melanoma is enrolled in a trial of indoximod. He had his primary tumor removed 2 years ago and has lung metastases. The drug blocks an enzyme some tumors use to hide from the immune system, the same enzyme the placenta uses during implantation. He has had fatigue and a cough. What does this enzyme do?
A. It degrades the zona pellucida and exposes the embryo
B. It oxidizes tryptophan and activates regulatory T cells
C. It produces hCG and maintains the corpus luteum
D. It activates NF-κB and starts inflammation
E. It transports IgG across the placenta to the fetus
Answer: B
Why this is correct: IDO1 catalyzes L-tryptophan oxidation, is needed for invasion into the endometrium, and is immunosuppressive through Treg activation, blocking conversion of Tregs into Th17-like cells. Some cancers make IDO1 to evade immunity, and IDO inhibitors like indoximod enhance anti-tumor responses.

Why this is correct: APS-1 (APECED) is caused by mutations in AIRE, the thymic library, which appears to be involved in tolerance to fetal antigens. More than 60% of women with APS-1 are affected by infertility or fetal loss.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 849
A newborn girl born at term has protective levels of IgG against measles and tetanus in her blood, matching her mother's antibodies. She is breastfeeding well. Her antibodies reached the baby before birth. She was born at 39 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her mother is fully vaccinated. Her own immune system hasn't yet made these antibodies. A. The ZP3 receptor
B. TLR4
C. The Brambell receptor (FcRn)
D. The IgA secretory component
E. CCR5
Answer: C
Why this is correct: The Brambell receptor (FcRn) actively transports maternal IgG across the placenta to the fetus. No mechanism protects the fetus from maternal pathologic autoantibodies.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 850
A 28-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy has blood type O negative. Her husband is O positive. Her first child was Rh positive, and she didn't receive any immune globulin after that delivery. Her antibody screen is now positive for anti-D. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, and her fetus is growing normally on ultrasound. What is the risk to this fetus, and how could it have been prevented?
A. Anti-RhD IgG can attack an Rh-positive fetus; RhoGAM after delivery
B. Risk of neural tube defects; folic acid before the next pregnancy
C. Risk only to the mother; RhoGAM now to protect her
D. Risk of hydatidiform mole; hCG monitoring in the next pregnancy
E. No risk, because IgG can't cross the placenta
Answer: A
Why this is correct: In Rh disease, an RhD-negative mother makes anti-Rh antibodies after delivering an RhD-positive infant. In later pregnancies, maternal anti-RhD crosses the placenta and attacks the fetus. RhoGAM (anti-RhD immune globulin) prevents this.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 851
A 26-year-old woman goes into labor at 39 weeks. She is healthy and takes a prenatal vitamin. Labor is a pro-inflammatory state driven by the innate immune system, and one trigger comes from the fetus's maturing lungs. Her contractions are every 3 minutes, and her cervix is 5 cm dilated. Her membranes are intact. Her pregnancy was uncomplicated, and the fetal heart rate is 140/min. What is that trigger?
A. Surfactant protein A activating TLR4, which drives NF-κB
B. IDO1 oxidizing tryptophan, which activates regulatory T cells
C. hCG activating regulatory T cells, which drive inflammation
D. FcRn transporting IgG, which activates the complement cascade
E. Estradiol shifting the response to Th2, which drives NF-κB
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Labor is a pro-inflammatory state initiated by the NF-κB pathway. One trigger is TLR4 activation by surfactant protein A from the fetal lung, and another is endogenous DAMPs.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 852
A 27-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation develops fever, muscle aches, and headache after eating soft unpasteurized cheese. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). Blood cultures grow a gram-positive rod. Her pulse is 108/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Fetal heart rate is 160/min. She has no other symptoms. Which group of infections is pregnancy listed as increasing maternal susceptibility to?
A. Influenza, measles, and hepatitis E
B. Rubella, CMV, and HSV
C. Group B strep only
D. All infections equally
E. Listeriosis, tuberculosis, and malaria
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Pregnancy increases maternal susceptibility to listeriosis, tuberculosis, and malaria. It increases severity of influenza, VZV, HSV, measles, hepatitis E, malaria, and others. Pregnancy doesn't cause global immunosuppression.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 853
A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation develops fever, cough, and shortness of breath during flu season. She didn't receive the influenza vaccine. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), and oxygen saturation is 91%. Her rapid influenza test is positive. Her pulse is 112/min, and respiratory rate is 26/min. She has crackles at both bases. She has asthma and uses an albuterol inhaler. Her fetal heart rate is 150/min. How does pregnancy affect this infection?
A. Influenza can't affect the fetus
B. Pregnancy increases the severity of influenza
C. Pregnancy protects against influenza
D. Pregnancy causes global immunosuppression
E. Influenza is a TORCH infection
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Pregnancy increases maternal severity of infections including H. influenzae, group A strep, pneumococcus, influenza, VZV, HSV, measles, hepatitis E, malaria, dengue, Lassa fever, and Ebola.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 854
A 32-year-old woman is 9 days past ovulation during an IVF cycle, and her embryo transfer was 4 days ago. She has had one prior miscarriage and takes vaginal progesterone. Three steps must happen for her embryo to implant, and the last step resembles something malignant cells do. She has regular cycles and takes estradiol and progesterone. Her blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg. Which sequence is correct?
A. Invasion, adhesion, then apposition
B. Adhesion, apposition, then invasion
C. Apposition, adhesion, then invasion
D. Compaction, cavitation, then hatching
E. Capacitation, acrosome reaction, then fusion
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Implantation has three steps. In apposition, the trophoblast contacts the progesterone-prepared endometrium, influenced by IL-1 and IL-6. In adhesion, the blastocyst attaches to the uterine epithelium with adhesion molecules. In invasion, stromal and immune cells produce inflammation (IL-6, IL-8, IL-15, GM-CSF, TNF, TGF-β), facilitated by hCG, similar to what malignant cells do.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities
Question 855
A 26-year-old woman comes for her first prenatal visit. The first day of her last menstrual period was 10 weeks ago, and she has regular 28-day cycles. She takes a prenatal vitamin. A. 6 weeks
B. 9 weeks
C. 12 weeks
D. About 8 weeks
E. 10 weeks
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Gestational age is measured from the first day of the last normal menstrual period, and pregnancy lasts 280 days (40 weeks). Embryonic age is measured from conception, which usually occurs about 14 days after the period starts, so it's about 2 weeks less.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities
Question 856

Why this is correct: In week 4, the rostral and caudal neuropores close, pharyngeal arches begin to form, the embryo has a C-shaped curve, upper and lower limb buds appear, and organ systems begin developing.

Question 857

Answer: B
Why this is correct: Weeks 5 to 8 establish all major organs and carry maximum susceptibility, and the organogenetic period (4 to 8 weeks) is when teratogens can produce major congenital anomalies.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities
Question 858

Why this is correct: The fetal period begins at 9 weeks. Between 9 and 12 weeks the urinary system becomes functional, and the external genitalia are distinguishable at 12 weeks.

Why this is correct: At 17 to 20 weeks, fetal movement (quickening) begins and vernix caseosa appears as a protective coating. The fetus is covered in lanugo hair, which lets the vernix adhere to the skin.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities
Question 860

Answer: A
Why this is correct: Surfactant production begins at 21 to 25 weeks. By 26 to 29 weeks, fetuses usually survive if born prematurely because the lungs are developed enough for gas exchange; the fetus practices breathing movements and the eyelids can open.

Why this is correct: Chorionic villus sampling biopsies trophoblastic tissue to detect chromosomal abnormalities and X-linked disorders and can be done sooner than amniocentesis, which samples amniotic fluid after 15 weeks.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities
Question 862
A newborn girl born at 37 weeks has both feet turned inward. Her mother had very low amniotic fluid for the last 8 weeks of pregnancy. The feet can be gently moved toward normal position. The rest of her exam is normal. Her kidneys are normal on ultrasound, and her chromosomes are normal. Her hips are stable. She weighs 2.8 kg, and her Apgar scores are 8 and 9. How is this birth defect classified?
A. A syndrome from a single underlying cause
B. A malformation from abnormal tissue formation
C. A deformation from mechanical forces
D. A disruption from breakdown of normal tissue
E. A dysplasia from abnormal cell organization
Answer: C
Why this is correct: A deformation is a body defect caused by mechanical forces, often from oligohydramnios, and can cause clubfoot. A malformation is intrinsically abnormal development, a disruption is an extrinsic problem with originally normal development, and a dysplasia is abnormal tissue organization.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities
Question 863

D. A disruption, from breakdown of normal tissue
E. An association, with nonrandom co-occurrence and unknown cause
Answer: E
Why this is correct: An association is a nonrandom group of anomalies with an unknown cause, like VACTERL. A syndrome has a specific common cause, like Down syndrome.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities
Question 864

B. Thalidomide; heart defects

Answer: B
Why this is correct: Thalidomide was used as a sedative and tranquilizer in the late 1950s and 1960s. It classically causes meromelia or amelia (partial or complete absence of a limb) and can also cause heart defects.

Why this is correct: Retinoic acid can cause craniofacial dysmorphism (wide-set eyes, ear abnormalities), cardiovascular anomalies like transposition of the great vessels, and CNS abnormalities including neural tube defects, hydrocephalus, and microcephaly.

Why this is correct: Fetal alcohol syndrome disrupts fetal growth and morphogenesis, causing a thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, small palpebral fissures, growth deficits, CNS abnormalities, and heart defects.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities
Question 867
A 29-year-old woman who smokes a pack a day is at 32 weeks' gestation. Ultrasound shows the fetus is below the 5th percentile for weight. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Why this is correct: Cigarette smoking causes growth restriction, premature delivery, low birth weight, placental abruption, and stillbirth. Nicotine constricts uterine vessels, lowering perfusion, and carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen.

Why this is correct: Radiation can cause chromosomal damage and kill rapidly dividing fetal cells. It's associated with microcephaly, intellectual disability, growth restriction, and malignancy.

Question 869

Why this is correct: Toxoplasma gondii is an intracellular parasite acquired from undercooked meat or cat feces, usually asymptomatic in the mother. Congenital infection causes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities
Question 870

Why this is correct: Rubella (German measles) crosses the placenta, with the highest risk in the first trimester. It causes eye defects (cataracts, glaucoma), cardiac defects, sensorineural hearing loss, and a blueberry muffin rash. It's rare in the US because of vaccination.

Why this is correct: CMV is the most common viral infection in fetuses, often acquired through body fluids or contact with children in daycare. Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Prenatal Timeline & Congenital Abnormalities

Question 876

Why this is correct: In the placenta accreta spectrum, villi embed into the myometrium (accreta) or penetrate through it (percreta). It raises the risk of postpartum hemorrhage and maternal death because the placenta fails to separate at delivery.

Why this is correct: Placental abruption is complete or partial separation of the placenta from the uterus before delivery, with abrupt, painful bleeding. It can present with hypertension and vaginal bleeding.

Why this is correct: Potter sequence results from abnormal kidney growth causing oligohydramnios, which leads to pulmonary hypoplasia and limb deformations.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes

A 3-year-old boy comes to the emergency department with painless, dark red rectal bleeding. He is otherwise well. A technetium scan shows an outpouching of the ileum containing ectopic tissue. Why this is correct: The yolk sac forms anterior to the embryo, is lined by hypoblast-derived endoderm, and provides early nutrients. When the embryo folds, it's incorporated into the gut, and the vitelline duct connecting it to the gut typically atrophies.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 883
A 30-year-old woman is pregnant with identical twins. Ultrasound at 12 weeks shows one placenta and one chorion but a thin membrane separating two amniotic sacs. C. At the morula stage

E. At the blastocyst stage
Answer: E
Why this is correct: In monozygotic twins, timing of cleavage sets the membranes. Early cleavage (morula) gives 2 chorions and 2 amnions, cleavage of the blastocyst gives 1 chorion and 2 amnions, and late cleavage gives 1 chorion and 1 amnion. D. A trisomy affecting limb development
E. Failure of lateral body wall folding
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Amniotic band syndrome occurs when fibrous amniotic bands encircle part of the fetus, causing ring constrictions or amputations. This is an extrinsic problem affecting originally normal development.

Question 887
A 29-year-old woman delivers a healthy boy at 39 weeks. The baby weighs 3.5 kg. The mother had no bleeding and a normal delivery. The obstetrician examines the side of the placenta shown, which is shiny, covered by membranes, and has the umbilical cord attached with large vessels branching across it. From which tissue does this side of the placenta form? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a8/Human_placenta_baby_side.jpg" alt="Photograph of a delivered placenta">
A. The decidua capsularis
B. The smooth chorion
C. The chorion frondosum
D. The yolk sac
E. The decidua basalis
Answer: C
Why this is correct: The placenta has a fetal part formed from the bushy chorion frondosum and a maternal part formed from the decidua basalis. The shiny side with the cord and branching vessels is the fetal side.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 888
A 33-year-old woman delivers at term, and her placenta is examined, shown. She had an uncomplicated pregnancy. The obstetrician points to the cord inserted near the center of this surface. The baby weighs 3.2 kg and is healthy. The placenta weighs 520 g. Her blood pressure was normal throughout pregnancy. The placenta delivered spontaneously. Where is normal cord insertion, and why does it matter? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a8/Human_placenta_baby_side.jpg" alt="Photograph of a delivered placenta">
A. Anywhere on the disc, since location doesn’t affect flow
B. Within 1 cm of the edge, where blood flow is highest
C. On the membranes outside the disc, where vessels are protected
D. Only on the maternal side, where the spiral arteries enter
E. In the central two-thirds of the disc, where oxygenation is best
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Normal cord insertion is within the central two-thirds of the placental disc. Moving away from the center, oxygenation may be less efficient; peripheral insertion is within 3 cm of the edge and marginal within 1 cm.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 889
A 27-year-old woman delivers at term, and the midwife inspects the placental surface shown, which is dark red and divided into lobes by shallow grooves. She checks that no lobes are missing. The mother had no bleeding and delivered vaginally. Her uterus is firm. She is 27 and this was her first baby. Her blood pressure was normal. The placenta delivered spontaneously. What are these lobes, and how did they form? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d8/Placenta_001.jpg" alt="Photograph of a delivered placenta">
A. Villi of the smooth chorion, formed as the abembryonic villi regressed
B. Cotyledons, formed as erosion of the decidua basalis created septa
C. Molar vesicles, formed as the villi swelled with fluid
D. Cotyledons on the fetal surface, formed by the umbilical vessels
E. Amniotic bands, formed as the amnion tore and wrapped the disc
Answer: B
Why this is correct: As villi invade the decidua, decidual tissue erodes to form the intervillous space. Erosion of the decidua basalis produces placental septa projecting toward the chorionic plate, forming cotyledons visible on the maternal surface after delivery.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 890
A 31-year-old woman delivers at term. She had normal fetal growth throughout pregnancy. Her blood pressure was normal. She is 31 and had one prior delivery. The placenta delivered spontaneously. The surface of her placenta shown was attached to her uterine wall. During pregnancy, maternal blood entered the spaces between the villi on this side. Where does maternal blood come from, and where does it go? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d8/Placenta_001.jpg" alt="Photograph of a delivered placenta">
A. From the umbilical vein into the villi and back to the mother
B. From the umbilical arteries into the fetal capillaries directly
C. From the yolk sac into the amnion and then to the fetus
D. From spiral arteries into the intervillous space around the villi
E. Through the cord, where maternal and fetal blood mix freely
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Maternal blood enters the intervillous space from spiral endometrial arteries and flows over the branching villi for gas exchange. Fetal blood arrives through two umbilical arteries and exchanges at fetal capillaries in the villi.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 891
A newborn girl is delivered at term, and a section of her umbilical cord is examined, shown. Her mother had an uncomplicated pregnancy. The baby weighs 3.4 kg with Apgar scores of 9 and 9. The cord has three vessels. The mother is 29 and healthy. She had normal fetal growth throughout pregnancy. The cord was clamped after 60 seconds. Which vessel in this cord carried the most oxygen-rich blood? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e8/Cross_section_of_the_umbilical_cord.jpg" alt="Umbilical cord cross-section">
A. The vitelline duct
B. The allantoic duct
C. The spiral arteries
D. The umbilical vein
E. The umbilical arteries
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Poorly oxygenated fetal blood travels through the two umbilical arteries to the placenta. The umbilical vein returns oxygen-rich blood to the fetus, the opposite of the usual artery-vein pattern.

Question 892
A newborn boy's umbilical cord section is shown. A small epithelial remnant sits between the umbilical arteries. His urinalysis is normal. He was born at 39 weeks and is healthy. A. The vitelline duct, which connected the yolk sac to the gut
B. The allantois, which initially drained the bladder
C. The decidua, which fed the embryo
D. The amnion, which surrounded the embryo
E. The notochord, which induced the neural plate
Answer: B
Why this is correct: The allantois is an endodermally lined outpouching of the hindgut that initially drains the urinary bladder. Its remnant can be seen in the cord.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 893
A 30-year-old woman delivers at term, and a section of her placenta is examined, shown. The outer layer of the villus is a continuous multinucleated layer without cell borders. This layer produced a hormone detected by her pregnancy test. Her pregnancy was uncomplicated. The baby weighs 3.3 kg. She is 30 and had no hypertension or diabetes. The placenta was sent to pathology as part of a teaching review. Her baby is healthy. What is this layer? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7d/Histology_of_chorionic_villus_at_term.jpg" alt="Histology section">
A. Cytotrophoblast
B. Syncytiotrophoblast
C. Amnion
D. Extraembryonic mesoderm
E. Decidua basalis
Answer: B
Why this is correct: The syncytiotrophoblast doesn't complete cytokinesis, so it's multinucleated. It invades the uterine wall and secretes hCG, the basis for pregnancy tests. The cytotrophoblast is the inner layer of mononucleate cells.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 894
A pathologist examines the term placental villus shown from a 34-year-old woman with an uncomplicated pregnancy. Inside the villus are small vessels filled with red cells. The baby weighs 3.3 kg and is healthy. The placenta weighs 500 g. She had one prior delivery. Her blood pressure was normal. The placenta delivered spontaneously. What stage of villus development includes fetal blood vessels, and what does it do? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7d/Histology_of_chorionic_villus_at_term.jpg" alt="Histology section">
A. Smooth chorion villi, which have degenerated
B. Lacunae, which contain maternal blood
C. Primary villi, which contain only trophoblast
D. Secondary villi, which contain mesoderm without vessels
E. Tertiary villi, which supply the embryo with nutrients and oxygen
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Cytotrophoblasts penetrate the syncytiotrophoblast to form primary villi, which develop into secondary and then tertiary villi as the baby develops blood vessels. Villi supply the embryo with nutrients and oxygen.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 895
A 29-year-old woman delivers twins at 36 weeks. She conceived after IVF with two embryos transferred. Both twins are healthy. The twins are a boy and a girl. She is 29 and had no hypertension. The membranes were sent to pathology. A section of the membrane dividing the two sacs is shown. The twins' placentas were separate. How many chorions and amnions did these twins have? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1e/Diamniotic-dichorionic_twin_placenta_-_low_mag.jpg" alt="Histology section">
A. Two chorions and one amnion
B. One chorion and two amnions
C. Two chorions and two amnions
D. They're conjoined
E. One chorion and one amnion
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Dizygotic twins come from two eggs and two sperm and have 2 chorions, 2 amnions, and 2 placentas. Monozygotic twins split at the morula also have 2 chorions and 2 amnions.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placental Pathology
Question 896
A 31-year-old woman delivers at 37 weeks, and the umbilical cord is found to attach to the membranes several centimeters outside the placental disc. The umbilical cord inserts into the membranes rather than the placental disc. The baby is healthy, weighing 2.9 kg. The placenta is otherwise normal. She had an uncomplicated pregnancy with normal fetal growth. Her blood pressure was normal. Why is this insertion risky?
A. It causes a single umbilical artery that lacks blood flow
B. It's never clinically significant, since the vessels are protected
C. It means the placenta is molar and needs hCG follow-up
D. The exposed vessels are at risk for compression or rupture
E. The cord is too short to reach the placenta directly
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Normal insertion is within the central two-thirds of the disc. Peripheral is within 3 cm of the edge, and marginal within 1 cm. Velamentous insertion attaches to membranes outside the placenta, so vessels travel farther and risk compression or disruption. All velamentous insertions are furcate, but not all furcate are velamentous.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placental Pathology
Question 897
A 22-year-old woman at 38 weeks' gestation has a fever of 38.8°C (101.8°F), fetal tachycardia, and foul-smelling amniotic fluid 20 hours after her water broke. Her baby is delivered, and the placenta is examined. The infection most likely ascended from the vagina. Her pulse is 116/min, and her uterus is tender. Her WBC is 19,000/mm³. Her Apgar scores were 7 and 8. In the fetal inflammatory response, what is the first stage?
A. Necrotizing chorioamnionitis with membrane necrosis
B. Necrotizing funisitis with cord necrosis
C. Umbilical arteritis with arterial wall inflammation
D. Chorionic plate vasculitis with umbilical phlebitis
E. Acute chorionitis with inflammation under the chorion
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Ascending infection is much more common. The fetal response, which is more common, progresses from chorionic plate vasculitis and umbilical vein phlebitis, to inflammation of one or both arteries, to necrotizing funisitis. The maternal response progresses from acute chorionitis and subchorionitis to chorioamnionitis to necrotizing chorioamnionitis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placental Pathology
Question 898
A 1-day-old boy born at 42 weeks develops respiratory distress. He was covered in green-stained fluid at delivery. Chest x-ray shows patchy infiltrates. The placenta is green, and the pathologist sees damage to the large vessels of the placental surface and cord. His Apgar scores were 4 and 7. His oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. He was delivered vaginally after a long labor. What passed too early, and what vascular damage can follow?
A. Blood; placental abruption with retroplacental clot
B. Meconium; meconium-associated vascular necrosis
C. Surfactant; placental infarction from hypoxia
D. Vernix; chorioamnionitis from ascending infection
E. Amniotic fluid; oligohydramnios from leakage
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Meconium is the first stool, usually passed 24 to 48 hours after birth. If passed in utero and inhaled, it causes meconium aspiration syndrome. Meconium-associated vascular necrosis affects the large vessels of the placenta and cord and can turn the placenta green.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placental Pathology
Question 899
A 20-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation has an ultrasound showing a fetus with an enlarged, echogenic placenta. Her β-hCG is moderately elevated. Genetic testing of the tissue shows 69,XXY, and p57 immunostaining is positive. She has had severe nausea and vomiting. Her blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg. She has no prior pregnancies. Her uterus is appropriate for her dates, and her thyroid tests are normal. What is the diagnosis?
A. Placenta accreta
B. Choriocarcinoma
C. Complete hydatidiform mole
D. Hydropic villi
E. Partial hydatidiform mole
Answer: E
Why this is correct: A partial mole has fetal tissue that dies as an embryo, a triploid genome (69,XXY), a somewhat increased hCG, and positive p57 staining because a maternal copy is present. A complete mole is 46,XX with two paternal genomes, markedly high hCG, p57 negative, and a 2–8% risk of choriocarcinoma.

Question 924
An 8-year-old boy presents to the ED in acute distress with chest pain and difficulty breathing. Two days ago, the patient flew on a 15-hour flight to the United States with his family. Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 4
Question 925
A 28-year-old single mother of an intellectually disabled boy with an ADHD (Image below) presents to her gynecologist with a 3-month history of amenorrhea and hot flashes. A learning disability, particularly in math and sciences, prevented her from finishing high school. Which of the following is most likely to be found in the mother?
A. Trisomy 21
B. >200 CAG repeats
C. Premutation in FMR1 gene
D. Maternal uniparental disomy at chromosome region 15q11.2
E. Hypermethylation of the CCG repeats that silences FMR1 gene expression
Answer: C
Why this is correct: This patient most likely has Fragile X syndrome which is an X-linked dominant disease caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene. This can cause intellectual disability, facial anomalies (long face, large ears), mitral valve prolapse, and hypermobility. The phenotype is dependent on the number of repeats. This is the most common inherited intellectual disability. His mother (who has a mild intellectual disability) likely has a premutation that she passed to her son who inherited and increased number of CGG repeats and has a more severe phenotype.

Question 927
A diagnosis is made in a 17-year-old man with intellectual disability, long face, long ears and large testicles. DNA analysis is performed in his maternal grandfather and father and in the patient. Which pattern of trinucleotide repeats in the FMR1 gene is most likely to be found?

Answer: E
Why this is correct: This describes Fragile X syndrome which is a X linked dominant disease. Since it is X-linked it had to be passed to the patient by his mother, so his father likely has a normal number of repeats while his grandfather may or may not have an increased number of repeats. Option E is the only possible option where the patient has a large number of repeats (>200 creates the phenotype), his father has a normal number of repeats, and his grandfather has an increased number of repeats that could have been passed to his mother and then the patient each gaining increasing numbers of repeats that ultimately lead to the patient having Fragile X syndrome.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 6
Question 941
A 59-year-old woman was diagnosed with breast cancer 4 months ago after she noted her left breast was significantly larger than her right. She underwent mastectomy and has been receiving chemotherapy. During her visit, she reports nausea that is alleviated by ondansetron therapy. She admits to decreased sleep and poor appetite for the past 4 weeks. She states that she has been feeling down and that chemotherapy makes her feel so tired that she doesn’t want to do anything. She spends most of her time at home. She states she is too drained to go out with her friends or talk to her family. She has lost interest in gardening and feels guilty for relying on her husband throughout this time. What is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
A. Explain that feeling fatigued is normal during chemotherapy and schedule a follow-up in 2 weeks
B. Reach out to the patient’s husband to ask for more information on the patient’s mood
C. Refer the patient to a support group
D. Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for major depressive disorder
E. Start the patient on a benzodiazepine for anxiety
Answer: D
Why this is correct: A common comorbidity to cancer is major depressive disorder (MDD). MDD is diagnosed by 5 or more of the following with one being either depressed mood or anhedonia: 1) depressed mood 2) anhedonia 3) weight/appetite changes 4) sleep disruption 5) psychomotor changed 6) fatigue 7) feeling worthless 8) cognitive issues 9) suicidal ideation. This patient is experiencing sleep disturbances, poor appetite (which could be related to chemo or MDD), depressed mood, fatigue (again could be related to MDD or chemo), and anhedonia. While her fatigue and appetite changes can also be side effects of chemotherapy, it is important to recognize the other symptoms that suggest her symptoms are likely related to MDD rather than chemotherapy alone.

Question 943

B. Aromatase inhibitor
C. Estrogen receptor agonist
D. HER2 receptor inhibitor
E. Progesterone receptor agonist
Answer: B
Why this is correct: This patient has breast cancer that is positive for estrogen receptors and progesterone receptors, which means her cancer will be receptive to medications that block these receptors or the hormones that bind to them. From the answer choices, the only one that would decrease estrogen is B) aromatase inhibitor. Why this is correct: Patient is over 30 years old and therefore mammogram is first line for palpable breast masses.

Question 948
A 63-year-old woman with recently diagnosed Her2+ breast cancer presenting to the ER at 2 a.m. with mild SOB that is worse with exertion and began 2 days ago. Question 949
A 42-year-old woman comes to the office for a follow-up after a modified radical mastectomy. Her incision site is healing well without complication. She reports an uncomfortable feeling in her back. Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 6
Question 950
A 34-year-old woman is being evaluated for a mass found in her breast during a self-exam a few days ago. The patient had a bilateral breast reduction about 2 years ago. In the clinic her breast exam shows a firm and fixed mass in the upper region of the left breast. A mammogram shows a 2 X 4 cm mass with coarse calcifications in the upper region of the left breast. A. Ductal Carcinoma in Situ
B. Galactocele
C. Fat Necrosis

Answer: C
Why this is correct: Fat Necrosis is a benign condition resulting from injury to breast tissue. It can occur due to blunt trauma or from trauma associated with surgical procedures. Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 6
Question 951
A 42-year-old woman presents to clinic with concerns for a lump on her right breast for one month. She notes that the lump is non-tender and notes no changes during her menstrual cycle. A. Core needle biopsy
B. Fine needle aspiration
C. Monitor for six months
D. MRI
E. Reassurance
Answer: A
Why this is correct: This question features a 42-yo female with a breast mass with suspicious characteristics (irregular borders, measuring >1cm). Ultrasound shows a solid mass and mammogram was negative; furthermore, mammograms can have a false negative rate of up to 15% especially with high breast density. A 20-year-old, G0 woman with no PMH presents to an OB-GYN clinic for a new patient visit. Her menstrual cycles began at age 14 and occur regularly every 28 days with light bleeding. Question 953
A 37-year-old G0 F presents to her OBGYN clinic for a 2-cm, tender breast mass first noticed 2 months ago on a self-breast exam. Answer: D
Why this is correct: A small mass showing reassuring characteristics on both physical exam and mammography in a pre-menopausal woman is highly unlikely to be a malignancy. Invasive procedures should be reserved at this time until the mass begins to show non-reassuring signs.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 6
Question 954
A 29-year-old woman, three months postpartum, presents to the clinic with a palpable lump in her left breast that she noticed two weeks ago while breastfeeding. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer. The lump is located in the upper outer quadrant, measures approximately 4 cm, is firm, non-tender, and not mobile. There are no associated skin changes, erythema, or nipple discharge. The patient is otherwise healthy and has no symptoms of mastitis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A. Initiate antibiotics and advise continued breastfeeding
B. Obtain a breast ultrasound
C. Obtain a mammogram
D. Perform a fine-needle aspiration (FNA)
E. Reassure the patient and recommend warm compresses
Answer: B
Why this is correct: In a 29-year-old woman who is postpartum with a new and palpable immobile breast mass, the best next step is to get an ultrasound. In women under the age of 30, guidelines recommend an ultrasound rather than a mammogram for evaluation of a mass, even if there is high suspicion for malignancy. This is in part due to the higher density of breast mass in younger women where ultrasound provides better visualization to differentiate between benign conditions like fibroadenoma or cyst and malignancies.

Question 955
A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency department with nausea, generalized weakness, and decreased urine output for the past 24 hours. He was recently diagnosed with Hodgkin’s lymphoma and was initiated on a treatment regimen that includes Venotoclax, a BCL2 inhibitor. His labs prior to starting treatment were all normal and he has no other remarkable past medical history. He takes no medications at home. On examination, he appears fatigued but is alert and oriented. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure is 108/64 mmHg, pulse is 102/min, and respirations are 18/min. Mucous membranes are dry. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal exams are unremarkable. Neurologic exam reveals mild hand tremors. Urinalysis is positive for crystals. CMP: Sodium 138 mEq/L (135–145); Potassium 6.4 mEq/L (3.5–5.0); Chloride 103 mEq/L (98–106); Bicarbonate (CO₂) 18 mEq/L (22–28); BUN 40 mg/dL (7–20); Creatinine 2.2 mg/dL (0.6–1.2); Glucose 95 mg/dL (70–110); Calcium 6.8 mg/dL (8.5–10.5); Phosphate 6.5 mg/dL (2.5–4.5); Total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL (0.1–1.2); AST 24 U/L (10–40); ALT 28 U/L (10–55); Alkaline phosphatase 90 U/L (40–120); Albumin 4.2 g/dL (3.5–5.0). Which of the following describes a drug that could have prevented this presentation if it was given to this patient as prophylaxis?
A. A drug that leads to increases renal excretion of potassium and retains calcium
B. A drug that leads to decreased prostaglandin synthesis and impaired renal vasodilation
C. A drug that inhibits an enzyme which leads to less formation of a renally excreted product
D. A drug that converts an insoluble product to a soluble product for easier excretion
E. A drug that inhibits an enzyme that leads to impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells
Answer: C
Why this is correct: This describes allopurinol which inhibits xanthine oxidase, an enzyme active in the process of metabolizing nucleic acids to uric acid. Excess uric acid, which is hinted at in the urinalysis findings, alongside hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperphosphatemia are indicative of Tumor Lysis Syndrome. Allopurinol is often given as prophylaxis to anticipate the large cell turnover from chemotherapy.

Question 956
A 52-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a routine checkup. She has no children and experienced menarche at age 11 and menopause at age 55. Her mother was diagnosed with breast cancer at age 45. Question 957

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 958
A 43-year-old man with a history of hypertension (HTN) comes to clinic due to his concern about dry cough that began 5 weeks ago soon after starting Lisinopril. He has tried OTC cold medications without relief. He denies sick contacts, recent travel, or history of similar episodes. He does not smoke and takes Lisinopril and Amlodipine as prescribed. B. Angioedema; switch to Enalapril
C. Peripheral edema; switch to ARB
D. Peripheral edema; switch to Enalapril
Answer: A
Why this is correct: While the exact cause is unknown, it is believed that ACEi angioedema and cough are both due to increased concentrations of bradykinin/ substance P. Cough can generally be controlled with discontinuation of ACEi, switching to another antihypertensive or an ARB.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 960
A 23-year-old woman with past medical history of multiple allergies leading to facial swelling presents with dyspnea and swelling of the face and neck. On physical exam, her extremities are also noted to be markedly swollen. She is immediately sedated for intubation to maintain patency of the airway. Chart review reveals newly started ACE-inhibitor. She is given 2 doses of Icatibant and IV steroids. What is the mechanism of action for Icatibant?
A. Competitive agonist of the bradykinin type 1 receptor
B. Competitive antagonist of the bradykinin type 1 receptor
C. Competitive antagonist of the bradykinin type 2 receptor
D. Noncompetitive antagonist of the bradykinin type 2 receptor
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Bradykinin receptors are G-protein coupled receptors, type 2 receptors. Both participate in the maintenance of normal vasoregulation or to development of hypertension. However, most treatment modalities focus on type 2 bradykinin receptors.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 961
20-year-old Hispanic woman presents to the ED with facial edema. She is Spanish-speaking, and the attending physician suggests that you call the medical interpreter. She also has her husband present in the room, who speaks both Spanish and English. Which of the following is true when working with a medical interpreter?

Answer: D
Why this is correct: When using a medical interpreter, a triangle should be made between the patient, interpreter, and physician. The patient should be spoken directly to in the first person while maintaining eye contact. Questions should not be directed to the interpreter. Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 962
A 55-year-old man with a PMH of HTN and hyperlipidemia presents to an outpatient clinic with a 3-day history of facial swelling. He does not have dyspnea or known allergies. Two weeks ago, he was started on an ACE inhibitor for his uncontrolled hypertension. He has a family history of edema due to an unknown “heart medication” but cannot provide any further information. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for this patient’s facial swelling?
A. Antigen-antibody complex build up in facial tissue
B. Decrease in bradykinin degradation
C. IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
D. Increase in B2 cell receptor concentration
E. Increase in bradykinin production
Answer: B
Why this is correct: ACE inhibitors are widely known for their ability to prevent conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II, but they also exhibit the ability to prevent the degradation of bradykinin into non-active metabolites. This results in the build-up of bradykinin leading to increased vasodilation and vascular permeability. ACE inhibitors have no effect on the production of bradykinin, nor its action or concentration of its receptors.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 963
A 32-year-old woman with past medical history of multiple allergies leading to facial swelling presents with abdominal pain and swelling of the face and extremities for the past 2 days. On physical exam, she shows no apparent distress or dyspnea, and her extremities are also noted to be markedly swollen. Chart review reveals a recently added ACE-inhibitor. What is the next most appropriate step in the treatment of this patient?
A. Stop the ACE-inhibitor and follow up in an outpatient clinic
B. Intubate and admit to the ICU
C. Oral antihistamine medications
D. Nebulized Albuterol Treatment
E. Perform a chest x-ray
Answer: A
Why this is correct: This is a patient presenting with a non-emergent angioedema likely due to the recent addition of an ACE-inhibitor. The most appropriate response is to discontinue the use of any ACE-inhibitors. Most patients will see a resolution of swelling within 48-72 hours. Follow-up with a PCP is sufficient to confirm resolution.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 964
A 17-year-old female patient presents to the ED due to acute swelling of the face and neck which she has never experienced before. It began a few hours ago without any apparent trigger. She reports that she started oral contraception last week due to a history of irregular menstrual periods since menarche at age 13. She was stung by a bee two days ago but has previously had bee stings without any major reaction. Which of the following would lead you to suspect a bradykinin-mediated process?
A. Acute onset following identifiable trigger
B. Family history of atopy
C. Negative response to epinephrine
D. Severe hypotension
E. Urticaria and pruritus
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Angioedema can be mediated by histamine or bradykinin. Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is mediated by bradykinin and can be triggered by high-estrogen states, such as OCPs. Bradykinin-mediated attacks tend to be slower in onset (over the course of hours), last longer (48 hours+), and do not respond to epinephrine. They are less likely than histaminergic episodes to involve urticaria, hypotension, or bronchospasm. Histamine is released by mast cells and is commonly associated with IgE related processes (type 1 hypersensitivity reactions, anaphylaxis). Histaminergic reactions are typically acute in onset, include skin changes (urticaria and pruritis), may include anaphylaxis with severe hypotension, and resolve with administration of epinephrine. Atopic conditions are typically found in families. They include allergic rhinitis, eczema, and asthma (the atopic triad) and are associated with IgE-mediated reactions.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 965
A 28-year-old man with PMH of Hereditary Angioedema Type 1 presents to the emergency room after the onset of significant facial swelling. He was diagnosed with HAE1 15 years ago and has been hospitalized several times with severe swelling, requiring intubation once. He has not had an attack like this in several years after starting regular C1 inhibitor concentrate injections, but he recently moved to the area and missed his last two injection appointments. On exam he has significant edema of the eyelids, lips, and mouth, and he is found to have stridor on chest auscultation. His BP is 118/76, HR is 104, and RR is 24. What is the best next step in the management of this patient?
A. Administer IM Epinephrine and admit to the floor
B. Administer C1-INH concentrate and Icatibant and schedule follow up with an allergist next week
C. Admit to the ICU for close monitoring
D. Endotracheal intubation and admission to the ICU
E. Establish a surgical airway with tracheostomy and admit to the ICU
Answer: D
Why this is correct: This patient with a history of HAE1 has previously had severe attacks requiring intubation and has not been receiving his prophylactic C1-INH concentrate. His exam reveals signs concerning for upper airway edema. He has acute progression of this attack during your exam as evidenced by onset of stridor which could easily progress further to acute loss of airway. If there is concern for significant airway involvement, the best next step is to secure his airway with endotracheal intubation. Epinephrine is not indicated in the management of HAE. C1-INH and icatibant are appropriate medications, but it would not be appropriate to discharge this patient who is at risk of airway compromise. A surgical airway is not necessary at this time, but HAE patients have particularly challenging airways which can acutely worsen with repeated failed intubation attempts. It is advisable to have a clinician experienced with cricothyrotomy available during the intubation.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 966
A 54-year-old man presents to the ED with a facial edema and abdominal cramps of one-week duration. He is also wheezing with increased difficulty breathing. He denies any rash or pruritus. He states that he has not made recent changes to his diet; however, he started taking a new medication a couple months ago for hypertension. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
A. Administer IM epinephrine
B. Administer IV antihistamines
C. Intubate for airway protection
D. Obtain C4 level
E. Stop patient’s ACE inhibitor
Answer: C
Why this is correct: This patient is in respiratory distress and action should be taken to establish an airway in the case of progressing laryngeal edema causing obstruction. Administering epinephrine would be the associated treatment with anaphylaxis; however, this patient does not have an urticarial rash and his swelling is likely due to the antihypertensive (ACE inhibitors) he was recently started on. IV antihistamines, C4 levels, and stopping offending agents can all be considered in treatment and workup for angioedema; however, are not the critical next step when a patient has threatening airway obstruction.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 967
A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for butterfly-like rash and symmetric joint pain and swelling in the knees, wrists, and hands of two-week duration. Lab findings include pancytopenia (decreased numbers of all blood cell types), elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and high titers of anti-Sm and anti-dsDNA antibodies. Deficiency of which of the following components of complement system classical pathway is likely to be found in this patient?
A. C1q and C4
B. C1-INH
C. C3
D. CD55 and CD59
E. Factor H
Answer: A
Why this is correct: This patient likely has systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) given her butterfly rash, symmetric joint pain, joint swelling, and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP). High titers of anti-Sm and anti-DNAse are highly suggestive (and should confirm) the diagnosis of SLE. In SLE there is activation of the complement, resulting in low levels of C1q and C4 (also often low C3) as they are used up due to the chronic activation.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 968
A 45-year-old Hispanic man with limited English proficiency presents to the family practice clinic with low-grade fever and cough of 24-hr duration. The receptionist requests an interpreter service. Prior to using the service, it is prudent for the health care provider to arrange a brief meeting with the interpreter to inquire about the patient’s
A. Citizenship
B. Permanent residency
C. Ability to afford health care
D. Culture and cultural taboos
E. Sexual orientation
Answer: D
Why this is correct: When treating different patients, it is important to consider how their culture impacts their views on healthcare, medications, etc. In some cultures, there may be different modesty standards that can impact the patient’s ability to feel safe during exams. Other cultures have different views on family involvement when making medical decisions. It is important to be aware of this and recognize when your cultural beliefs may differ from those of your patients so that they feel comfortable receiving care.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 969
Which of the following is a correct statement regarding the immune status of patients afflicted with the most common complement deficiency?
A. An insufficient level of alternative pathway complement levels predisposes patients to infections
B. An insufficient level of classical pathway complement levels predisposes patients to infections
C. An insufficient level of alternative pathway complement levels predisposes patients to SLE
D. An insufficient level of classical pathway complement levels predisposes patients to SLE
E. C3 deficiency results in altered alternative pathway response only
Answer: D
Why this is correct: The most common complement deficiency is C2, which is strongly associated with SLE. Homogeneous hereditary deficiencies in the early classical complement pathway (C1q, C1r, C1s, C4, C2) is one of the strongest risk factors for developing SLE.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 970
A 27-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician due to a history of recurrent episodes of non-pitting swelling involving her extremities, face, and abdomen. These episodes are often triggered by minor trauma or stress and are not associated with urticaria or pruritus. She reports that her father has experienced similar symptoms. Laboratory evaluation during an acute attack reveals low levels of serum C4 and low levels of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH). Which of the following best explains the underlying pathophysiology of this patient's condition?
A. Decreased degradation of histamine due to a genetic mutation
B. Deficiency in C5 convertase, leading to decreased complement activity
C. Excessive production of bradykinin due to unregulated kallikrein activity
D. Increased activation of the classic complement pathway
E. Overproduction of C1q protein due to C1-INH deficiency
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a disorder caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH). C1-INH normally inhibits kallikrein, an enzyme that converts kininogen into bradykinin. Without functional C1-INH, there is unregulated kallikrein activity, leading to excessive production of bradykinin. Bradykinin increases vascular permeability, resulting in the characteristic non-pitting angioedema seen in these patients. The lack of urticaria and pruritus, her family history, and the involvement of the complement system with low C4 levels further support the diagnosis.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 971
A 42-year-old woman who recently immigrated to the United States from Mexico presents to the clinic with her 17-year-old daughter. The patient speaks only Spanish, while her daughter is fluent in both Spanish and English. The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. She is here for a routine follow-up appointment. The physician needs to discuss recent lab results indicating poor glycemic control and adjust her treatment plan. The clinic does not have an on-site medical interpreter. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in ensuring effective communication during this visit?
A. Ask the patient’s daughter to serve as an interpreter during the visit
B. Connect with the telephone interpreting service provided by the clinic
C. Give the patient written instructions in Spanish and discuss the results in English
D. Proceed with the conversation in English and use non-verbal cues to communicate
E. Use a bilingual staff member who is not certified in medical interpretation
Answer: B
Why this is correct: In the setting of not having an in-person medical interpreter, the most appropriate next step is to use a virtual interpreting service that provides a trained medical interpreter via phone or video to ensure accurate and effective communication. Trained interpreters are familiar with medical terminology and are skilled in translating complex medical information without introducing errors or bias. This approach respects the patient’s language needs and ensures that she fully understands her condition and treatment plan.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 972
A 19-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of swelling of her lips and face. She has no urticaria or pruritus. Her father has had similar episodes of swelling in the past requiring hospitalization. Examination shows marked periorbital and tongue swelling. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect in this patient?
A. Deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor
B. Deficiency of C3 convertase
C. Deficiency of C5a
D. Deficiency of C9
E. Excessive histamine release from mast cells
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Hereditary angioedema (types 1 and 2) occurs due to a deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor of the complement pathway. This leads to unregulated activation of complement, further leading to an increase in bradykinin. The increase in bradykinin is what leads to the angioedema.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 973
A 45-year-old man with a history of hereditary angioedema presents with increased facial and laryngeal swelling. He was recently prescribed a medication from his primary care provider for increased blood pressure. Which of the following drugs most likely triggered this exacerbation?
A. Hydrochlorothiazide
B. Propranolol
C. Enalapril
D. Nifedipine
E. Furosemide
Answer: C
Why this is correct: ACE inhibitors are a common cause of exacerbating hereditary angioedema. This occurs due to ACE inhibitors blocking bradykinin degradation, leading to increased bradykinin and worsening of swelling. Hydrochlorothiazide, propranolol, Nifedipine, and Furosemide do not typically affect bradykinin levels, and have no effect on hereditary angioedema.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 974
A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with severe, crampy abdominal pain that began while at school this morning. He describes feeling bloated. He has had several episodes of nausea and vomiting but no diarrhea. He denies fever, sick contacts, or recent travel. His past medical history is unremarkable aside from childhood eczema. On exam, he appears uncomfortable and has diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. No rash or urticaria is present. Bowel sounds are decreased. Initial work-up for acute abdomen has been negative. When interviewed, his mother shares her son has been relatively healthy aside from recent complaints of acne and growing pains. She can recall this happened once before when she took her son to the dentist for a cavity filling. Of note, his father unexpectedly passed away at age 33 from complications of a genetic condition. Laboratory studies, including CBC and basic metabolic panel, and abdominal imaging are all within normal limits. Which of the following describes the underlying mechanism responsible for his clinical presentation?
A. Ischemia of the intestinal mucosa due to mesenteric arterial thrombosis
B. Obstruction of the lumen leading to bacterial overgrowth, inflammation, and neutrophilic infiltration
C. Inflammatory cytokine-mediated edema of the intestinal wall from viral gastroenteritis
D. Unregulated production of a potent vasodilator that affects smooth muscle
E. Excess histamine release from mast cell and basophil degranulation
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Abdominal angioedema is a potential presentation in cases of hereditary angioedema. The genetic mutation underlying HAE leads to uncontrolled and unregulated production of bradykinin which causes increased vascular permeability from bradykinin. The lack of negative acute abdomen workup, history of a similar episode, and family history support this suspected diagnosis. HAE is likely to first occur in childhood with or without triggers. Examples of increased stress or hormonal changes have been shown to be potential triggers.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 7
Question 975
A 27-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of worsening skin irritation. She has a past medical history of asthma for which she takes fluticasone. She denies having started any new medicines and only endorses seasonal allergies. In her social history, she reports drinking alcohol and occasionally smokes marijuana. Currently employed and started a new job at as a maid cleaning and disinfecting rooms at a hotel four days ago. She notes the itching began on the backs of her hands and spread. A. IL-5
B. IL-4 and IL-13
C. IL-2 and IFN-γ
D. TNF-α and C5a
E. IL-17 and IL-23
Answer: C
Why this is correct: IL-2 promotes T-cell proliferation and IFN-γ activates macrophages. These are key responses in a Type IV Hypersensitivity Response. This clinical vignette best describes contact dermatitis. The patient had a possible exposure four days ago with symptoms appearing two days ago. This matches the delayed presentation of Type IV HSRs and could be attributed to her new job with a workplace exposure to cleaning solvents.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 8
Question 988
A 65-year-old male presents to his PCP for a health maintenance exam. Physical exam reveals marked splenomegaly, and labs are remarkable for a leukocytosis of 123,000 and low LAP. Peripheral smear reveals significant presence of myelocytes and basophils. Which chromosomal translocation is most likely associated with this patient’s disorder?
A. t(8;14)
B. t(9;22)
C. t(11;14)
D. t(14;18)
E. t(15;17)
Answer: B
Why this is correct: This patient likely has CML, which often presents with splenomegaly, leukocytosis, and dysregulated production of mature and maturing granulocytes, as evidenced by the myelocytes and basophilia on peripheral smear. t(9;22) is associated with CML. Also known as the Philadelphia chromosome, this translocation causes the BCR-ABL fusion gene. It presents with dysregulated production of mature and maturing granulocytes such as neutrophils, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, and basophils. It is associated with splenomegaly and responds to BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors like imatinib.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 8
Question 989
A 4-year-old boy with newly diagnosed ALL is admitted for his first cycle of chemotherapy. One day after treatment initiation, he develops nausea, vomiting, and muscle weakness. Laboratory studies show: Potassium: 6.2 mEq/L [3.5-5]; Phosphate: 5.7 mg/dL [2.5-4.5]; Calcium: 7.1 mg/dL [8.5-10.5]; Glucose: 150 mg/dL [70-100]; Uric acid: 12.3 mg/dL [2.5-7]; Creatinine: 2.2 mg/dL [0.6-1.2]. Which of the following is most appropriate for immediate management?
A. IV fluids & allopurinol
B. IV fluids & rasburicase
C. IV insulin & glucose
D. IV sodium bicarbonate
E. Urgent hemodialysis
Answer: B
Why this is correct: The patient is suffering from Tumor Lysis Syndrome. Treatment initiation in leukemia and lymphomas can cause massive lysis of tumor cells, causing increases in serum potassium, phosphate, and uric acid. Increased serum phosphate then causes hypocalcemia as phosphate sequesters Ca. The uric acid crystals and calcium phosphate crystals can then damage the renal tubules to cause AKI. Rasburicase is a recombinant uricase that metabolizes uric acid to allantoin, helping to clear elevated uric acid levels. Aggressive hydration helps to dilute and excrete elevated serum electrolytes and promote renal perfusion.

B. Development of resistance due to mutations in a viral DNA polymerase
C. Inability to convert drug into active form due to missing viral thymidylate kinase
D. Use of an antiviral to treat a likely bacterial infection
E. Use of an antiviral to treat a likely fungal infection
Answer: C
Why this is correct: This patient with uncontrolled HIV likely has CMV retinitis, evidenced by painless nature of visual loss, severe degree of immunosuppression, and characteristic fundoscopic findings. Use of acyclovir in the treatment of CMV infections is not effective as CMV does not encode a viral thymidylate kinase required to convert acyclovir into its active form.

Foundations of Medicine / CBL / Week 9
Question 1001
A 24-year-old man presents to the clinic with a fever, sore throat, and generalized lymphadenopathy. He reports unprotected sexual contact with multiple partners in the last month. Physical examination reveals a maculopapular rash on his trunk. Concerned about acute HIV infection, the physician orders an HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody test. The result is negative. Given the patient’s high-risk behavior, the physician suspects the test result may be a false negative. Which of the following best explains the sensitivity of the HIV test in this patient?
A. The test is less sensitive due to the presence of generalized lymphadenopathy
B. The test is less sensitive in patients with multiple sexual partners
C. The test lacks sensitivity due to a mutation in the HIV virus
D. The test may be falsely negative during the "window period" before enough antibodies are produced
E. The test requires confirmation with a Western blot to increase sensitivity
Answer: D
Why this is correct: HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination tests detect both p24 antigen (present early in infection) and antibodies (which appear later). However, in the early phase of infection (often called the "window period"), the level of antibodies may be too low to detect, leading to a false-negative result. During this period, only the p24 antigen or HIV RNA tests are reliable.

A 34-year-old man with a history of rheumatic fever has fever and fatigue for 4 weeks. He had a dental cleaning with scaling 6 weeks ago and has several dental caries. Blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic, gram-positive cocci in chains that aren't typeable by Lancefield grouping and grow despite an optochin disk. Which organism is most likely?
A. Streptococcus pneumoniae
B. Viridans streptococci
C. Enterococcus faecalis
D. Staphylococcus epidermidis
E. Streptococcus pyogenes
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Viridans streptococci are alpha hemolytic and not Lancefield typeable. They cause caries (sugar-driven acidification and demineralization) and infective endocarditis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Cocci
Question 1008
A 72-year-old man with COPD has high fever, shaking chills, and a cough with rust-colored sputum for 2 days. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), and he has crackles and egophony over the right lower lobe. Chest x-ray shows lobar consolidation. Sputum Gram stain shows lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci. On blood agar the colonies are alpha hemolytic with a clear zone of no growth around an optochin disk. What is the most likely organism?
A. Viridans streptococci
B. Streptococcus pyogenes
C. Streptococcus pneumoniae
D. Klebsiella pneumoniae
E. Staphylococcus aureus
Answer: C
Why this is correct: S. pneumoniae causes pneumonia and is alpha hemolytic with a zone of inhibition around optochin. Pneumolysin creates pores and reduces ciliary motility.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Cocci
Question 1009
A 70-year-old man develops fever and right upper quadrant pain 5 days after biliary surgery. He has diabetes and takes insulin. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in chains that don't hemolyze blood agar, grow in 6.5% NaCl broth, and turn bile esculin agar black. He was receiving a cephalosporin at the time the fever began. Which organism is most likely?
A. Streptococcus pneumoniae
B. Viridans streptococci
C. Staphylococcus aureus
D. Streptococcus agalactiae
E. Enterococcus faecalis
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Enterococcus (group D strep) lives in the GI, GU, and biliary tracts, is gamma hemolytic, grows in 6.5% NaCl, and reacts with iron to turn black on bile esculin agar. Aminopenicillins cover E. faecalis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1010
A 29-year-old man who injects heroin has a swollen, painful thigh at an injection site for 3 days. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), pulse is 118/min, and blood pressure is 94/58 mm Hg. The skin is red and tense with a fluctuant abscess, and the pain extends beyond the redness. His heroin supply was traced to a batch contaminated with animal-derived material. A. Injectional anthrax
B. Cutaneous anthrax
C. Inhalational anthrax
D. Gastrointestinal anthrax
E. Clostridium perfringens gas gangrene
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Injectional anthrax causes cellulitis, abscess, and necrotizing fasciitis, beginning with flu-like symptoms and progressing to dyspnea, confusion, and eventually shock.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1011
A 35-year-old metalworker is struck in the eye by a metal fragment. Within 24 hours the eye becomes severely painful with rapidly worsening vision. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). E. Clostridium tetani
Answer: D
Why this is correct: B. cereus causes food poisoning linked to fried rice and rapid eye toxicity with post-traumatic endophthalmitis. It's a large, motile, beta-hemolytic rod.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1012
A 70-year-old man who gardens without gloves has jaw tightness and trouble swallowing 8 days after a deep thorn puncture to his hand. He hasn't had a tetanus booster in decades. Temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F). He has a fixed grimace, rigid abdominal muscles, and painful spasms triggered by noise. Gram stain of the wound shows rods with terminal spores in a tennis-racket shape. Which organism is responsible?
A. Clostridium botulinum
B. Clostridium perfringens
C. Clostridium tetani
D. Bacillus anthracis
E. Listeria monocytogenes
Answer: C
Why this is correct: C. tetani is found in soil. Its toxin inhibits glycine and GABA, causing spastic paralysis with risus sardonicus, spasms, and asphyxiation or pneumonia.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1013
A 45-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with double vision, drooping eyelids, and trouble swallowing that began 18 hours after eating home-canned green beans. Her husband ate the same beans and has similar symptoms. She is afebrile and alert. She has bilateral ptosis, fixed dilated pupils, and descending weakness of her arms. Her reflexes are decreased. Which mechanism explains her weakness?
A. Inhibited glycine and GABA release causing spastic paralysis
B. Blocked acetylcholine release causing flaccid paralysis
C. Inactivation of elongation factor 2 causing nerve damage
D. A superantigen binding MHC II causing cytokine release
E. Increased cGMP in neurons causing loss of muscle tone
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Clostridium botulinum spores are found in canned food, honey, corn syrup, soil, and water. Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1014
A 68-year-old woman in a nursing home has had 8 watery stools a day for 5 days. She finished a course of a fluoroquinolone for pneumonia 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), and WBC is 21,000/mm³. Her abdomen is distended and tender. Abdominal x-ray shows a markedly dilated colon. A. Clostridium perfringens food poisoning
B. Shigella dysentery with toxic megacolon
C. Bacillus cereus food poisoning
D. Enterotoxigenic E. coli diarrhea
E. C. difficile colitis with toxic megacolon
Answer: E
Why this is correct: C. difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis, diarrhea, and megacolon after fluoroquinolone or clindamycin use lets it overgrow, especially with prolonged antibiotic use in healthcare settings.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1015
A 26-year-old man who lives in a shelter has an ulcer on his shin that hasn't healed for 5 weeks. It has a gray membrane at its base. He recently had a sore throat. Temperature is 37.8°C (100°F). A swab grown on Loeffler medium shows gram-positive rods with metachromatic granules, and the organism forms black colonies on blood agar. Which organism is most likely?
A. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
B. Bacillus anthracis
C. Streptococcus pyogenes
D. Listeria monocytogenes
E. Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Answer: A
Why this is correct: C. diphtheriae causes pharyngitis, bull neck, myocarditis, cranial neuropathy, and necrotic cutaneous infection, with epidemics in the homeless. It forms black colonies, shows metachromatic granules on Loeffler medium, and its toxin inactivates EF-2.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1016
A 72-year-old man on prednisone for polymyalgia rheumatica has fever, headache, and confusion for 2 days. He eats deli meats daily. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), and he has neck stiffness. A. Streptococcus pneumoniae
B. Neisseria meningitidis
C. Clostridium perfringens
D. Listeria monocytogenes
E. Haemophilus influenzae
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Listeria is a small, aerobic, beta-hemolytic gram-positive rod with tumbling motility from actin rockets and umbrella-shaped growth in agar. It causes flu-like illness, puerperal fever, neonatal sepsis, and meningitis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1017
A 30-year-old woman develops 6 watery stools a day on the third day of a trip to Southeast Asia. She has mild cramps but no fever or blood in her stool. Pulse is 96/min, and her mucous membranes are dry. Stool culture grows a motile, glucose-fermenting, oxidase-negative gram-negative rod that makes heat-labile and heat-stable toxins. What type of diarrhea do these toxins cause?

B. Pseudomembranous colitis from C. difficile
C. Osmotic diarrhea from enterotoxigenic E. coli
D. Vomiting from B. cereus’s cGMP toxin
E. Typhoid fever from Salmonella typhi
Answer: C
Why this is correct: ETEC's heat-labile and heat-stable toxins cause osmotic diarrhea. E. coli is motile.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1018
A 3-year-old boy has had fever, cramping, and frequent small stools with blood and mucus for 3 days. His daycare has had several similar cases. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). His abdomen is tender without guarding. Stool culture grows a non-motile, oxidase-negative gram-negative rod that ferments glucose. Five days later his urine output drops and he becomes pale. Which toxin is responsible for his complications?
A. Heat-labile toxin
B. Shiga toxin
C. TSST-1
D. Exotoxin A
E. Lecithinase (alpha toxin)
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Shiga toxin from Shigella causes bloody diarrhea, HUS, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Shigella is non-motile.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1019
A 24-year-old man returns from a month in South Asia with fever that has climbed stepwise over 10 days, abdominal pain, headache, and constipation. He didn't receive travel vaccines. Temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), but pulse is 84/min. His spleen is palpable, and he has faint pink spots on his abdomen. Blood cultures grow a gram-negative rod that ferments glucose and is oxidase negative. What is the diagnosis?
A. Shigella dysentery
B. Enterotoxigenic E. coli
C. Leptospirosis
D. Brucellosis
E. Typhoid fever from Salmonella typhi
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Salmonella typhi is a member of the Enterobacteriaceae (glucose fermenters, nitrate reducers, oxidase negative) and causes typhoid fever.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1020
A 45-year-old man returns from a trip to India with 12 days of fever, abdominal pain, and malaise. Temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F). Blood cultures grow Salmonella typhi. The microbiology lab confirms the organism is a facultative anaerobe. Which set of biochemical features is shared by this organism and the rest of its family?
A. Ferments glucose, reduces nitrate, and is oxidase negative
B. Oxidase positive and a non-fermenter of glucose
C. Coagulase positive and catalase positive
D. Requires X and V factors for growth
E. Acid-fast staining with a waxy cell wall
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Enterobacteriaceae are facultative anaerobes that all ferment glucose, reduce nitrate to nitrite, and lack cytochrome c oxidase (oxidase negative). The family includes Salmonella typhi, Yersinia pestis, E. coli, Shigella, Proteus, Serratia, Enterobacter, and Klebsiella.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1021
A 66-year-old man with diabetes has a high fever and cough productive of currant-jelly sputum. He drinks heavily. Temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), and he has crackles in the right upper lobe. C. Lipooligosaccharide
D. A thick capsule
E. Urease
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a non-motile member of the Enterobacteriaceae with a thick capsule.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1022

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1023
A 58-year-old woman has fever and a foul-smelling abscess in her pelvis 8 days after a colon resection. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). CT shows gas within the collection. D. Proteus mirabilis
E. Clostridium tetani
