Why this is correct: Bacteroidetes are anaerobes that contain endotoxin and make beta-lactamase. Anaerobic infections occur near mucosa with mixed flora, foul odor, and tissue gas.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1024
A 16-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has increased sputum and worsening cough. His sputum has a sweet, grape-like odor and is greenish. Culture on agar shows blue-green pigmented colonies of an aerobic gram-negative rod that is oxidase positive. Which organism is most likely?
A. Klebsiella pneumoniae
B. Proteus mirabilis
C. Haemophilus influenzae
D. Bordetella pertussis
E. Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic, oxidase-positive gram-negative rod found in soil and water, with blue-green pigment and a grape-like odor. It has elastase, alkaline protease, exotoxin A, and exoenzyme S.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 1025
An 18-year-old college student shared a dorm room for 3 weeks with a roommate who was just diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. He feels well and has no fever, headache, or rash. He takes no medications. His vital signs and exam are normal. Which chemoprophylaxis options are appropriate for him, and which drug-interaction concern applies to one of them?
A. No prophylaxis, since only household contacts need it
B. Doxycycline or minocycline; doxycycline causes photosensitivity
C. Vancomycin or linezolid; vancomycin causes red man syndrome
D. Rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or azithromycin; rifampin induces CYP450
E. Metronidazole or tinidazole; metronidazole causes a disulfiram reaction
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Close contacts of meningococcal disease get chemoprophylaxis with rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or azithromycin. Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer, which matters for drug interactions.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 1026
A 19-year-old woman will start college in the fall and live in a dormitory. She received the quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine at 16. She is healthy and takes no medications. Her vital signs are normal, and her other childhood vaccines are up to date. Her vaccine covers four serogroups. Against which serogroup does she still need a separate vaccine for short-term protection before college?
A. Serogroup B
B. Serogroup W
C. Serogroup Y
D. Serogroup C
E. Serogroup A
Answer: A
Why this is correct: The quadrivalent polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccine covers serogroups A, C, Y, and W. Serogroup B vaccine is given at ages 18 to 23 for short-term protection in groups like military recruits and college students, and a pentavalent vaccine covers A, B, C, Y, and W.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 1027
A 30-year-old woman has had a cough for 5 weeks. It started like a cold, then turned into fits of coughing that end in a gasp and sometimes vomiting. Her infant nephew was just hospitalized with the same illness. She never got a Tdap booster. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), and her lungs are clear between fits. A. Erythromycin
B. Parenteral ceftriaxone
C. Doxycycline and gentamicin
D. Vancomycin
E. Rifaximin
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Bordetella pertussis is spread by aerosol and passes through catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages. It causes a very high WBC with lymphocytosis, is cultured on Regan-Lowe, is treated with erythromycin, and is prevented with Tdap.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 1028
A 68-year-old man with COPD has a worsening productive cough and fever for 4 days. He smokes. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), and he has coarse crackles. Chest x-ray shows a patchy infiltrate. Sputum shows many neutrophils and oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococci that don't use any carbohydrates. Which organism is most likely?
A. Neisseria meningitidis
B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae
C. Haemophilus influenzae
D. Moraxella catarrhalis
E. Streptococcus pneumoniae
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that doesn't use carbohydrates. LOS is its key virulence factor, and it causes otitis media and pneumonia.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 1029
A 55-year-old man has fever, fatigue, and a new murmur for 3 weeks. He has a prosthetic aortic valve. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F). Echocardiography shows a vegetation. Routine blood cultures stay negative for several days, but PCR of the blood identifies an oxidase-positive gram-negative coccobacillus with pili and a capsule that also causes septic arthritis in toddlers. Which organism is most likely?
A. Haemophilus influenzae
B. Moraxella catarrhalis
C. Kingella kingae
D. Bordetella pertussis
E. Brucella
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Kingella kingae is an oxidase-positive gram-negative coccobacillus with pili, a capsule, and a toxin. It causes septic arthritis in toddlers, endocarditis, and osteoarticular infection, and PCR-based assays are used for diagnosis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 1030
A 34-year-old man with AIDS has 6 weeks of fever, night sweats, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. He has lost 10 kg. His CD4 count is 25/μL, and he takes no prophylaxis. He has hepatosplenomegaly and cervical lymphadenitis. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL. Blood cultures grow slow-growing acid-fast bacilli that don't make pigment in light or dark. Which organism is most likely?
A. Mycobacterium kansasii
B. Mycobacterium scrofulaceum
C. Mycobacterium abscessus
D. Nocardia asteroides
E. Mycobacterium avium complex
Answer: E
Why this is correct: MAC causes disseminated infection in AIDS with CD4 under 50, with cervical lymphadenitis, hepatosplenomegaly, diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal pain, anemia, fever, and night sweats. It's a slow-growing non-chromogen, and prophylaxis is azithromycin, clarithromycin, or rifabutin.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 1031
A 48-year-old woman with a heart transplant takes tacrolimus and prednisone. She has 2 weeks of cough, fever, and a new severe headache. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Chest CT shows a cavitating nodule, and brain MRI shows a ring-enhancing abscess. Bronchoscopy samples show gram-positive, weakly acid-fast, branching filaments. Biopsy shows no granulomas. How does this organism survive inside phagocytes?
A. It inactivates elongation factor 2 inside the phagocyte
B. It prevents phagosome acidification and phagolysosome fusion
C. It forms a thick capsule that blocks phagocytic killing
D. It binds MHC II as a superantigen and disables the phagocyte
E. It produces pneumolysin that forms pores in the phagosome
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Nocardia is a gram-positive, weakly acid-fast, branching filamentous organism. N. asteroides causes lung infections in immunocompromised patients that can spread to the brain. It prevents phagosome acidification and phagolysosome fusion and doesn't form granulomas.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 1032
A 66-year-old man who never smoked has had a cough and 5-kg weight loss for 3 months. He is HIV negative and has no TB exposure. Chest CT shows a thick-walled cavity in the right upper lobe. His tuberculin test is weakly positive. Sputum grows a slow-growing mycobacterium that turns yellow only after light exposure. The same organism is regularly isolated from his home's tap water. Which organism is most likely?
A. Mycobacterium kansasii
B. Mycobacterium avium complex
C. Mycobacterium gordonae
D. Mycobacterium abscessus
E. Mycobacterium leprae
Answer: A
Why this is correct: M. kansasii causes TB-like lung disease with cavitation and a right upper lobe predilection, prevents phagolysosome fusion, is consistently isolated from tap water, and is a slow-growing photochromogen.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 1033
A 4-year-old boy has a painless swelling in his neck for 2 months that hasn't improved with amoxicillin. He is healthy and HIV negative. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). He has a firm, non-tender 3-cm submandibular node with purplish overlying skin. Excision shows granulomatous inflammation, and culture grows a slow-growing mycobacterium that produces yellow-orange pigment even when kept in the dark. How is this organism classified?
A. A slow-growing photochromogen
B. A rapid-growing non-pigmented organism
C. A non-chromogen
D. A slow-growing scotochromogen (M. scrofulaceum)
E. A non-grower
Answer: D
Why this is correct: M. scrofulaceum and M. gordonae are slow-growing scotochromogens, which make pigment in the dark. M. kansasii and M. marinum are photochromogens, and MAC is a non-chromogen.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Mycobacteria & Nocardia
Question 1034
A 55-year-old woman has a lung disease that resembles MAC on CT, with nodules and bronchiectasis. She has lost 4 kg. She has no HIV. Sputum grows a non-pigmented mycobacterium that forms colonies within 5 days. She has a fish tank and gardens often. Which organism is most likely?
A. Mycobacterium avium complex
B. Mycobacterium kansasii
C. Mycobacterium abscessus
D. Mycobacterium scrofulaceum
E. Nocardia asteroides
Answer: C
Why this is correct: M. abscessus resembles MAC disease, is found in soil, dust, water, and wild or domestic animals and fish, and is non-pigmented and rapid growing.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 1035
A 60-year-old man from Arkansas has fever, headache, and muscle aches for 6 days. He removed several ticks after deer hunting 2 weeks ago. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F). He has a faint maculopapular rash on his trunk. WBC is 2,600/mm³, platelets are 70,000/mm³, and ALT is elevated. A peripheral smear shows clusters of bacteria inside vacuoles of monocytes. Which organism is most likely?
A. Anaplasma phagocytophilum
B. Ehrlichia chaffeensis
C. Rickettsia
D. Coxiella burnetii
E. Brucella
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Ehrlichia chaffeensis causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis. It's an obligate intracellular organism that replicates in host cell vacuoles, rarely causes vasculitis, and has a rash in about a third of cases. It's treated with doxycycline.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 1036
A 58-year-old woman from Minnesota has had fever, chills, headache, and muscle aches for 5 days after a hike. She has no rash and few GI symptoms. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). Hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL, WBC is 2,900/mm³ with increased bands, and platelets are 80,000/mm³. A smear shows clusters of organisms inside neutrophil vacuoles. What is the treatment?
A. Doxycycline
B. Doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine
C. Penicillin G
D. Supportive care
E. Doxycycline plus gentamicin
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Anaplasma phagocytophilum causes human granulocytic anaplasmosis, with nonspecific symptoms, fewer GI symptoms, a rash in 10%, mild anemia, leukopenia with bands, and low platelets. It's treated with doxycycline.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 1037
A 52-year-old sheep farmer has had fatigue, night sweats, and fevers for 6 months after an episode of pneumonia last year. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). His liver and spleen are enlarged, and a new murmur is heard. Echocardiography shows an aortic valve vegetation, but routine blood cultures are negative. Serology shows high antibody titers to an organism acquired from infected aerosols and raw milk. What is the diagnosis?
A. Brucellosis with undulant fever
B. Viridans streptococcal endocarditis
C. Leptospirosis with Weil disease
D. Psittacosis with endocarditis
E. Chronic Q fever endocarditis
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever from infected aerosols, raw milk, or ticks, and chronic disease causes endocarditis, myocarditis, and hepatosplenomegaly. With heart disease it's treated with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 1038
A 35-year-old man who works in a city sewer system has fever, severe headache, and calf pain for 6 days. He has cuts on his hands. His eyes are red without discharge. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F). He is jaundiced, his creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL, and he coughs up blood. Darkfield microscopy of his blood shows highly motile spirochetes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome
B. Q fever
C. Rocky Mountain spotted fever
D. Weil disease from Leptospira
E. Typhoid fever
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Leptospira comes from rats and contaminated food, soil, or water and enters through skin defects. Weil disease is often biphasic, with jaundice, conjunctival suffusion, flu-like symptoms, and pulmonary hemorrhage. It's diagnosed by darkfield microscopy, culture, or microscopic agglutination test.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 1039
A 42-year-old veterinarian who treats parrots has had high fever, headache, dry cough, sore throat, and diarrhea for 6 days. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). He has faint pink macules on his face. Chest x-ray shows lobar consolidation, and a sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils but no organisms. What is the most likely organism?
A. Coxiella burnetii
B. Chlamydophila psittaci
C. Streptococcus pneumoniae
D. Leptospira
E. Hantavirus
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Psittacosis is caused by Chlamydophila psittaci, carried by parrots and other birds. Poultry workers, veterinarians, pet store workers, and bird owners are at risk. It causes fever, dry cough, diarrhea, facial Horder spots, lobar pneumonia, and a sputum Gram stain with many polys.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 1040
A 36-year-old man with HIV comes for follow-up after missing several appointments and doses of his antiretrovirals. He feels well except for mild fatigue. His vital signs are normal, and he has no thrush, weight loss, opportunistic infections, or other AIDS-defining conditions. His CD4 count is 180 cells/μL, and his viral load is 48,000 copies/mL. Does he meet the definition of AIDS?
A. No, because his CD4 count must be below 50
B. Yes, because his CD4 count is below 200 cells/μL
C. No, because he has no opportunistic infection
D. Yes, but only if his viral load is high
E. No, because AIDS requires Kaposi sarcoma
Answer: B
Why this is correct: AIDS is defined by a CD4 count below 200 cells, or the presence of an opportunistic infection or other AIDS-defining condition.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 1041
A 39-year-old woman with AIDS has had headache and fever for 3 weeks and is now confused. Her CD4 count is 30/μL. She has mild neck stiffness but no focal deficits. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 30 cm H2O, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and a slightly low glucose. An India ink preparation of her CSF shows round yeast cells with clear halos. Which organism is responsible?
A. Toxoplasma gondii
B. JC virus
C. Cryptococcus neoformans
D. Epstein-Barr virus
E. Neisseria meningitidis
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Cryptococcal meningitis is caused by Cryptococcus neoformans or gattii and diagnosed by cryptococcal antigen, PCR, culture, or India ink stain. It's treated with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then fluconazole.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 1042
A 44-year-old man with HIV has raised purple plaques on his legs and similar lesions on his palate and in his mouth. His CD4 count is 120/μL. CT shows enlarged lymph nodes. Biopsy of a plaque shows a vascular tumor. His oncologist stages it as advanced disease beyond what antiretrovirals alone should control. What is the treatment?
A. Antiretrovirals alone
B. Antiretrovirals plus radiation
C. Antiretrovirals plus ganciclovir
D. Antiretrovirals plus amphotericin B
E. Antiretrovirals plus liposomal doxorubicin
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and involves skin, oral mucosa, and lymph nodes (visceral involvement in about half). Stage T0 is treated with antiretrovirals alone, and stage T1 with antiretrovirals plus liposomal doxorubicin.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 1043
A 42-year-old man with HIV hasn't taken antiretrovirals or prophylaxis for a year. He has had a dry cough and worsening shortness of breath for 3 weeks. His CD4 count is 90/μL. His room-air PaO2 is 64 mm Hg. Chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage with a direct fluorescent antibody stain is positive. Which organism is responsible?
A. Pneumocystis jirovecii
B. Streptococcus pneumoniae
C. Cryptococcus neoformans
D. Mycobacterium avium complex
E. Toxoplasma gondii
Answer: A
Why this is correct: PCP occurs with CD4 below 200 (or 14%), shows ground-glass opacities, and is diagnosed by bronchoalveolar lavage, PCR, stains, or DFA. Moderate to severe disease (PaO2 below 70) is treated with TMP-SMX plus corticosteroids.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 1044
A 46-year-old man with AIDS has had headache, fever, and new left-sided weakness for 2 weeks. He has two cats. His CD4 count is 55/μL, and he takes no prophylaxis. MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions, most in the basal ganglia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. CNS lymphoma
B. PML
C. Cryptococcal meningitis
D. Cerebral toxoplasmosis
E. Kaposi sarcoma
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Toxoplasmosis occurs with CD4 below 100, is associated with cats and litter boxes, and shows multiple lesions with a basal ganglia predilection. A presumptive diagnosis rests on a consistent presentation, anti-Toxoplasma IgG, and response to treatment.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 1045
A 40-year-old woman with AIDS has had worsening balance, confusion, and trouble seeing things on her left for 6 weeks. Her CD4 count is 35/μL. She has no fever or headache. D. Cryptococcal meningitis
E. CMV retinitis and encephalitis
Answer: C
Why this is correct: PML causes gait disturbance, confusion, or homonymous hemianopsia from white matter demyelination, usually with CD4 under 50. It's caused by JC virus and treated by treating the HIV.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 1046
A 50-year-old man with AIDS has had headaches and personality changes for 5 weeks and had a seizure yesterday. His CD4 count is 40/μL. He is afebrile. Why this is correct: CNS lymphoma causes headaches, seizures, and focal deficits, with enhancing lesions and edema on CT or MRI. It's associated with EBV, diagnosed by EBV PCR from CSF, and treated with radiation.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Beta-Lactam Antibiotics
Question 1047
A 30-year-old teacher has a sore throat and fever for 2 days. She has no drug allergies and takes an oral contraceptive. Temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), her tonsils have exudates, and she has tender anterior cervical nodes. Her rapid strep test is positive, and she is prescribed penicillin. Two days later her fever resolves. By which mechanism did this drug kill the organism?
A. They bind PBPs and block transpeptidation, so the cell wall fails
B. They form cation channels in the membrane, so the cell depolarizes
C. They bind the 30S ribosome, so proteins are misread
D. They bind D-ala-D-ala, so cell wall polymerization is blocked
E. They inhibit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, so transcription stops
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams) bind PBPs, inhibit transpeptidation, and block cell wall synthesis, causing lysis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Beta-Lactam Antibiotics
Question 1048
A 40-year-old woman is bitten on the hand by a dog. She has no allergies and takes no medications. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). The wound is swollen, and redness spreads 3 cm from the bite. Why this is correct: Aminopenicillins plus a beta-lactamase inhibitor include amoxicillin-clavulanate (oral), which covers anaerobes, and ampicillin-sulbactam (IV), used for Acinetobacter.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Beta-Lactam Antibiotics

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Beta-Lactam Antibiotics
Question 1050
A 60-year-old man with diabetes and chronic kidney disease has a deep foot ulcer with surrounding redness. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), and his creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL. He has no drug allergies. Deep tissue culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which cephalosporin covers this organism?

C. Cefepime
D. Cefazolin
E. Cefuroxime
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Cefepime is a fourth-generation cephalosporin with Pseudomonas coverage. It's a zwitterion, with positive and negative charges and a net charge of zero.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Beta-Lactam Antibiotics

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Beta-Lactam Antibiotics

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Other Cell Wall & Membrane Antibiotics
Question 1054
A 60-year-old woman with hypertension is admitted with MRSA pneumonia. She takes lisinopril. She is started on daptomycin. Three days later her fever persists at 38.6°C (101.5°F), chest x-ray shows a larger right lower lobe infiltrate, and her WBC has risen to 19,000/mm³. Her creatinine and CK are normal. Why did this treatment fail?
A. It causes nephrotoxicity
B. It causes serotonin syndrome
C. It has no MRSA activity
D. It only works in urine
E. It's inactivated by lung surfactant
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Daptomycin covers gram-positive organisms like S. aureus by forming cation channels that release potassium and depolarize the cell. It's inactivated by lung surfactant, and its main adverse effect is rhabdomyolysis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Other Cell Wall & Membrane Antibiotics

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / DNA & RNA Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 1057
A 34-year-old woman with a penicillin allergy has fever and flank pain and is diagnosed with pyelonephritis. Her creatinine is normal. She is started on a fluoroquinolone, but after 3 days her fever is 38.9°C (102°F) and her flank pain is worse. Her urine culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / DNA & RNA Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 1058
A 70-year-old woman is admitted with a urinary infection and cellulitis of her leg. She has a penicillin rash history. She is started on ciprofloxacin. Her urine culture grows Enterobacterales, and her urinary symptoms improve, but the leg redness spreads and a wound swab grows Streptococcus pyogenes. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Which statement explains this outcome?

B. It covers strep but not Pseudomonas, like moxifloxacin
C. It covers only gram-positive organisms, like vancomycin
D. It covers MRSA and anaerobes but not gram-negative rods
E. It covers Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas but not gram-positives
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Ciprofloxacin covers Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas but has poor gram-positive coverage. Levofloxacin adds strep coverage and has a long half-life.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Protein Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 1059
A newborn boy fails his hearing screen twice. His mother had a Pseudomonas urinary tract infection at 12 weeks' gestation and was treated with a drug that binds the 30S ribosome and causes mRNA misreading. She also developed vertigo and a rise in creatinine during treatment. The baby's other exam findings are normal. Which antibiotic class was she most likely given?
A. Aminoglycosides
B. Fluoroquinolones
C. Macrolides
D. Oxazolidinones
E. Beta-lactams
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, plazomicin) bind the 30S subunit, causing mRNA misreading and defective membranes. They cause nephrotoxicity, neuromuscular blockade, ototoxicity, and vertigo and should be avoided in pregnancy.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Protein Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 1060
A 26-year-old woman from North Carolina has a rash on her wrists and ankles after a tick bite and is started on doxycycline. She takes an iron supplement for heavy periods and swallows both pills together each morning. After 3 days her fever persists, and her platelets are 90,000/mm³. How do tetracyclines work, and why did her iron interfere with treatment?
A. They block tRNA binding to the 30S ribosome; they chelate metals
B. They bind the 50S ribosome; they induce CYP
C. They form cation channels; they're inactivated by surfactant
D. They inhibit DHFR; they cause hyperkalemia
E. They bind PBPs; they cause nephrotoxicity
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Tetracyclines prevent tRNA from binding the 30S ribosome during elongation. Doxycycline covers MRSA, atypical organisms, protozoa, Rickettsia, and syphilis. Tetracyclines chelate, and toxicities include photosensitivity, tooth discoloration, GI distress, and pill esophagitis. They're contraindicated in pregnancy.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Membrane Transport
Question 1061
A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is starting a walking program. He takes metformin and has a BMI of 33. Exercise, like insulin, would bring more of a certain transporter to the surface of his muscle cells so they can take up glucose. His HbA1c is 7.9%, and his blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg. He works at a desk job and rarely exercises. Which transporter is this?
A. GLUT5
B. SGLT2
C. GLUT4
D. GLUT1
E. GLUT2
Answer: C
Why this is correct: GLUT4 is in muscle, heart, and fat and responds to insulin and exercise. It doesn't appear on the cell surface until activated, which is why people with type 2 diabetes are encouraged to exercise.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 2 / Patterns of Inheritance
Question 1062
A 35-year-old woman is screened for carrier status for a recessive condition common in her population. In her population, 36% of people are homozygous for the normal allele. She is healthy and 16 weeks pregnant. Her vital signs and exam are normal. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, what is the frequency of the recessive allele?
A. 0.4
B. 0.48
C. 0.64
D. 0.6
E. 0.16
Answer: A
Why this is correct: p² is the frequency of AA homozygotes. If p² = 0.36, then p = 0.6, and q = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 3 / Cellular Energetics
Question 1063
A 26-year-old man fasts overnight before a lipid panel. In his liver, the citric acid cycle keeps oxidizing fuels while also supplying citrate and other intermediates used to build new molecules. Which of the following terms describes a pathway that works this way?
A. Amphibolic, because it takes part in both catabolism and anabolism
B. Catabolic, because it only breaks molecules down
C. Anaerobic, because it runs without oxygen
D. Anabolic, because it only builds molecules
E. Cytoplasmic, because it occurs only outside the mitochondria
Answer: A. Amphibolic, because it takes part in both catabolism and anabolism
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: ATP generation and creatine phosphate; Citric acid cycle regulation
Why this is correct:
An amphibolic process involves both anabolism and catabolism. The citric acid cycle handles the aerobic catabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, and amino acids and supplies intermediates for biosynthesis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The cycle also supplies intermediates for building molecules.
C. The citric acid cycle is aerobic.
D. The cycle also breaks molecules down.
E. The citric acid cycle runs in the mitochondria.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 3 / Energy Balance & Nutrition
Question 1064
A 28-year-old woman who lifts weights 4 days a week notices she feels warm after meals. Indirect calorimetry shows her metabolic rate rises after each meal, and the size of the rise depends on what she eats. Her BMI is 22. Which of the following macronutrients has the greatest thermic effect?
A. All macronutrients equally
B. Lipid
C. Protein and lipid equally
D. Protein
E. Carbohydrate
Answer: D. Protein
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Total daily energy expenditure
Why this is correct:
The thermic effect of food is the rise in metabolic rate from eating. It's greatest for protein and smallest for lipid, because protein takes more energy to break down.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. The effect differs by macronutrient.
B. Lipid has the smallest thermic effect.
C. Protein's effect is greater than lipid's.
E. Carbohydrate's effect is smaller than protein's.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 3 / Disorders of the Urea Cycle
Question 1065
A 60-year-old woman with cirrhosis from fatty liver disease is drowsy but arousable. She takes lactulose. Serum ammonia is high, BUN is low, and albumin is low. In her brain, glutamate dehydrogenase is running in reverse to trap the excess ammonia as glutamate. Which of the following best explains how this reaction harms her neurons?
A. It depletes alpha-ketoglutarate, which can shut down the citric acid cycle
B. It blocks glycogen phosphorylase, which starves neurons of glucose
C. It raises BUN, which is directly toxic to neurons
D. It increases NADPH production, which causes oxidative damage
E. It produces excess urea in the brain, which draws in water
Answer: A. It depletes alpha-ketoglutarate, which can shut down the citric acid cycle
Order: Second
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Ammonia handling in brain, muscle, and kidney
Why this is correct:
At high ammonia levels, glutamate dehydrogenase runs in reverse and makes glutamate from ammonia. This uses up alpha-ketoglutarate and can shut down the citric acid cycle in the brain.
Why the other answers are wrong:
B. The reaction doesn't act on glycogen phosphorylase.
C. Her BUN is low, and BUN isn't the toxic molecule.
D. The reaction doesn't increase NADPH.
E. The brain doesn't make urea; the urea cycle is in the liver.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 3 / Disorders of the Urea Cycle
Question 1066
A researcher studies how the brain handles ammonia produced during normal metabolism. Before ammonia leaves the brain, one enzyme combines it with glutamate so it can travel safely to the liver. Which of the following enzymes is this?
A. Alanine transaminase
B. Glutamate dehydrogenase
C. Glutaminase
D. Glutamine synthetase
E. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
Answer: D. Glutamine synthetase
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Ammonia handling in brain, muscle, and kidney
Why this is correct:
In the brain, glutamine synthetase captures ammonia as glutamine for safe transport. In the liver, glutaminase turns glutamine back into glutamate, and glutamate dehydrogenase releases the ammonia for the urea cycle.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Alanine transaminase converts alanine to pyruvate.
B. Glutamate dehydrogenase releases ammonia from glutamate in the liver.
C. Glutaminase releases ammonia from glutamine rather than capturing it.
E. CPS-I runs the first step of the urea cycle in the liver.
Objective: Interpret the role of protein, carbohydrate, lipid, and nucleic acid metabolisms in normal and pathophysiological states (CBO 1.1)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 4 / Nucleus & Genome Organization
Question 1067
A 55-year-old man has a liver biopsy that shows tumor cells with larger, more prominent nucleoli than normal cells. His pathologist explains that the tumor cells are making more ribosomes. Which of the following processes takes place in the nucleolus?
A. Glycosylation of proteins
B. Removal of introns by the proteasome

Foundations of Medicine / Week 4 / DNA Replication & Repair
Question 1068
A 50-year-old woman receives radiation therapy for cancer. Which of the following is the main way ionizing radiation such as X-rays and gamma rays damages DNA?
A. Inserting transposons into genes
B. Adding alkyl groups to O6-guanine
C. Generating reactive oxygen species that cause single- or double-strand breaks
D. Dimerizing adjacent pyrimidines
E. Deaminating methylcytosine to thymine
Answer: C. Generating reactive oxygen species that cause single- or double-strand breaks
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Sources of DNA damage and the Ames test
Why this is correct:
Ionizing radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, cosmic rays) generates ROS that cause single- and double-strand breaks and base loss.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Transposon insertion is an endogenous source of mutation.
B. Alkylation comes from alkylating chemicals.
D. Pyrimidine dimers come from UV radiation.
E. Deamination is spontaneous damage.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 4 / DNA Recombination
Question 1069
A 40-year-old woman with a family history of breast and ovarian cancer is found to carry a BRCA1 mutation. Which of the following best describes how BRCA1 normally keeps double-strand break repair accurate?
A. It binds DNA and prevents excessive nuclease activity, promoting error-free repair
B. It removes O6-alkylguanine without a template
C. It starts meiotic recombination by making double-strand breaks
D. It removes thymine dimers by excising a short segment
E. It recognizes mismatches and nicks the new strand
Answer: A. It binds DNA and prevents excessive nuclease activity, promoting error-free repair
Order: First
Difficulty: Medium
Reference: Non-homologous end joining and BRCA1; Familial cancer syndromes
Why this is correct:
BRCA1 promotes error-free NHEJ or homologous recombination. It binds DNA and prevents excessive nuclease activity; when it's lost, error-prone repair takes over.
Why the other answers are wrong:

C. Spo11 starts meiotic recombination.
D. Thymine dimers are removed by nucleotide excision repair.
E. Mismatch recognition is done by Mut proteins.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 4 / Transcription
Question 1070
A research team designing a new antiviral studies how mRNAs are processed in human cells. Nuclear mRNAs carry a 7-methylguanosine at their 5' end, but mitochondrial mRNAs don't. Which of the following is a function of this 5' cap?

Foundations of Medicine / Week 5 / Cancer Screening & Diagnosis
Question 1071
A study of a new screening test for a cancer is reviewed. On average, the test finds the cancer 15 years before symptoms would have. Patients diagnosed by screening survive 20 years after diagnosis, compared with 5 years for those diagnosed by symptoms, but both groups die at about 65. No treatment changes the course of this cancer. Which of the following biases best explains the apparent survival benefit?
A. Length-time bias
B. Lead-time bias
C. Negative predictive value
D. Selection bias from high specificity
E. Poor sensitivity
Answer: B. Lead-time bias
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Lead-time and length-time bias
Why this is correct:
Lead-time bias makes survival look longer when screening moves diagnosis earlier without changing the time of death, and it's most likely when treatment doesn't change mortality.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Length-time bias comes from preferentially finding slow-growing cancers.
C. Negative predictive value is a test property, not a bias.
D. Specificity doesn't create this survival pattern.
E. The test finds the cancer early, so sensitivity isn't the issue.
Objective: Identify risk factors and evidence-based screening methods for cancer and discuss opportunities for disease prevention and patient education (CBO 1.5)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 5 / Cancer Screening & Diagnosis
Question 1072
A screening program for a cancer is reviewed. Tumors found by screening are mostly small and slow growing, while aggressive tumors tend to show up with symptoms between screenings. The screened group appears to have much better outcomes than people diagnosed by symptoms. Which of the following biases explains this?
A. High positive predictive value
B. Low specificity
C. Low sensitivity
D. Length-time bias
E. Lead-time bias
Answer: D. Length-time bias
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Lead-time and length-time bias
Why this is correct:
Length-time bias happens because screening picks up a disproportionate number of slow-growing, indolent cancers, while aggressive ones appear between screens.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. PPV is a test property, not a bias.
B. Specificity doesn't explain the tumor mix.
C. Sensitivity doesn't explain the tumor mix.
E. Lead-time bias comes from earlier diagnosis without a change in death.
Objective: Identify risk factors and evidence-based screening methods for cancer and discuss opportunities for disease prevention and patient education (CBO 1.5)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 5 / Cancer Screening & Diagnosis
Question 1073
A 45-year-old woman asks about a new blood test she saw advertised that's accurate, inexpensive, and detects a rare cancer years before symptoms. Her physician finds that no treatment changes the course of the disease once it's found, and early detection doesn't improve cancer-specific mortality. Which of the following best explains why this test shouldn't be used for population screening?

Reference: Principles of cancer screening

Screening makes sense only when effective treatment exists and improves cancer-specific mortality, along with an accurate test, balanced cost, and continuous screening.
Why the other answers are wrong:

Foundations of Medicine / Week 6 / Basics of Innate Immunity
Question 1074
A 9-month-old boy has recurrent oral thrush and a Candida diaper rash that keeps returning despite treatment. Studies show his macrophages and dendritic cells can't recognize carbohydrates such as beta-glucan on the fungal cell wall. Which of the following receptor families is defective?
A. Toll-like receptors such as TLR4
B. C-type lectin receptors such as dectin-1
C. NOD-like receptors such as NOD2
D. Coreceptors such as CD4
E. Fc receptors such as FcεRI
Answer: B. C-type lectin receptors such as dectin-1
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Inflammasome and cytosolic sensors
Why this is correct:

A 61-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes and recent ketoacidosis has fever, cough, hemoptysis, and a cavitary lung lesion on CT. A lung biopsy shows broad, ribbon-like hyphae that branch at wide angles and lack regular cross walls. Which of the following fungi is most likely?
![Tissue biopsy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/74/Histopathology_of_pulmonary_mucormycosis.jpg)
A. Aspergillus
B. Mucor or Rhizopus, a zygomycete
C. Candida
D. Cryptococcus
E. Trichosporon
Answer: B. Mucor or Rhizopus, a zygomycete
Order: Second
Difficulty: Easy
Why this is correct:
Zygomycetes such as Mucor and Rhizopus have broad aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching and infect people with ketoacidosis.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Aspergillus is septate with acute-angle branching.
C. Candida is a yeast.
D. Cryptococcus is an encapsulated yeast.
E. Trichosporon is a basidiomycete yeast.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 1122
A 30-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has an ultrasound showing a developing placenta. She is healthy and takes a prenatal vitamin. Her ultrasound shows a normal embryo. The chorion forms the fetal portion of her placenta. Her vital signs are normal, and her β-hCG is rising appropriately. She works as a pharmacist. Her fetal heart rate is 160/min. Which layers make up the chorion?
A. Cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast, and extraembryonic mesoderm
B. Ectoderm, endoderm, and intraembryonic mesoderm
C. Decidua basalis, decidua parietalis, and decidua capsularis
D. Amnion, yolk sac, and connecting stalk
E. Epiblast, hypoblast, and primitive streak
Answer: A
Why this is correct: The chorion forms the fetal portion of the placenta and is made of the two trophoblast layers and the extraembryonic mesoderm, which also forms blood vessels for the amnion, umbilical cord, yolk sac, and chorion.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 1123
A 30-year-old woman undergoing IVF has the day-5 embryo shown, with its outer layer and inner cluster of cells visible. She has tubal factor infertility. Her embryos were cultured to day 5. Her husband's semen analysis is normal. She is 30 and has had two prior miscarriages. Her blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg. What will the outer layer marked T form? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a8/Mouse_blastocyst-microscopy.png" alt="Light micrograph of an embryo">
A. The primary yolk sac, which supplies early nutrients
B. The embryo proper, which forms all three germ layers
C. The amnion, which surrounds the embryo with fluid
D. The notochord, which induces the neural plate
E. The fetal chorion, which leads to the placenta
Answer: E
Why this is correct: In the blastocyst, the trophoblast (outer layer) contributes to the fetal chorion and placenta, and at 5 to 6 days it makes enzymes that break down the zona pellucida. The inner cell mass forms the epiblast (embryo and amnion) and hypoblast (primary yolk sac).

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Fertilization & Implantation
Question 1124
A 35-year-old woman's day-5 embryo, shown, is ready for transfer. She has endometriosis and takes a prenatal vitamin. The inner cluster of cells is marked I. It will soon split into two layers. She has had two previous IVF attempts. Her endometrium measures 10 mm on ultrasound. Which layer lies closest to the cavity, and what does it form? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a8/Mouse_blastocyst-microscopy.png" alt="Light micrograph of an embryo">
A. The trophoblast, which forms the placenta
B. The hypoblast, which forms the primary yolk sac
C. The hypoblast, which forms the embryo
D. The epiblast, which forms the yolk sac
E. The syncytiotrophoblast, which makes hCG
Answer: B
Why this is correct: The inner cell mass splits into the epiblast, which forms the embryo proper and amniotic sac, and the hypoblast, which is closest to the blastocyst cavity and becomes the primary yolk sac.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 1125
A 30-year-old woman is followed through an uncomplicated pregnancy. She is at 8 weeks and healthy. Her immune response changes across three stages. She has no autoimmune disease and takes a prenatal vitamin. Her vital signs are normal. She has had one prior uncomplicated pregnancy. Which sequence describes the immune changes across her pregnancy?
A. Th17 during implantation, Th1 during growth, and Th2 during labor
B. Th1 during implantation, Th2 during fetal growth, and Th1 during labor
C. Th1 during implantation, Th1 during growth, and Th1 during labor
D. Th2 during implantation, Th1 during growth, and Th2 during labor
E. Th2 during implantation, Th2 during growth, and Th2 during labor
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Implantation and placenta formation happen in a Th1 pro-inflammatory state, fetal growth in a Th2 anti-inflammatory state, and labor and delivery in a Th1 pro-inflammatory state.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 1126
A 31-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has an uncomplicated pregnancy without an immune attack on the fetus. She is healthy and takes a prenatal vitamin. A placental hormone that rises as pregnancy progresses shifts her immune response toward an anti-inflammatory profile. She has no autoimmune disease. Her ultrasound shows normal fetal growth. Her blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg. Which hormone is it?
A. Surfactant protein A
B. hCG
C. Cortisol
D. Estradiol
E. Progesterone
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Estradiol increases from the placenta as pregnancy progresses and shifts the maternal immune response from Th1 to Th2.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Immunology of Pregnancy
Question 1127
A 30-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation has an uncomplicated pregnancy. She is healthy. During fetal growth, specialized immune cells quietly clear dying trophoblast cells without provoking an immune reaction. She takes a prenatal vitamin and has no autoimmune disease. Her ultrasound shows normal growth. She works as a teacher. Her blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Which cells do this, and why does it matter?
A. Eosinophils, releasing IL-5
B. Neutrophils, preventing infection
C. Macrophages, preventing release of paternal antigens
D. B cells, making antibodies to trophoblast
E. Cytotoxic T cells, killing paternal cells
Answer: C
Why this is correct: During fetal growth, inflammation is controlled by specialized macrophages, NK cells, and Tregs. Macrophages remove dying trophoblast cells, preventing release of paternal antigens, and Tregs recognize paternal antigens and protect fetal cells.

E. Folic acid; about a 50% reduction in neural tube defects and cleft lip
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Folic acid (B9) is critical for neural tube development between days 18 and 33. Taking it during pregnancy leads to about a 50% reduction in neural tube defects and a 50% reduction in cleft lip.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 1129
A 28-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation has an ultrasound showing the chorion fused with the uterine lining. She is healthy. As the fetus grew, the endometrium covering the embryo thinned and disappeared, and the fetal membranes fused with the endometrium lining the rest of the uterus. She takes a prenatal vitamin and her ultrasound is normal. Which layers are these?
A. The chorion frondosum degenerated, and the smooth chorion fused with the basalis
B. The decidua basalis degenerated, and the chorion fused with the capsularis
C. The amnion degenerated, and the chorion fused with the basalis
D. The decidua capsularis degenerated, and the smooth chorion fused with the decidua parietalis
E. Nothing degenerated, and the chorion fused with the capsularis
Answer: D
Why this is correct: The decidua capsularis overlies the embryo and degenerates as it grows. The smooth chorion then contacts and fuses with the decidua parietalis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 10 / Placenta & Extraembryonic Membranes
Question 1130
A 26-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation has an ultrasound showing the placenta on one side of the uterus, although villi once covered the entire chorion. She is healthy. Her ultrasound shows a normal placenta on the posterior wall. She takes a prenatal vitamin and has no bleeding. Which statement explains this pattern?
A. All villi persisted, and the placenta shifted to one side as the uterus grew
B. The decidua capsularis formed the placenta, and the other villi degenerated
C. The smooth chorion formed the placenta, and the frondosum degenerated
D. Embryonic-pole villi formed the frondosum; the rest became smooth chorion
E. Embryonic-pole villi degenerated, and abembryonic villi formed the placenta
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Villi initially cover the whole chorion. As pregnancy advances, villi on the embryonic pole keep growing into the bushy chorion frondosum, which forms the fetal placenta, while villi on the abembryonic pole degenerate, forming the smooth chorion.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 6 / Inflammation
Question 1131
A 34-year-old man had severe burns to his right elbow 6 months ago without skin grafting. The burns healed, but the skin across the joint is thick, tight, and puckered and pulls the elbow into flexion, so he can't straighten his arm. Which of the following best explains his limited movement?

B. Ulceration from poor blood flow

Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Abnormal wound healing
Why this is correct:
A contracture is exaggerated wound contraction that deforms the wound and surrounding tissue, often after burns, and it can limit joint movement.
Why the other answers are wrong:

Why this is correct:

C. Saponification is fat necrosis.
D. Granulomas surround caseous necrosis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 8 / Pathology of Cell Injury & Death
Question 1155
A 30-year-old man with a patent foramen ovale and a recent long flight has sudden kidney pain from a renal infarct. A biopsy 2 days later shows cells without nuclei, but the tubule outlines are still visible and deeply pink. Which of the following explains why the architecture is preserved?
A. Fibrin coats the vessels
B. Granulomas wall off the area
C. Lysosomal enzymes digest the tissue
D. Intracellular acidosis denatures proteins, including enzymes
E. Lipase saponifies fat
Answer: D. Intracellular acidosis denatures proteins, including enzymes
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Types of necrosis
Why this is correct:
In coagulative necrosis, intracellular acidosis denatures proteins, including lytic enzymes, so outlines stay visible and the tissue stains deeply eosinophilic.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Fibrin deposition is fibrinoid necrosis.
B. Granulomas are caseous necrosis.
C. Digestion would erase the outline.
E. Saponification is fat necrosis.
Objective: Integrate basic science knowledge with clinical information to begin developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for diagnosing and managing patients (CBO 2.6)

Foundations of Medicine / Week 8 / Pathology of Cell Injury & Death
Question 1156
A 45-year-old man who drinks a liter of vodka daily has an enlarged liver and high liver enzymes. His biopsy shows many cells with clear cytoplasmic droplets and others with pale, swollen, water-filled cytoplasm, and his enzymes normalize after he stops drinking. Which of the following classifies these changes?
A. Irreversible injury with karyolysis
B. Coagulative necrosis
C. Fibrinoid necrosis
D. Reversible injury with fatty change and hydropic swelling
E. Caseous necrosis
Answer: D. Reversible injury with fatty change and hydropic swelling
Order: First
Difficulty: Easy
Reference: Reversible vs. irreversible cell injury
Why this is correct:
Reversible injury on light microscopy shows cellular swelling, hydropic degeneration, and fatty change, and it resolves when the insult stops.
Why the other answers are wrong:
A. Karyolysis is irreversible.
B. His cells aren't dead.
C. Fibrinoid necrosis involves vessels.
E. Caseous necrosis is TB.

Question 1157
A 60-year-old woman who had no pulse for 25 minutes before resuscitation later develops heart failure with a large akinetic ventricular region. Biopsy shows extensive myocyte death with loss of cell membranes and digestion of the tissue. Which of the following leads to this enzymatic digestion?
A. Koilocytosis

Irreversible injury depletes ATP and damages membranes, letting calcium in and lysosomal enzymes out, which digest the tissue and cause necrosis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1159
A 58-year-old farmer stepped on a nail in his barn 10 days ago and didn't seek care. He never received a tetanus booster. He now has jaw stiffness, a fixed grin, and painful spasms that arch his back when he hears loud noises. He is awake and alert. Temperature is 37.8°C (100°F). A Gram stain of the wound shows gram-positive rods with terminal spores shaped like tennis rackets. How does this organism's toxin cause his spasms?
A. It inhibits release of glycine and GABA
B. It inactivates elongation factor 2
C. It raises cGMP
D. It blocks acetylcholine release
E. It acts as a superantigen
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Clostridium tetani is a tennis racket-shaped gram-positive rod from soil. Its toxin inhibits glycine and GABA, causing spastic paralysis with risus sardonicus, spasms, and asphyxiation or pneumonia.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1160
A 4-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of constipation for 5 days, a weak cry, and poor feeding. His parents have been putting honey on his pacifier to calm him. He was born at term. He is afebrile, has drooping eyelids, and is floppy with poor head control. His blood glucose and electrolytes are normal. He has a weak suck and poor gag. Which tests confirm the diagnosis, and how does the toxin work?
A. Stool culture; the toxin raises cAMP in enterocytes
B. CAMP test; the toxin lyses red cells in the gut
C. Blood culture; the toxin inhibits glycine release
D. Stool culture and toxin assay; the toxin blocks ACh release
E. Loeffler culture; the toxin inactivates EF-2
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Clostridium botulinum spores are found in honey, corn syrup, soil, and canned food. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis. Infant botulism (floppy baby syndrome) is confirmed by positive stool culture and toxin assay.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1161
A 7-year-old boy who recently arrived from a country with low vaccination rates has a sore throat, fever, and a swollen neck. He hasn't received any vaccines. Temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F). He has a gray membrane over his tonsils and massive neck swelling. A week later he has a new arrhythmia. The organism forms black colonies on blood agar, and on Loeffler medium it shows metachromatic granules. His throat membrane bleeds when scraped. He has decreased palate movement when he says 'ah.' What is the treatment?
A. Supportive care only, with airway monitoring
B. Rifampin prophylaxis alone, with airway monitoring
C. Penicillin or erythromycin plus diphtheria antitoxin
D. Vancomycin alone, with airway monitoring
E. Doxycycline alone, with airway monitoring
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Corynebacterium diphtheriae causes pharyngitis, bull neck, myocarditis, and cranial neuropathy. Its toxin inactivates elongation factor 2. It's treated with penicillin or erythromycin plus antitoxin, and prevented with Tdap.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1162
A 30-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of fever, muscle aches, and fatigue for 3 days. She ate deli meats and soft cheese last week. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), and fetal heart rate is 164/min. Blood cultures grow a small, aerobic, beta-hemolytic gram-positive rod. In wet mounts the organism tumbles, and in semisolid agar it grows in an umbrella shape. Her WBC is 14,200/mm³. She has no urinary symptoms or rash. Which complications is her baby at risk for?
A. Infant botulism
B. Neonatal sepsis and meningitis
C. Rheumatic fever
D. Scarlet fever
E. Gonococcal conjunctivitis
Answer: B
Why this is correct: Listeria monocytogenes is a small aerobic beta-hemolytic gram-positive rod with tumbling motility from actin rockets and umbrella-shaped growth in agar. It causes flu-like illness, puerperal fever and sepsis, neonatal sepsis, and meningitis.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Positive Bacilli
Question 1163
A 35-year-old man in a rural village where several animals recently died develops fever, chills, sore throat, and trouble swallowing. He ate undercooked meat from one of the animals 3 days ago. Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1164
A 60-year-old woman with pyelonephritis has a urine sample plated on selective media. She has type 2 diabetes. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), and she has left flank tenderness. Gram-positive organisms don't grow on the plate, and the gram-negative colonies turn pink-red as shown below. She takes metformin and has had two urinary infections this year. Her WBC is 15,200/mm³, and urinalysis shows nitrites. What does the pink color indicate? <img src="https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/05/Raoultella_planticola_MacConkey_colonies_32.jpg" alt="MacConkey agar plate">
A. The organism is oxidase positive, so the dye changes color
B. The organism ferments lactose, dropping the pH below 6.8
C. The organism produces urease, raising the pH above 6.8
D. The organism is gram positive, so it takes up the dye
E. The organism raised the pH above 6.8 by using peptones
Answer: B
Why this is correct: MacConkey agar is selective media with lactose as the sole carbohydrate. Bile salts and crystal violet prevent gram-positive growth. Lactose fermentation drops the pH below 6.8, turning colonies red; above 6.8 there's no color.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Bacilli
Question 1165
A 45-year-old man is admitted with fever and abdominal pain 10 days after surgery for a perforated appendix. He has hypertension. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F), and CT shows a pelvic abscess. Culture grows an anaerobic gram-negative rod that contains endotoxin and makes beta-lactamase. His WBC is 18,200/mm³. He received cefazolin at surgery. Which features point to an anaerobic infection?
A. A positive CAMP test with a single organism on culture
B. Coagulase-positive cocci in clusters on the Gram stain
C. Mixed flora near a mucosal surface, with foul odor and gas
D. Growth only on MacConkey agar with pink colonies
E. A single organism with no odor and no tissue gas
Answer: C
Why this is correct: Anaerobic infections occur near mucosa and show mixed flora on Gram stain, a malodorous infection, and tissue gas. Bacteroidetes are anaerobes that contain endotoxin and make beta-lactamase.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 1166
A 3-day-old boy has red, swollen eyelids and a thick purulent discharge from both eyes. He was born vaginally to a mother who had no prenatal care. He is otherwise feeding well. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F). Gram stain of the discharge shows gram-negative diplococci that ferment glucose only and have no capsule. His mother had a vaginal discharge late in pregnancy that wasn't treated. Why isn't a tetracycline or fluoroquinolone used for this organism?
A. Chromosomal resistance from efflux pumps, porin changes, and gyrase changes
B. It’s a gram-positive organism, so the drugs can’t reach their targets
C. It lacks a cell wall, so the drugs have nothing to act on
D. It has a thick capsule that blocks both drugs from entering the cell
E. It lives inside host cell vacuoles, where neither drug can reach it
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonococcal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum). It has chromosomal resistance: efflux pumps affect tetracyclines, PenA mutations change PCN-binding proteins, and PenB porin and DNA gyrase changes affect fluoroquinolones. It's treated with parenteral ceftriaxone.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 1167
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of fever and ear pain for 2 days. He attends daycare and hasn't completed his vaccines. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), and his right tympanic membrane is red and bulging. Which antibiotic is appropriate for his ear infection?
A. Vancomycin or linezolid
B. A third-generation cephalosporin only
C. Dapsone or clindamycin
D. Ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or TMP-SMX
E. Doxycycline or azithromycin
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Haemophilus influenzae is a pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacillus with a capsule and LOS, diagnosed by culture with X and V factors. Otitis media and sinusitis are treated with ampicillin, Augmentin, or TMP-SMX, and meningitis with a third-generation cephalosporin.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 1169
A 3-month-old unvaccinated girl is brought to the emergency department because of coughing fits that end with a high-pitched whoop and vomiting. She had a runny nose for a week before the cough started. Between spells she looks well. During a spell she turns blue. WBC is 40,000/mm³ with 70% lymphocytes. The organism is grown on Regan-Lowe medium. Her oxygen saturation is 97% between spells. How does its toxin work?
A. It inactivates elongation factor 2, stopping protein synthesis
B. It binds MHC II as a superantigen, releasing cytokines
C. It blocks acetylcholine release, causing paralysis
D. It raises cGMP, causing fluid secretion
E. It ADP-ribosylates Gαi, raising cAMP
Answer: E
Why this is correct: Bordetella pertussis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative coccobacillus spread by aerosol. It goes through catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages. Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Gram-Negative Cocci & Coccobacilli
Question 1170
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of ear pain and fever for 2 days. She attends preschool and has had three ear infections this year. C. M protein, which blocks complement
D. Pneumolysin, which forms membrane pores
E. Lipooligosaccharide, with toxic lipid A

Why this is correct: Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that doesn't use carbohydrates. LOS is its key virulence factor, with lipid A as the toxic moiety, and it causes otitis media and pneumonia.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 1171
A 30-year-old woman is admitted in Argentina with fever, cough, and respiratory failure from a hantavirus. She has no history of rodent exposure in the past month. Her platelets are low. What is unusual about the strain that caused her illness?
A. It’s the only hantavirus spread person to person
B. It responds to doxycycline, unlike other hantaviruses
C. It only affects the kidneys, unlike other hantaviruses
D. It’s spread by mosquitoes, unlike other hantaviruses
E. It’s spread by ticks, unlike other hantaviruses
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Andes hantavirus is the only hantavirus with human-to-human transmission. Others are spread by inhaling rodent saliva, urine, or feces.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Zoonotic, Tick-Borne & Intracellular Infections
Question 1172
A 7-year-old girl from Tennessee is admitted in July with fever, headache, and a spreading rash for 4 days after a camping trip. The rash started on her wrists and ankles. Temperature is 39.4°C (103°F). Platelets are 76,000/mm³, and CSF shows pleocytosis. She is started on doxycycline immediately. Her ALT is elevated, and her WBC is normal. B. Regan-Lowe culture of the blood
C. Rose Bengal agglutination test
D. Darkfield microscopy of the blood
E. India ink stain of the skin biopsy
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is diagnosed with the indirect fluorescent antibody (IFA) or direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test, and treatment shouldn't wait for results because delay increases fatality.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV

A 38-year-old man with AIDS comes to the emergency department because of headache and fever for 2 weeks. He hasn't taken antiretrovirals for 2 years. His CD4 count is 40/μL. Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 1174
A 34-year-old man has had several sexual partners with HIV but has never been infected despite repeated exposures. He is healthy and takes no medications. His CD4 count is normal, and HIV testing is negative. Genetic testing shows he is homozygous for a deletion in a co-receptor that HIV uses to enter cells. For which other infection is he at increased risk?
A. Hantavirus
B. Pneumocystis pneumonia
C. Kaposi sarcoma
D. Toxoplasmosis
E. Symptomatic West Nile virus
Answer: E
Why this is correct: HIV binds CD4 through gp120, causing a conformational change in gp120 and gp41 that leads to membrane fusion. Homozygous CCR5 Δ32 makes a person HIV resistant but increases the risk of symptomatic West Nile virus.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV
Question 1175
A 43-year-old woman with AIDS is brought to the emergency department with headache, fever, and new weakness in her left arm for 2 weeks. She has two cats. Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / HIV

Why this is correct: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy causes gait disturbance, confusion, or homonymous hemianopsia from demyelination of white matter, usually with CD4 under 50. It's caused by JC virus and treated by treating the underlying HIV.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Other Cell Wall & Membrane Antibiotics
Question 1179
A 70-year-old man with MRSA bacteremia is started on IV vancomycin. He has chronic kidney disease. During a rapid infusion he develops flushing and itching of his face and upper body. Why must his drug levels be monitored?

B. Vancomycin is a CYP inducer that lowers levels of his other drugs

Why this is correct: Vancomycin covers only gram-positive organisms and prevents polymerization at the D-ala-D-ala site. Its adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, and vancomycin infusion syndrome (related to the infusion rate), and its narrow therapeutic index requires monitoring.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / DNA & RNA Synthesis Inhibitors

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / DNA & RNA Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 1181
A 25-year-old woman is diagnosed with bacterial vaginosis and prescribed metronidazole. She drinks wine on weekends. Two days later she has a glass of wine and develops flushing, nausea, and a pounding headache. She has a thin gray discharge with a fishy odor. She takes no other medications. How does metronidazole kill organisms, and what caused her reaction?
A. It binds the 30S ribosome and causes misreading; it causes ototoxicity with alcohol
B. It blocks DHFR and stops folate synthesis; it causes hyperkalemia with alcohol
C. It binds D-ala-D-ala and blocks cell wall building; it causes flushing with alcohol
D. It inhibits RNA polymerase and stops transcription; it turns fluids orange with alcohol
E. It’s reduced inside the organism and breaks DNA; it causes a disulfiram-like reaction

Why this is correct: Metronidazole, a nitroimidazole, diffuses into bacteria, is activated by reduction, and transfers electrons that break DNA strands. It covers anaerobes, bacterial vaginosis, protozoa, and C. diff, and its adverse effects include a disulfiram-like reaction, gynecomastia, and peripheral neuropathy.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / DNA & RNA Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 1183
A 34-year-old man with HIV is started on TMP-SMX to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia. He also takes lisinopril. Three weeks later his potassium is 5.9 mEq/L and his sodium is 131 mEq/L. He also has a new rash. His CD4 count is 150/μL, and his creatinine is normal. He has no fever. How does TMP-SMX work, and what serious reaction can the rash progress to?

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Protein Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 1185
A 30-year-old woman with walking pneumonia from an atypical organism is prescribed azithromycin. She has no allergies and takes an oral contraceptive. Temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), and chest x-ray shows patchy infiltrates. She has had a dry cough for a week and a mild headache. Her WBC is normal. How do macrolides work?
A. They bind the 50S subunit and inhibit transpeptidation
B. They block tRNA binding to the 30S subunit during elongation
C. They break DNA strands after being reduced inside the cell
D. They bind the 30S subunit and cause misreading of mRNA
E. They inhibit DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and stop transcription
Answer: A
Why this is correct: Macrolides cover atypical organisms, non-tuberculous mycobacteria, and some STIs. They bind the 50S subunit and inhibit transpeptidation in the elongation phase.

Foundations of Medicine / Week 9 / Protein Synthesis Inhibitors
Question 1186
A 45-year-old woman is treated with clindamycin for a dental abscess. She has hypothyroidism and takes levothyroxine. Ten days later she has 10 watery stools a day, fever, and cramping. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), and her WBC is 18,000/mm³. Colonoscopy shows yellow-white plaques on the colon wall. How does clindamycin work, and what caused her diarrhea?
A. It breaks DNA strands; a disulfiram-like reaction
B. It binds the 30S subunit; nephrotoxicity
C. It binds PBPs; allergic colitis
D. It binds the 50S subunit; C. difficile infection
E. It inhibits RNA polymerase; hepatotoxicity
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Clindamycin, a lincosamide, binds the 50S subunit to prevent peptide bonds. It covers staph, strep, anaerobes, toxoplasmosis, and pneumocystosis. Its main adverse effects are C. diff infection and diarrhea.

Foundations of Medicine / Biostatistics / Study Designs
Question 1187
Investigators want to know whether night-shift work is associated with breast cancer. A. Case-control study
B. Cohort study
C. Cross-sectional study
D. Meta-analysis
E. Randomized controlled trial
Answer: A
Why this is correct: The study starts by choosing people based on whether they have the disease (breast cancer or not) and then looks back in time through records to find the exposure (night-shift work). Starting with disease status and looking backward is what defines a case-control study.

Which of the following best describes this study design?

C. Cross-sectional study

E. Randomized controlled trial

Why this is correct: Participants are grouped by exposure (adding salt or not) while free of the disease, then followed forward to see who develops hypertension. That's a prospective cohort study.

Foundations of Medicine / Biostatistics / Study Designs
Question 1190
Four hundred adults with newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation are enrolled at 12 centers. A computer program assigns each patient to either a new anticoagulant or warfarin, and patients are followed for 12 months for stroke. Which of the following features of this study most directly distinguishes it from a prospective cohort study?
A. Outcomes are measured after the exposure begins
B. Participants are followed forward in time
C. Relative risk can be used to compare the groups
D. The investigators assign the exposure using randomization
E. The study includes a comparison group
Answer: D
Why this is correct: Both RCTs and cohort studies follow people forward in time and compare an exposed group with an unexposed group. What makes this an RCT is that the investigators randomly assign who gets the treatment, which removes bias in who ends up in each group.

Foundations of Medicine / Biostatistics / Study Designs
Question 1191
Fourteen randomized trials of a new migraine preventive have been published, and their results disagree about how well the drug works. Which of the following best describes this study?
A. Case-control study
B. Cohort study
C. Cross-sectional study
D. Meta-analysis
E. Randomized controlled trial
Answer: D
Why this is correct: A meta-analysis is a study of studies. It pools published results to guide further research and to identify reasons for heterogeneity (disagreement) between studies.

Foundations of Medicine / Biostatistics / Study Designs
Question 1192

E. Relative risk
Answer: E
Why this is correct: This is a case-control study, which is retrospective. Relative risk is only used in prospective studies, because you need to start with exposed and unexposed groups and watch who develops disease to know the risk in each group.
